pages.title: Business service health
pages.description: How OpsKnight decides whether a business service is operational, degraded or down, and how impact history drives uptime.
pages.intro: A business service (such as Checkout ) is healthy or not because of open incidents , not because of the status someone set on a technical service. One engine computes it, and the catalog, /m/status , incident Impacts , follower notifications, REST v2 and MCP all read the same result. Only open and acknowledged incidents count. Snoozed, suppressed and maintenance-held incidents never make a busines

sections.heading: Thresholds
sections.text: Each business service decides which incidents matter. An incident counts when its urgency is at least the minimum urgency or its priority is at least as severe as the maximum priority. Criticality Counts when -------------- ---------------------------------- TIER 0 High urgency, or priority P1 or P2 TIER 1 High urgency, or priority P1 or P2 TIER 2 High urgency, or priority P1 TIER 3 High urgency n

sections.heading: Freshness
sections.text: Health is computed once for the whole organization and cached for 20 seconds; a change to incidents starts a new computation, and a cached result up to 5 minutes old can be served while a fresh one is computed. Each reader then sees only the business services in their scope.

sections.heading: Impact history and uptime
sections.text: Every impact is also recorded as an interval (incident, business service, reason, start, end). It is written off the paging path when an incident is created, acknowledged, resolved or otherwise changes, and a reconcile every minute repairs anything missed. pages.title: Incident response
pages.description: How OpsKnight coordinates awareness, ownership, escalation, mitigation, resolution, and learning.
pages.intro: OpsKnight keeps one authoritative incident state and projects it into notification providers, ChatOps cards, war rooms, Jira, status pages, analytics, and postmortems. Responders should make lifecycle decisions against the incident page and treat external representations as potentially delayed views.

sections.heading: Response model
sections.text: A practical response moves through six concerns that may overlap: 1. Awareness — an integration or person creates the incident and responders receive context. 2. Ownership — somebody acknowledges response and an individual or team is assigned. 3. Coordination — responders use notes, watchers, action items, and an optional war room to share current truth. 4. Mitigation — the team reduces impact whi

sections.heading: Acknowledgement and assignment
sections.text: Acknowledgement records that a responder accepted the response and preserves the first acknowledgement measurement. It completes the active escalation generation. Assignment records the current coordinating owner and can point to a user or team. Either can happen first. During handoff, keep the acknowledgement history and change the assignee with a timeline note rather than unacknowledging solely

sections.heading: Escalation generations
sections.text: Escalation work belongs to a generation of the incident. Lifecycle transitions increment or complete that generation so a delayed worker cannot page targets from stale state. - Open incidents execute scheduled policy escalation automatically. Capability-enabled Microsoft Teams cards can request manual escalation; Web and standard Slack do not expose that action in 2.0. - Acknowledgement completes

sections.heading: Snooze and suppression
sections.text: Snooze is a time-bounded pause with a wake time and optional reason. Use it when work is intentionally waiting and the incident should return to active response automatically. Suppression is an explicit operational hold without the same time-bounded meaning. Use it for known noise or a controlled condition that should remain paused until a person unsuppresses it. Neither state resolves the inciden

sections.heading: Communication and projections
sections.text: The incident timeline is the durable response narrative. Record observations, decisions, mitigations, handoffs, and resolution evidence without placing secrets or unnecessary personal data in it. Connected systems serve different purposes: - Notifications attract attention and can expose delivery failures. - Slack and Teams cards offer authenticated response actions and can create war-room collabo

sections.heading: Resolution and reopening
sections.text: Human resolution requires a meaningful note and any required custom fields. It records a terminal response event, completes escalation, and preserves timing history. Automated event resolution follows the ingestion contract and is not a substitute for human verification when an operator is closing the incident. Reopening returns a resolved incident to active response with a new escalation generati

sections.text: During a live response: - Verify service, urgency, visibility, and scope before acting. - Use the incident page to resolve disagreements between projections. - Submit mutating actions once, then refresh before retrying. - Treat authorization and concurrency errors as safety boundaries. - Keep handoffs explicit and verify the incoming owner can access the incident. - Confirm provider delivery separ

sections.text: Visibility is PUBLIC or PRIVATE . The service supplies the default for new manual and integration incidents, and responders can make an intentional per-incident choice. - Public incidents can participate in status-page/customer communication when the relevant status configuration includes the service. - Private incidents remain internal and have tighter scoped-user visibility. sections.text: These signals are independent: - Assignment identifies the current responsible user or team. - Acknowledgement records that response awareness has been accepted and stops active escalation for that generation. - Watching gives a user a relationship to updates and can contribute to scoped incident visibility. An incident can be acknowledged while unassigned, or assigned while still open/unacknowled

sections.text: The supported operational states are: State Meaning --- --- OPEN Active and unacknowledged; escalation can run ACKNOWLEDGED Active response accepted; escalation completed/stopped SNOOZED Active but temporarily paused until a future time SUPPRESSED Active but intentionally excluded from active escalation RESOLVED Active response ended with resolution context Supported commands are Acknowledge, Reso

sections.heading: Escalation generations prevent stale work
sections.text: Lifecycle transitions that resume/restart response increment an escalation generation. Workers re-check this token before assignment, delivery, and final mutation. Work claimed for an earlier generation must become stale rather than page after acknowledgement, resolution, snooze, suppression, or a newer reopen. This is why operators should avoid repeated clicks while a command is pending. Idempote

sections.heading: SLA contract and clocks
sections.text: At creation, OpsKnight resolves the incident's SLA targets from current policy and stores a contract on the incident. Later edits to service tier or SLA policy must not rewrite historical targets silently. The lifecycle maintains: - immutable first-ack elapsed time; - current/final resolve elapsed time; - accumulated paused time; - an open pause start when snoozed/suppressed; and - indexed next-tr

sections.heading: Timeline and side effects
sections.text: Every meaningful transition appends a timeline event. Resolution with a human note also creates retained note/comment context. In the same transaction, OpsKnight enqueues lifecycle side effects for downstream processing. sections.heading: Sources and authorization
sections.text: Lifecycle commands can originate from web, mobile, REST API, bulk operations, ChatOps, voice, inbound events, or system automation. The shared lifecycle engine enforces transition invariants; each adapter must authenticate and authorize the actor before calling it. Interactive responders need the relevant incident capability and resource scope. API keys also need the corresponding explicit scope.

pages.title: Runbooks and safe remediation
pages.description: Understand immutable workflows, service bindings, outbound Agents, risk-aware approval, execution semantics, and uncertain outcomes.
pages.intro: Beta — Runbooks is Beta in v2.1. Qualify your deployment, Agent topology, and target permissions before enabling automatic writes in production. A Runbook is an ordered, reusable incident-response workflow that captures diagnostic, recovery, and verification steps in a single versioned definition. Authors build and iterate on drafts ; publishing produces an immutable version with a SHA-256 checksu

sections.heading: Architecture overview
sections.text: The Control Plane hosts the Runbook Builder, handles preview and approval, and validates all inputs. The Runbook Worker plans, dispatches, and reconciles executions using a durable PostgreSQL job queue. Outbound Agents are deployed near execution targets (hosts, containers, Kubernetes clusters) and perform allowlisted actions. Agents do not expose inbound command endpoints — they poll the control

sections.heading: Workflow lifecycle
sections.text: A Runbook progresses through these stages: 1. Draft — Author creates and iterates on steps, inputs, and configuration. 2. Published — An immutable version is created with a SHA-256 checksum of the canonical definition. Published versions cannot be edited. 3. Bound — A service automation rule connects the published version to a service with concrete input values, an execution target, and a trigger.

sections.heading: Binding modes and versions
sections.text: Mode Behavior ------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Manual A responder starts the workflow from an incident. No trigger evaluation. Suggested A matching incident-created trigger produces a suggestion; a responder decides whether to start it. Automatic A matching trigger starts the workflow. Requires a pinned pu

sections.heading: Risk model and approval
sections.text: Risk is derived from executable semantics , not only an author's label: Risk class Meaning Example actions ------------------ -------------------------------------- ------------------------------------ READ ONLY Observes without changing target state Diagnostics, inspect, status, health IDEMPOTENT WRITE Changes state in a repeatable way Start, stop, scale NON IDEMPOTENT Cannot safely retry Restart

sections.heading: Target semantics
sections.text: Use a specific Agent for machine-specific writes. A LOCAL HOSTS pool contains different machines; a multi-member pool cannot be used as an ambiguous write target. A SHARED TARGET pool is appropriate only when every member can reach the same shared target. Pool membership alone does not grant platform access.

sections.heading: Execution model
sections.text: Each execution follows a deterministic state machine: Steps within an execution proceed in order. Each step can have prechecks (run before the action) and verification (run after). A failed precheck prevents the action. Failed verification fails the remediation workflow even when the action itself succeeded.

sections.heading: Unknown outcomes
sections.text: Loss of an Agent or its lease after a write starts can leave an UNKNOWN step outcome. This does not mean the write failed or never ran. Inspect the actual target before starting another execution. Cancellation requests stop further work through reconciliation; they cannot undo an already-completed write.

sections.heading: Safety guarantees
sections.text: OpsKnight's Runbook system enforces multiple safety boundaries: - Immutable versions — Published workflows cannot be modified. - Cryptographic plan digest — Approval is bound to the exact plan hash. - Signed execution envelopes — Agents verify the control plane's signature before executing any step. - Replay protection — Nonce-based request deduplication prevents replay attacks. - Remediation budg

sections.text: - Disabled ( DISABLED ): no service automation evaluation; ordinary incident classification and service routing continue. - Shadow ( SHADOW ): evaluate the published configuration and record how its result differs from ordinary routing and priority. sections.text: All matching enrichment rules run in configured order. They can set priority, write declared custom context, and add tags. Later rules see earlier context writes; later writes to the same field win. Tags are deduplicated. Routing evaluates the enriched context. The first matching routing rule wins, and evaluation stops. pages.title: Administration

pages.intro: Common tasks: - Find the correct Settings area - Manage users and permissions - Review and revoke sessions - Create and rotate API keys - Review Audit Logs and Event Logs - Configure custom fields Use least privilege and keep a tested break-glass path outside automated identity-provider deprovisioning.

pages.title: Manage API keys
pages.description: Create, scope, rotate, inspect, and revoke OpsKnight API credentials.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as an administrator and identify the consumer owner, endpoints, minimum scopes, expiration, and secret manager. Effective authority is the intersection of key scopes and its owner's current product permissions.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → API keys . Review existing name, prefix, owner, scopes, expiry, status, and last-used evidence.

sections.heading: Configure and create a key
sections.text: 1. Open Settings → API keys and create a key. 2. Name the system/environment/owner. 3. Select minimum scopes and an operational expiration. 4. Copy the secret once directly into a secret manager. 5. Make a test request and verify Last used changes. The secret is displayed once. Store it in a secret manager; OpsKnight retains a keyed hash, the visible prefix, owner, scopes, expiration, and last use

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight stores a keyed hash rather than a retrievable secret, plus prefix, owner, scopes, expiration, and last-used evidence. Owner deactivation or permission changes can reduce/stop key authority.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Confirm the expected response and Last used update. Where safe, verify an operation outside scope returns 403 .

sections.heading: Revoke or rotate
sections.text: 1. Create a replacement with the same minimum scopes. 2. Update the consumer and verify its last used value changes. 3. Revoke the old key. 4. Confirm the revocation in the audit log. Revocation is immediate. It does not delete audit history. If a secret is exposed, revoke it before investigating the consumer.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - 401 : the secret is missing, malformed, expired, revoked, or owned by an inactive user. - 403 : authentication succeeded but the key lacks a required scope or its owner lacks product permission. - No last used update: verify the header, endpoint, and that the request reached this OpsKnight installation. See Permissions and API scopes.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Record owner, expiry, and rotation schedule. - Review audit logs and permissions.

pages.title: Review audit logs
pages.description: Search administrative changes, inspect record details, and export the current result page as CSV.
pages.intro: The Audit Log records security-sensitive and administrative actions. Use it to identify the recorded actor, action, entity, timestamp, source, and before/after details. It is distinct from application System Logs, notification delivery history, and an incident timeline.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as an ADMIN or AUDITOR . Collect the action name, entity identifier, actor name/email/identifier, or a phrase likely to appear in the visible record. The current page has no time-range, outcome, or correlation-ID filter.

sections.heading: Search and filter in the UI
sections.text: 1. Open Audit Log ( /audit ). 2. Use Search to match action, entity ID, stored actor name/email, or the current actor relation's name/email. 3. Select an Entity type to limit results to that resource category. 4. Select an Action when the filter offers the relevant action. 5. Open a row to inspect its full details and old/new values. 6. Move through results with Previous and Next . The page loads

sections.heading: Export CSV
sections.text: Use Export CSV in the filter toolbar to export the records supplied to the current page. Treat the export as a page/result export, not proof that every matching record across all pages was included. Record the active filters and page with the evidence package.

sections.heading: Understand a record
sections.text: For authentication policy, filter action=auth.policy.migrated to inspect the one-time legacy import, or action=auth.policy.changed for an administrator mode change. These events use entity type SYSTEM CONFIG and entity ID default . The change event includes old/new mode and version and the actor's authentication method. Policy updates and their mandatory audit commit in the same transaction. user.

sections.heading: What a missing event means
sections.text: A missing row does not prove the action never occurred. Confirm the entity/action spelling, clear filters, search adjacent pages, and inspect the relevant application and delivery logs. Some read operations and failed requests may not emit the mutation event you expected. Preserve application logs before restarts when investigating an apparent gap.

sections.heading: Security and retention
sections.text: Audit data can contain user and resource identifiers plus operational metadata. Restrict access, store CSV exports in an approved evidence location, and apply the organization's retention and legal-hold policy. Never paste credentials into investigation notes or enrich audit records with secrets.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - No results after filtering: clear filters, then add one exact entity/action/actor criterion at a time. - An actor is blank: historical/system activity may retain captured actor fields without a current user relation; inspect the row details. - CSV contains fewer records than expected: paginate and export the required result pages or use the approved evidence-export workflow for the broader case.

sections.heading: Authentication security events
sections.text: Review System → SSO / Authentication → Diagnostics for recent staged-provider tests/activation, emergency enrollment/sign-in/failure/revocation, explicit password restoration and targeted session revocation. Production mutations commit their audit and durable high-priority alert intent in one transaction. Failed audit/intent writes reject the mutation. Tokens, secrets and private keys are excluded

pages.title: Configure incident custom fields
pages.description: Create, validate, display, edit, and safely remove organization-specific incident fields.
pages.intro: Custom fields add structured, organization-specific metadata to incidents—for example environment, customer impact, change URL, or incident commander email. Administrators define fields; permitted responders enter values during incident creation or on the incident detail page.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as an ADMIN . Decide the field owner, data classification, permanent key, type, default, and whether responders need it in the incidents table. Avoid secrets and sensitive personal data: field values can appear in operational views, exports, and—only when separately enabled—status-page output.

sections.heading: Create a field
sections.text: 1. Open Settings → Custom Fields . 2. Select Add Custom Field . 3. Enter a display Name of 1–200 characters. 4. Enter a unique Key of 1–100 letters, digits, or underscores. Spaces, hyphens, and punctuation are rejected. 5. Choose one of the seven types: TEXT , NUMBER , DATE , SELECT , BOOLEAN , URL , or EMAIL . 6. For SELECT , add the allowed options in the order responders should see them. 7. Opt

sections.heading: Validation and stored values
sections.text: - TEXT : leading and trailing whitespace is removed; the remaining text is stored. - NUMBER : the value must be a finite JavaScript number. It is normalized with String(number) , so 01.50 becomes 1.5 ; NaN and infinity are rejected. - DATE : the value must be accepted by Date.parse . OpsKnight stores the normalized UTC ISO timestamp. - SELECT : when options exist, the value must exactly equal one

sections.heading: Edit a definition
sections.text: From Settings → Custom Fields , edit the name, required flag, default, select options, incident-list visibility, or order. Existing stored values are not rewritten when a default or option list changes. Before removing a select option, search retained incidents and integrations for that value.

sections.heading: Incident-list and status-page visibility
sections.text: Show in incident list controls the compact internal incidents table; it does not make the field public. Status-page publication is configured separately on the single status page through its privacy settings: custom fields must be enabled and the field must be in the allowed list. Keep customer identifiers, security context, emails, and internal runbook data out of public projections.

sections.heading: Delete a field
sections.text: Deletion is destructive. The API deletes every CustomFieldValue associated with the definition and then deletes the definition itself. Those historical values disappear from existing incidents; a later field with the same key does not restore them. Before confirming deletion, export anything that must be retained, remove the field from status-page privacy settings and external workflows, and check

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - “A custom field with this key already exists”: locate the existing definition or choose a genuinely new stable key. - Key validation fails: use only letters, numbers, and underscores, with no spaces or hyphens. - A number changes format: normalization stores the numeric value, not presentation formatting; use TEXT when leading zeros are meaningful. - A date shifts timezone: date input is normali

pages.title: Review and revoke signed-in sessions
pages.description: Inspect account sessions and recent device activity, revoke access, and respond to an untrusted device.
pages.intro: System authentication policy is enforced when an existing session makes its next protected server request. Password Only rejects OIDC sessions; SSO Required rejects ordinary password sessions. Method-specific revocation cutoffs also keep sessions revoked after a mode is relaxed again. Emergency sessions are independent recovery capabilities with a one-hour hard cap and 15-minute idle timeout. They

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in from a trusted device and preserve a break-glass access path. 1. Review unfamiliar session and device activity. 2. Revoke the affected session or all sessions. 3. Remediate the password or identity provider. 4. Verify revoked browsers must authenticate again.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings - Security and find Signed-in Sessions . Each row is an authentication session, not merely a device profile. Review the browser, operating system, device type, authentication kind ( Password , Trusted PWA , or Enterprise SSO ), creation time, last activity, expiry, opaque display ID, and whether the row is the current session. OpsKnight does not show an IP address, network, or inferr

sections.heading: Configure revocation
sections.text: Revoke a specific unfamiliar session first when the account remains under your control. Confirm it disappears and that the affected browser must authenticate again. Use Revoke all sessions for a lost device, suspected credential exposure, or uncertain scope. This increments the identity token version and invalidates existing browser sessions, including other trusted devices.

sections.heading: How session revocation works
sections.text: After emergency revocation, change the password when direct authentication is used, revoke/repair provider access when SSO is compromised, review audit and recent device activity, and re-enrol only trusted devices. Push subscriptions are per-device and separate from an interactive login session; review mobile Push device cleanup as part of a lost-device response.

sections.heading: Verify revocation
sections.text: Confirm the row disappears and the revoked browser must authenticate again.

sections.heading: Undo or restore access
sections.text: The old session cannot be restored. Authenticate again after securing the account and device.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: If activity looks stale, reload before acting. If a revoked session continues to access data, capture the request time and session/device details, verify all web replicas share the current database/session state, and escalate as a security incident.

pages.description: Map each Settings group to its owner, purpose, and detailed workflow.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Identify whether the change is personal, workspace-wide, integration-specific, or operational. Settings cards are permission-aware; administrator/auditor badges identify areas that may be hidden or read-only for your account.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings or /settings . Use the Settings search when you know the feature or a related keyword. Read the card's description and live status before opening it.

sections.heading: Configure through Settings
sections.text: 1. Select the group that owns the change using the map below. 2. Open the card and confirm its scope, current state, and required role. 3. Follow the linked feature guide before changing a credential, identity rule, routing policy, retention setting, or other high-impact control. 4. Save the smallest intended change and verify it in the consuming workflow. 5. Record and audit the result according

sections.heading: Choose the correct settings area
sections.text: Account and identity - Profile & Preferences: personal name, timezone, delivery preferences, quiet hours, and current membership/on-call context. - Security & Sessions: personal password and signed-in session review/revocation. Password controls are unavailable when the system policy requires SSO. - System → SSO / Authentication: administrator-only provider configuration and database-backed sign-i

sections.heading: How Settings works
sections.text: The landing page is an information architecture and status surface, not a bulk configuration form. Cards can display connection or record summaries, but the owning page performs the change. Permissions are enforced again by the target page/API; hiding a card is not the security boundary.

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text: After a change, return to Settings and confirm the card/live summary reflects the expected state where one is provided. Then verify the feature itself: send a test notification, perform an identity test, inspect health, or exercise the relevant incident workflow. Record high-risk changes in the change ticket and Audit Log.

sections.heading: Change or undo it
sections.text: Undo a change in its owning page, following that guide's rotation, disconnect, or rollback procedure. Do not delete a provider, identity configuration, or API credential before dependents have moved to a tested replacement.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - A card is missing: verify role, account status, and required capability. - Settings search has no match: search by feature and synonym, then use the grouped map above; product-wide record search is a separate control. - A live status is stale: open the target page and verify the source record; return/reload after the change. - A save succeeds but behavior is unchanged: verify runtime configurati

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Manage permissions - Manage profile and preferences - Configure notification providers - Configure Slack - Configure Microsoft Teams

sections.heading: Choose a range
sections.text: Pick 24 hours , 7 days , 30 days (default), 90 days , 6 months , 12 months , 2 years or 3 years , or Custom for a start and end day (up to 3 years). - Preset ranges are rolling: "7 days" means the 7 × 24 hours ending now. - Custom ranges are whole calendar days, midnight to midnight in your timezone, and include the end day you pick. - Charts bucket by hour (up to 2 days), day (up to ~3 months), w

sections.text: Filter by Teams , Services , Urgency , Status , Priority and Assignee (including Unassigned ). Teams, services and priorities accept several values. Filters apply to every section and are kept in the URL, so you can bookmark or share a view; unknown or invalid values in a link are ignored. Selecting a row in Services filters the whole page to that service — the incident page's Service analytics li

Each tile shows the change in percent, coloured by whether it is an improvement for that metric; there is no percentage when the previous value is missing or zero. The Services table adds the change in incident count per service.

sections.text: - "No data" on a tile: nothing in the range qualifies (for example no resolved incidents for MTTR). Widen the range or clear filters. - Totals differ from the incident list: Analytics counts incidents created in the range; the incident list may filter by status or activity instead. - A section shows an error: use the retry button on that section; other sections are unaffected. - Export returns 403

pages.title: ChatOps and incident collaboration
pages.description: Configure provider policy, incident actions, and Slack or Microsoft Teams war rooms.
pages.intro: ChatOps projects incident state into Slack or Microsoft Teams and lets authorized responders act without losing the OpsKnight incident as the source of truth. Start in this order: 1. Connect Slack or Microsoft Teams. 2. Configure the global and service policy. 3. Test a provider destination and responder identity. 4. Create and operate a war room. 5. Verify actions, membership synchronization, rec

pages.title: Configure the global ChatOps and war-room policy
pages.description: Connect provider readiness to automatic war-room triggers, naming, lifecycle, and video bridges.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect and test Slack, Microsoft Teams, or both. For Teams war rooms, enable war rooms and at least one destination. Decide which incident priorities/urgencies justify automatic room creation and who owns room closure.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → Integrations → ChatOps as an administrator. Provider cards show actual connection/readiness; saving policy does not connect a provider.

sections.heading: Configure the policy
sections.text: 1. Enable War Room Provisioning only after provider tests pass. 2. Choose Slack , Microsoft Teams , or Both as the default provider set. 3. Enter a short channel prefix such as inc ; OpsKnight adds incident-derived identity. 4. Select automatic creation priorities ( P1 – P5 ) and/or urgencies ( HIGH , MEDIUM , LOW ). Empty selections mean manual creation. 5. Decide whether resolution automatically

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: The global policy determines provider requests and defaults. Service-level overrides can narrow or replace behavior. A provider conflict or disconnected provider prevents successful provisioning rather than silently creating a different room. War-room operations remain auditable and tied to the incident.

sections.heading: Verify the policy
sections.text: Create a synthetic incident matching exactly one configured trigger. Confirm the expected provider room(s), normalized name, incident card, bridge link, responder actions, and resolution-close behavior. Then create a nonmatching incident and confirm no automatic room is requested.

sections.heading: Change or undo
sections.text: Turn off provisioning to stop new automatic/manual requests; existing provider rooms are not retroactively deleted. Remove triggers for manual-only behavior. Disable automatic closure before changing provider retention procedures.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - No room: check global enablement, trigger match, provider connection, Teams destination readiness, and service override. - Two rooms unexpectedly: default is Both or a service override requests both. - Invalid bridge: correct the URL/template or use NONE ; never publish credentials in it. - Configuration conflict: reconcile global and service policies explicitly, then retest.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Create a war room - Slack war rooms - Teams war rooms

pages.title: Create and operate an incident war room
pages.description: Provision, verify, reconcile, and close an incident-scoped Slack or Microsoft Teams room.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect Slack or Microsoft Teams, configure a destination, and create an active test incident. Confirm the responder can read the incident and use collaboration actions. Automatic creation also requires an owning destination in the global or service ChatOps policy.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Incidents → select incident and locate the Create war room button in the action bar under the incident's title card, after the tags.

sections.heading: Configure manual or automatic creation
sections.text: - Manual: a responder opens an incident and explicitly creates the room. Use this when only selected incidents require a dedicated channel. - Automatic: the effective global/service policy creates a room when a qualifying incident begins. Only one destination should own automatic room creation for a service. Service policy overrides the global default. Test the effective policy with a new incident

sections.heading: Verify the room
sections.text: 1. On the incident's action bar, select Create war room . 2. Select the provider (Slack or Microsoft Teams) in the creation dialog, then confirm creation. 3. Wait for provisioning to finish. Do not retry while the operation is still pending; durable operation and provider markers prevent duplicate rooms. 4. Open the returned provider URL and confirm incident title, urgency, service, assignee, stat

sections.heading: Operate during the incident
sections.text: Treat OpsKnight as authoritative for incident state. Provider messages and cards project that state; manual channel edits do not replace incident actions. Use the room for coordination, pin or update incident context through supported controls, and keep sensitive credentials out of chat history. Participant synchronization depends on provider permissions, bot/app access, and identity availability.

sections.heading: How synchronization works
sections.text: OpsKnight stores the durable provider room and operation identity, projects incident state, and reconciles supported membership, messages, and cleanup.

sections.heading: Reconcile drift and avoid duplicates
sections.text: If the provider room was renamed, membership changed, a card is stale, or a request timed out, inspect collaboration health and the existing operation/room identifier first. Run reconciliation or retry the recorded operation. Do not delete the remote room and immediately create another: the first request may have succeeded even when its response was lost.

sections.heading: Remove or close the room
sections.text: Resolve the incident according to the response workflow, then use the OpsKnight collaboration control to close/archive the room. Verify terminal context is published and provider cleanup reaches a terminal state. Provider capabilities and policy determine whether the channel is archived, retained, or otherwise closed; do not assume manual deletion is equivalent.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Creation forbidden: verify destination, app installation, scopes/RSC, and public/private-channel permission. - Action rejected: link the provider identity and confirm product role and incident authorization. - Members missing: verify provider directory availability and membership read/write permission. - Ambiguous or timed-out create: inspect the durable operation and remote marker before retryi

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: Provider details: - Slack war rooms - Microsoft Teams war rooms - Configure global ChatOps policy

pages.title: Compliance Control Center
pages.description: Evaluate runtime controls, investigate drift, inspect evidence, and export audit packages.
pages.intro: Open Settings - Security & Compliance to inspect runtime controls, framework mappings, evidence integrity, drift, and compliance operations. OpsKnight supplies technical evidence; it does not certify the organization or replace scope, shared-responsibility, and external-control review. Use Evaluate controls and export evidence for the operational workflow. The tabs are: - Overview — posture, monit

pages.title: Evaluate controls, investigate drift, and export evidence
pages.description: Operate the Compliance Control Center without treating product evidence as automatic certification.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Use an authorized administrator/operator identity, define the audit scope, and prepare a protected destination for evidence archives. 1. Review posture and monitoring recency. 2. Investigate failing controls and drift. 3. Inspect evidence integrity. 4. Preview and export only the required scope.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings - Security & Compliance .

sections.heading: Configure and evaluate current posture
sections.text: Open Settings - Security & Compliance . On Overview , record the runtime revision, monitoring recency, failing/unknown controls, open drift, and evidence integrity warnings. Open Controls , select a control, and inspect its observed state, evaluation time, supporting evidence, and framework mappings. A mapping means the evidence is relevant; it does not satisfy an entire external standard. Trigger

sections.heading: Investigate drift
sections.text: Open Control Drift , select the episode, and compare baseline and current evaluations, evidence, and mapped requirements. Assign remediation outside the control center where appropriate. Acknowledge drift only to record that it was seen; acknowledgment does not make the control compliant. Verify remediation with a later passing evaluation and reviewable evidence.

sections.heading: Inspect evidence integrity
sections.text: Open Evidence Ledger . Search and filter by control, evidence type, and integrity result. Review collection time, source, payload summary, and digest. An integrity mismatch is an investigation condition: preserve the record, restrict export, and inspect storage/key/runtime history rather than deleting it.

sections.heading: How evaluation works
sections.text: Evaluations capture observed technical state; evidence supports the observation, and framework mappings relate it to requirements without granting certification.

sections.heading: Export a package
sections.text: Select Export Evidence Package . Choose all controls, selected controls, or a framework; then choose a current snapshot or a historical date range. Preview the counts and scope before export. The downloaded archive includes observed technical state, mappings, supporting evidence, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. Store the archive as sensitive audit material. Record the product revision, export tim

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text: Confirm archive counts match the preview and that manifest, digests, revision, scope, and evaluation window are present.

sections.heading: Remove or undo
sections.text: An export cannot be recalled. Quarantine an incorrectly scoped archive under your evidence-handling policy and generate a corrected package.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - No controls/evidence: verify authorization, runtime evaluation health, and monitoring completion. - Export unavailable: the signed-in role lacks export capability. - Historical export is empty: confirm time range and control/framework scope. - Integrity mismatch: preserve evidence and investigate; do not regenerate an archive merely to hide the mismatch. - Drift remains after acknowledgment: exp

sections.text: - Compliance evidence concepts - Audit Logs

pages.title: Command Center
pages.description: Use the OpsKnight home dashboard to understand operational state and choose the next response action.

A chrome-free Wallboard at /wallboard shows the same live data on office TVs. It is an operational view; use Analytics for deeper historical analysis and Reports for saved exe

pages.title: Use the Command Center
pages.description: Watch live incidents, focus the feed, and read operational trends on the OpsKnight home dashboard and TV wallboard.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in and confirm that your team membership and incident permissions are current. Everything on the page is authorization-scoped: two users can legitimately see different incidents and counts.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Select Dashboard in the main navigation or open / . The page has three zones, top to bottom: 1. Command Center : current state at a glance. 2. Live Incidents with Ops Pulse beside it, sized so the whole panel fits on a desktop screen without scrolling the page. 3. Trends & insights : historical analytics for a selectable period.

sections.heading: Configure the view
sections.text: 1. Select the operational scope ( All , My teams , or Mine ) from the top controls. 2. Filter the live incident feed by service, assignee, urgency, or keyword. 3. Choose the metrics card or queue item to focus on active priority incidents. 4. Select Wallboard when projecting to team TV displays.

sections.heading: How the Command Center works
sections.text: Read the Command Center indicators from left to right: - Status shows Operational , Degraded (active incidents, none critical), or Critical (a critical incident, an SLA deadline within 10 minutes, or an SLA breached in the last hour). - The summary line describes the situation in words, for example "5 critical on API Gateway / 2 due within 10 min / 3 critical unowned". Each phrase is a link that f

Narrow the feed with Search (press / ), Service , and Filters . Filters contains Show (All active, Critical, Mine, My teams, Unassigned, SLA risk), Team, Status, Urgency, and Assignment. Active choices appear as removable

Sort feed applies the same ordering to the live feed. - Hotspots : services with the most active and critical incidents; select a service to focus the feed on it. - On call

The section shows created versus resolved incidents over the period, MTTA and MTTR compared with the previous period, acknowledgement and resolution SLA compliance, an activity timeline with type filters, team load, and the incident heatmap. Empty or unavailable data

sections.text: Open Wallboard or /wallboard on the screen's browser and sign in once. The wallboard is read-only and has no navigation chrome. It: - enters true fullscreen with Fullscreen or F (hiding browser toolbars where the browser allows it; TV browsers that refuse the request keep working in a maximized window); - cycles through views every 20 seconds ( Space or Auto-cycle pauses; ?cycle=off disables it);

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text: 1. Create a test incident and confirm it appears at the top of the feed without a page refresh. 2. Acknowledge it and confirm the row updates in place; resolve it and confirm it leaves the feed. 3. Select a metric and compare the feed with the equivalent Incidents page filter ( View all incidents ). 4. Switch the scope to Mine and compare it with your assigned incidents. 5. Change the Trends & ins

sections.heading: Change or undo the view
sections.text: Scope, filters, sort, pause, pins, and density change only your view, never incident records. Select Clear all (or remove each chip) and switch the scope to All to return to the default. Incident actions taken from the feed are real mutations; reverse them from the incident itself where the workflow permits.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - A count differs from another user's count: compare roles, team membership, service access, scope, and filters. - The footer says Stale or Offline: the live channel is degraded. Data is re-read automatically when it recovers; do not treat a quiet feed as proof that nothing changed. - A new incident did not appear: check whether updates are paused, whether a filter or scope excludes it, and whethe

sections.text: - Respond to an incident - Use Analytics - Read a saved dashboard - Understand permissions

pages.title: Escalation policy tasks
pages.description: Create, test, attach, and troubleshoot escalation policies.
pages.intro: Follow Create a policy, define its steps and retries/delays, then test it before you attach it to a service. Use Configure a policy as the complete workflow and troubleshooting for stalled or unexpected escalation.

pages.title: Attach an escalation policy to a service
pages.description: Select, save, verify, and safely replace the escalation policy used by a service's new incidents.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Create/validate a policy and confirm its targets/channels are suitable for the service. Identify change window and current incidents affected by existing policy generations.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Services → select service → escalation/response configuration .

sections.heading: Configure the attachment
sections.text: 1. Select the intended escalation policy. 2. Review service ownership, urgency/notification context, and policy name. 3. Save the service. 4. Reopen/refresh and confirm the selected policy remains.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: New incident escalation uses the service's selected policy and records/executed generation according to product lifecycle. Changing the service does not recall notifications already sent for active incidents.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Create a controlled incident on that exact service and inspect attached policy/current step/target plus delivered notification. A policy directory view alone is insufficient.

sections.heading: Change or undo it
sections.text: Reattach the prior valid policy, save, and retest. Never leave a production service without a viable escalation route during replacement.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Policy absent from selector: verify it exists, access/tenant scope, and current validity. Incident uses unexpected policy: confirm incident service and creation time versus service change; inspect recorded generation/current state.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Test policy - Inspect notification delivery

pages.title: Configure an escalation policy
pages.description: Build, attach, and test ordered incident notification steps.
pages.intro: An escalation policy defines who OpsKnight contacts, through which personal channels, and how long it waits before trying the next step. Only Admins can change policies. Authorized Responders and Auditors can view them.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Prepare the targets: - a User must be an active Admin or Responder; - a Team needs active members, or an active lead for lead-only notification; - a Schedule needs effective coverage when an incident may page. Verify responder preferences and destinations too. Selecting SMS cannot deliver to a responder without an enabled, usable SMS endpoint.

sections.heading: 1. Create the policy
sections.text: 1. Open Escalation Policies and choose Create Policy . 2. Enter a unique name of at least two characters. 3. Describe its service or operational purpose. 4. Create and open the policy. A policy can be saved without steps, but it cannot page until a valid step exists.

sections.heading: 2. Add the first step
sections.text: Under Steps , choose Add Escalation Step and set: 1. Target Type: User, Team, or Schedule (On-Call). 2. Target: the exact object to page. 3. Delay: 0 for immediate paging. Values are whole minutes from 0 through 10,080. 4. Conditions: optionally match priority, urgency, or support-hours state. A step supports at most ten conditions. 5. Notification Channels: Email, SMS, Voice Call, Push, and/or Wh

sections.heading: 3. Add fallbacks and verify timing
sections.text: A practical starting sequence is primary schedule at 0 , backup team at 5 , and incident commander at 10 . Each value is the wait before a reachable step at that timeline position; the policy header shows the maximum total duration. Steps whose conditions fail or whose targets have no eligible responders are skipped immediately, without waiting their configured delay. OpsKnight advances while the

sections.heading: 4. Attach it to a service
sections.text: 1. Open Services and select the service. 2. Open general settings and select the policy under Escalation Policy . 3. Save, then confirm the service appears in the policy's Linked Services tab. An unattached policy never runs. A service with no policy, or a policy with no steps, cannot start policy-based paging.

sections.heading: 5. Test the route
sections.text: 1. Create a test incident whose priority, urgency, and support-hours state match the intended step. 2. Confirm the first target receives the expected channel. 3. If safe, leave it unacknowledged long enough to verify the fallback. 4. Acknowledge and resolve it, then inspect delivery details and the policy's Activity tab. Targets resolve at execution time. Matching steps run in displayed order, and

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: No notification: confirm the policy is attached, has a matching step, and the incident remains unacknowledged. Schedule resolves to nobody: check effective coverage at the incident time. An existing schedule still needs an active layer or override and eligible responder. Team reaches fewer people: check active membership and Notify only team lead . If enabled, verify the lead is active. One channe

pages.title: Create an escalation policy
pages.description: Create an ordered escalation policy with valid targets, channels, delays, retries, and a testable fallback path.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Only administrators can change policies. Prepare active user/team/schedule targets, usable personal endpoints, intended channel order, delays/retries, and fallback coverage.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Escalation policies and select Create policy .

sections.heading: Configure the policy
sections.text: 1. Enter a unique operational name/description. 2. Add the first policy step with target, channel, and timing. 3. Add fallback steps for non-response/provider failure according to policy design. 4. Save and review total timing/order. 5. Attach the policy to a service.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: For an open incident, OpsKnight evaluates the attached policy generation, resolves user/team/schedule targets at execution, and enqueues eligible personal notifications. Invalid targets/endpoints can yield skips/failures; a saved policy is not proof of deliverability.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Inspect policy order/targets/timing, attach it to a non-production service, and complete Test an escalation policy. Confirm notification, acknowledgement, and later-step suppression/advance behavior.

sections.heading: Change or undo it
sections.text: Edit only with impact review. Before deleting/replacing, identify every attached service and move it to a valid policy. Retest after target, schedule, channel, timing, or provider changes.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Target unavailable: activate/fix the user/team/schedule and endpoint; do not rely on an empty step. Timing unexpected: review per-step delay/retry semantics and total elapsed path.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Configure steps - Test policy

pages.title: Configure escalation retries and delays
pages.description: Set and validate escalation timing without creating alert storms, dead time, or impossible response objectives.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Know incident response objective, provider delivery characteristics, responder expectations, and total acceptable time before each fallback.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Escalation policies → select policy → Steps , then edit the intended step timing.

sections.heading: Configure timing
sections.text: 1. Set the wait/delay before advancement according to product fields. 2. Configure bounded retry behavior only where it improves delivery without duplicate storm risk. 3. Calculate cumulative elapsed time through all preceding steps/retries. 4. Save and review the full timeline.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: The escalation planner schedules eligible work for the current incident/policy generation. Acknowledgement or terminal state changes suppress/complete later work according to lifecycle rules. Provider retry and policy advancement are distinct concerns.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Run a controlled test with timestamps. Confirm first delivery, retry/advance time, acknowledgement stopping behavior, and no unexpected duplicate provider messages.

sections.heading: Change or undo timing
sections.text: Restore the prior reviewed timing values and retest. Already emitted notifications cannot be recalled; communicate accidental pages.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Next step is late: inspect scheduler/queue oldest age, configured cumulative delays, provider retries, and incident acknowledgement state. Duplicate storm: stop the test through correct incident lifecycle, inspect retry versus policy scheduling, and reduce unsafe repeated paths.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Attach policy to service - Test policy

pages.title: Configure escalation policy steps
pages.description: Select escalation targets and channels, order fallbacks, and verify runtime target resolution.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Prepare active targets and usable channel endpoints. A schedule needs effective coverage at incident time; a team needs eligible members/lead according to target mode.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Escalation policies → select policy → Steps .

sections.heading: Configure a step
sections.text: 1. Add or select a step position. 2. Choose target type and exact user/team/schedule. 3. Choose notification channel(s) supported by intended responders. 4. Configure delay/retries according to timing. 5. Save and add later fallback steps.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight resolves targets at execution, filters ineligible recipients/endpoints, and creates delivery work with the policy/incident generation. Changes affect later execution according to current state; they do not recall already emitted pages.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Review every target and total path, then run a controlled test at a time the schedule/team resolution is known. Confirm actual recipient/channel matches.

sections.heading: Remove or change a step
sections.text: Preserve at least one viable route and review service impact before reordering/deleting. Retest the complete fallback chain after changes.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Step saves but no recipient: inspect active user/team membership/schedule coverage and personal channel eligibility. Wrong member paged: inspect execution timestamp and runtime team/schedule target resolution.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Configure retries and delays - Test policy

pages.title: Test an escalation policy
pages.description: Validate target resolution, timing, notification delivery, acknowledgement behavior, and fallback progression end to end.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Use a test service/window, tell responders, attach the policy, verify schedule/team targets and endpoints, and decide whether the test should acknowledge first step or intentionally advance.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open the policy and attached test service, then record current targets/timing.

sections.heading: Configure the test
sections.text: Create a unique test incident title, expected recipient/channel/timestamps, acknowledgement actor, and cleanup plan. Avoid unintended production paging.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Trigger the controlled incident. 2. Observe policy/target resolution and first delivery. 3. Acknowledge or intentionally let the next step advance. 4. Inspect delivery history/timeline. 5. Resolve the test incident.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight evaluates current open state, policy generation, runtime target eligibility, scheduler timing, queue/provider delivery, and acknowledgement/terminal suppression.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Compare expected and actual recipients/channels/timestamps, delivery results, timeline, acknowledgement actor, later-step behavior, and final resolution. Retain objective evidence.

sections.heading: Change or undo the test
sections.text: Resolve and clearly label the test, remove temporary service/policy/override changes, and notify accidentally paged recipients. Preserve audit/delivery evidence.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: No delivery: trace service attachment → policy step → target resolution → endpoint preference → queue → provider result. Next step did not stop: verify acknowledgement state/time and incident/policy generation; inspect scheduler/worker logs/metrics.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Escalation troubleshooting - Inspect delivery

pages.title: Troubleshoot escalation policies
pages.description: Diagnose missing targets, wrong recipients, timing, duplicate pages, non-advancement, and acknowledgement suppression failures.

sections.heading: No recipient is resolved
sections.text: Check service policy attachment, active incident/current generation, target existence, team membership/lead mode, schedule coverage/override, user status, and personal endpoint eligibility. Correct the target and run a controlled test. Trace one incident from the service outward: service → attached policy → current policy generation → eligible step → resolved user/team/schedule → enabled user endp

sections.heading: Wrong responder is paged
sections.text: Check incident service/policy, execution timestamp, schedule zone/overrides, team membership, and recorded target resolution. Communicate accidental paging and correct the narrow source.

sections.heading: Next step is late or never advances
sections.text: Check incident remains open/unacknowledged, configured cumulative timing, scheduler heartbeat/lag, queue oldest age, database, provider retries, and worker health. Compute the expected due time from the incident's escalation start and cumulative step delays, in UTC. If the due time is still in the future, the policy is working as configured. If it passed and no claim exists, inspect scheduler owne

sections.heading: Acknowledgement does not stop later work
sections.text: Check acknowledgement time/state, concurrent step claim, incident/policy generation, and delivery already emitted before acknowledgement. An already sent provider notification cannot be recalled.

sections.heading: Duplicate notifications occur
sections.text: Check provider retry/idempotency, repeated manual escalation, duplicated targets across steps, concurrent workers, and projection/delivery operation IDs before retrying. Compare intent ID, delivery operation ID, recipient endpoint, provider message ID, and incident generation. The same provider message shown twice is a provider or client-display issue; two operation IDs indicate duplicate scheduli

sections.heading: Evidence to collect
sections.text: Preserve incident ID and generation, service and policy IDs, expected/due times, resolved target, scheduler heartbeat, queue age, intent/attempt IDs, provider status, and acknowledgement time. Redact endpoint addresses and credentials.

sections.heading: Recovery verification
sections.text: Use Test an escalation policy and confirm target, delivery, timing, acknowledgement behavior, fallback, and resolution evidence.

pages.title: Identity and single sign-on
pages.description: Set up single sign-on, decide who can sign in, give people roles and teams from your identity provider, and provision accounts with SCIM.
pages.intro: OpsKnight connects to one OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta, Auth0 or Keycloak. You set it up in Settings → System → SSO / Authentication , in four steps: Step What you do Guide ------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------

sections.heading: Choosing how people sign in
sections.text: - SSO Optional — people can use single sign-on or their password. Start here. - SSO Required — everyone must use single sign-on. This needs two emergency recovery identities first, so a provider outage can never lock you out. See authentication modes for exactly what each mode allows.

sections.heading: Provisioning with SCIM
sections.text: Single sign-on decides who can sign in. SCIM lets your directory create, update and deactivate accounts and keep team membership in sync, so people are ready before their first sign-in and lose access the moment they leave.

sections.heading: When something goes wrong
sections.text: Every sign-in problem shows a specific message and a reference ID. Look the message up in sign-in problems. If your own test sign-in fails, see administrator test failures.

sections.heading: More
sections.text: - Migrate the first administrator to SSO - Rotate provider credentials - Recover from an SSO lockout - Upgrade from v2.1

sections.text: An outage never turns passwords back on by itself. Use emergency access to repair the provider while staying on SSO Required, or follow SSO lockout recovery to restore password access deliberately.

sections.text: Older environment settings are imported once. Later environment changes do not override the policy you set in the console. An imported emergency password only opens the restricted recovery console at /recovery ; retire it after setting up two emergency recovery identities.

pages.title: Migrate an existing administrator to SSO

Enter the provider credentials (and role rules in 3 · Roles & teams ) and select Save changes . Nothing changes for anyone yet. 3. Open 4 · Test & activate . Tick Allow this SSO identity to link … only after confirming you control the identity at the provider. 4. Select Test my sign-in and sign in at the pro

sections.heading: Failures and rollback
sections.text: A mismatching verified email needs an explicit review of the original record and provider claim; do not change claims merely to bypass ownership checks. Missing ADMIN claims, Entra group overage, disabled users and changed token versions invalidate the test. Save again after issuer or client changes and repeat the test. Optional keeps ordinary password access available while piloting. Roll back a

sections.heading: Verify identity ownership and administrator continuity
sections.text: Record the existing administrator’s stable User ID, manual/IdP role source, team assignments, and the intended issuer/client. Do not create a duplicate administrator just to test SSO. Test from the acting normal administrator’s own account, or use independent emergency recovery to search and select the existing active admin. Administrator search is paginated and searches names/emails beyond the fi

sections.text: Sign out of the verification browser and perform a new production sign-in. Confirm the stable User ID, expected role source, team access, and registered OIDC session. Verify an unrelated identity with a matching unapproved email does not link itself. For Required, a prior password session must be rejected on its next protected request. Keep the two independent custodians available during migration

pages.title: Roles, permissions and access requests
pages.description: What each OpsKnight role and team role can do, why someone sees an Access denied page, how to request or grant access (including temporary and emergency access), and how administrators review and explain access.
pages.intro: Everyone in OpsKnight has one role for the whole organization, and a team role in each team they belong to. Administrators can also give someone a custom role (extra permissions) or temporary access that ends on its own. Every page and action is checked on the server. When something is not allowed you see an Access denied page that says what is needed, who can give it to you, and lets you ask for

sections.heading: When you see "Access denied"
sections.text: The page tells you: - what you tried to open and what it needs (for example "Requires Auditor or Admin"); - your role and teams; - who can give you access: the owners and admins of the team that owns the item, or your organization's administrators; - a Request access form. For a specific incident, service or team outside your teams, OpsKnight shows only which team owns it, never its contents.

sections.heading: Request access
sections.text: From the Access denied page or Settings → My Access , ask for a different role or to join a team. Choose how long you need it (1 hour to 7 days, or permanently) and say why. - Team requests go to that team's owners and admins; role requests go to administrators. - Approvers review requests in Settings → Access Requests . They can change the duration, approve or decline, and add a note. You get a n

sections.heading: Emergency access (break-glass)
sections.text: If an incident can't wait for an approver, anyone can give themselves Responder access for a short time (15 minutes to the organization's limit), for one incident or in general. It requires a reason and a recent sign-in, is limited to three times a day, alerts every administrator immediately, and everything done with it is in the audit log. Administrators can turn it off.

sections.heading: For administrators
sections.text: Settings → Access Management brings everything together: - Access checker — choose a person and a page, permission, or incident action to see whether it is allowed and exactly why (role, teams, temporary access, relationship to the incident). - Who has access — everyone holding a permission through their role, a custom role, or temporary access. - Temporary and emergency access — see and end activ

sections.text: Keep the current working provider registration and encryption key. Confirm two independent recovery identities are drilled if Required is active. Register both callback URIs on the replacement client. Sign in freshly or verify an emergency key before staging. Overlap old and new client secrets at the provider when supported.

sections.text: 1. Open 1 · Connect provider and enter the new credentials. A blank secret preserves the existing encrypted secret only when issuer and client ID match; it is never displayed. 2. Review organization/domain boundaries, scopes, role/profile mappings and session limits. Stage the revision. 3. Run a real administrator sign-in for that revision. Discovery alone cannot demonstrate that the secret works

This makes a new immutable revision using the current production base version. Run a fresh administrator test and activate it explicitly. A previously successful test is not reusable after a production change. If the old secret is revoked at the IdP, rollback requires a valid new secret;

Record the normal and administrator-test callback URLs shown in Connection. Provider-side secret overlap is preferable when supported, but confirm its exact behavior with your IdP administrator; the application cannot guarantee vendor overlap perio

A provider version change invalidates the proof; a cancelled/expired test requires a new state/nonce/PKCE ceremony. If all independent recovery credentials are lost and the imported bridge has been retired, application-level recovery is unavailable: use the separately governed infrastructure/database recovery procedure and review every change. Do not delete import markers, enable legacy variable

A deployment pin does not create DNS or ingress routing. 2. Set AUTH RECOVERY

pages.title: Incident response tasks
pages.description: Declare, coordinate, escalate, and resolve incidents in OpsKnight.
pages.intro: Start with Respond to an incident. For individual tasks use create, acknowledge, assign, escalate, and resolve. Give the response a commander, ops lead, comms lead and scribe with incident roles. Administrators can configure incident SLA, templates, and the SLA scheduler migration. Track operational follow-up through Action Items, then create a postmortem.

pages.title: Acknowledge an incident
pages.description: Take response ownership, verify escalation stops, and handle acknowledgement conflicts safely.
pages.intro: Acknowledgement tells OpsKnight that a responder has accepted the active response. It records response timing and completes the current escalation generation. It does not assign the incident, resolve the underlying problem, or make a private incident public.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: You must be signed in, able to view the incident, and have incident.acknowledge.scoped or broader incident-management access for it. Before selecting the action: 1. Confirm the incident title and service so you do not acknowledge a similarly named event. 2. Read the latest timeline entries and current status. 3. Check the assignee. Assignment and acknowledgement are independent, so decide whether

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Incidents → select the incident . Acknowledge is on the right of the action bar, under the incident's title card. On a phone it is in the bar fixed to the bottom of the screen.

sections.heading: Configure and acknowledge from the incident page
sections.text: 1. Open Incidents and select the incident. 2. Review the service, urgency, priority and current assignee in the Details card, and the Ack SLA chip under the title. 3. Select Acknowledge once. 4. Wait for the status update before taking the same action from another channel. OpsKnight applies lifecycle commands against the status you loaded. If another responder changed it first, the request can be

sections.heading: Verify acknowledgement
sections.text: Confirm all of the following: - The title card shows Acknowledged . - The timeline records the acknowledgement and actor. - The first acknowledgement timestamp and response measurement are present. Later status changes do not replace the original first-acknowledgement measurement. - The active escalation generation is complete, with no new step scheduled from that generation. - Any acknowledgement

sections.heading: Acknowledge from another response channel
sections.text: Mobile, supported ChatOps actions, voice workflows, and authenticated API clients can acknowledge an incident when the actor and integration have the required access. Regardless of channel, verify the canonical incident page when the action is operationally important. Provider cards and push notifications are views of incident state, not a separate source of truth. Never share an interactive actio

sections.text: The global banner includes active P1 , P2 , or high-urgency incidents created within the last four hours. It automatically dismisses after 12 seconds; hover over it to pause the countdown. Manual or automatic dismissal persists while navigating in the same browser session. A genuinely new or newly escalated P1 /high-urgency incident can reopen it. Realtime toast cards are for new, unacknowledged a

sections.heading: How acknowledgement works with other states
sections.text: - Open: acknowledgement changes the incident to Acknowledged and completes active escalation work. - Snoozed: acknowledgement accepts the response and leaves the incident acknowledged rather than waiting for the snooze to expire. A snooze always ends: when no end time is given (for example a mobile swipe, a bulk action or a REST status update), it lasts 60 minutes, and snoozing an already-snoozed

sections.text: Use Unacknowledge only when the incident genuinely needs to return to the open response path—for example, ownership was accepted by mistake and no responder is now handling it. 1. Open the acknowledged incident. 2. Confirm there is no active owner continuing the response. 3. Open the ⋯ menu at the right of the action bar and select Unacknowledge . 4. Verify the status returns to Open , a timeline

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: The action is unavailable Check the incident status, your effective permission, and service scope. The UI hides actions that are invalid for the current state. A suppressed or resolved incident needs its corresponding lifecycle action first. OpsKnight says the incident changed elsewhere Another actor won the concurrent update. Refresh, read the new status and latest timeline entry, then decide whe

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: Acknowledgement is the start of owned response work. Confirm assignment, communicate impact, add investigation notes, create action items where useful, and resolve only after service health is restored. See Assign an incident, Escalate an incident, and the incident lifecycle.

pages.title: Track incident action items
pages.description: Create, own, prioritize, review, export, and optionally link remediation work to Jira.
pages.intro: Action items turn incident and postmortem findings into accountable work. Use them for a measurable change that remains after live response—such as adding an alert, removing a failure mode, testing restore procedures, or revising an escalation policy. Do not use them as live lifecycle commands or as a replacement for timeline notes.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: Identify the parent incident or postmortem, the expected outcome, a responsible owner, and a realistic due date. Responder-level access or broader authorization is required to change action-item status; management options can be further limited by the user's effective permissions and scope. If the item will use Jira, the workspace Jira connection must be healthy and the parent service must have an

sections.text: Open the parent incident's Postmortem tab (or the related postmortem) to view and edit its action items, or select Action Items in the main navigation to manage work across all incidents.

sections.text: Action items are authored in postmortem action-item surfaces and then appear on the global Action Items board. 1. Open the related incident postmortem or postmortem editor. 2. Add an action item with a concise, outcome-oriented title. 3. Describe the failure being prevented, the required change, and how completion will be verified. 4. Set priority to High , Medium , or Low based on risk and urgenc

sections.text: OpsKnight keeps the action item attached to its incident/postmortem while also projecting it onto the global board for ownership, due-date, priority, and status review.

sections.heading: Use the global board
sections.text: Open Action Items to review work across postmortems. The summary separates total, open, in-progress, completed, blocked, overdue, and high-priority work. Incident-owned Jira issues may also appear as inherited, read-only context; they are not the action item's own link. To use an action-item link: 1. Open the item from its postmortem or global board. 2. Choose to create a Jira issue or link an existing issue key. 3. Verify the d

sections.text: Before marking an item completed: 1. Test the acceptance condition named in its description. 2. Capture durable evidence in the appropriate repository, change record, runbook, or ticket. 3. Confirm the parent postmortem and global board show the same status. 4. If linked to Jira, sync and reconcile meaningful status differences according to your team's source-of-truth policy. 5. Mark the item Comp

sections.heading: Undo or change an action item update
sections.text: Correct the supported owner, due date, priority, Jira link, or status from the action-item controls and record why a completed item was reopened. Do not delete or mark work complete merely to remove it from an active view; preserve the audit trail and create a replacement item when the required outcome changed materially.

sections.text: An item is missing from the board Clear search and status, owner, and priority filters. Confirm the postmortem was saved and that the item has a normalized record. During migration, once normalized records exist for a postmortem they are the read source, avoiding duplicate legacy and normalized entries. A status change fails Refresh, verify the item still exists, and confirm responder access. If t

pages.title: Assign an incident
pages.description: Assign, reassign, or unassign an incident without confusing ownership with acknowledgement.
pages.intro: Assignment records who is responsible for coordinating the incident. An incident can be assigned to one active user, one existing team, or nobody. A valid explicit priority or urgency supplied by the incident-creation path is retained. 2. Applicable scoped rules are evaluated before inherited/parent behavior. 3. A rule can set, inherit, derive/fallback, default, or explicitly clear its field as described above. 4. If urgency is stil

Add date exceptions for holidays, maintenance coverage, or exceptional staffed peri

sections.text: At incident creation, OpsKnight classifies the signal, selects the service or workspace priority rule (or base targets), and freezes the result. Both phases breach only when elapsed SLA time is strictly greater than the target. Incident outcome ACK result Resolution result --- --- --- Acknowledged within target, resolved within target Met Met Acknowledged after ACK target Breached Determined indep
