sections.text: Use a controlled non-production service or approved test window: 1. Simulate all normalized severities and save the expected priority, urgency, target source, and support state. 2. Send one representative provider event and open the created incident. 3. Confirm service, severity-derived urgency, priority, policy source/version, ACK deadline, and resolution deadline match the simulation. 4. Acknowl

sections.heading: Production rollout checklist
sections.text: - Policy meanings and achievable targets are approved by service owners. - Every provider severity is mapped and simulated. - Priority and urgency are explained separately to responders. - Workspace inheritance is the default; every service exception has an owner. - Timezone, holidays, overnight windows, and DST boundaries are tested. - At least one controlled end-to-end event matches the simulato

sections.heading: Roll back or change
sections.text: To roll back, save a new policy version using the previous values. There is no safe way to rewrite the contract of incidents already created under the changed version. Validate rollback with a newly created controlled incident. Remove a service exception by restoring inheritance, and restore the previous scoped classification/fallback selections explicitly. Policy configuration is separate from th

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Wrong priority: inspect explicit payload priority, the matched scoped rule, priority mode, clear semantics, fallback mode, and captured provenance. - Wrong urgency: inspect explicit urgency, scoped inheritance, severity normalization, the row's urgency mode, and the severity default. - P2 or P4 never appears: urgency fallback only produces P1, P3, or P5; set P2/P4 explicitly for the appropriate

sections.text: - Understand the incident SLA contract - Create and verify an incident - Acknowledge an incident - Resolve an incident - Migrate the SLA scheduler - Monitor SLA and response-policy metrics

pages.title: Create an incident
pages.description: Create a manual incident with the right service, response settings, ownership, and deduplication behavior.
pages.intro: Create an incident manually when a person identifies an operational problem before an integration does, or when you need a controlled exercise. For monitoring alerts, prefer the service integration so OpsKnight can deduplicate active events and resolve incidents from the source automatically. Reopening a recently resolved incident is supported for matching manual reports within the 30-minute dedup

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: You need incident.create.all or incident.create.scoped . Scoped access only permits services in your effective scope. Check the target service before a production test: - It has the intended escalation policy and responder ownership. - Its notification providers are enabled and healthy. - Its visibility default is appropriate for the event. - Its response targets and support hours are correct. The

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Incidents and select Create incident .

sections.heading: Configure and create the incident
sections.text: 1. Open Incidents . 2. Select Create incident . 3. Optionally choose an incident template. Review every value it supplies; a template is a starting point, not proof that the current service, urgency, or owner is correct. 4. Enter a title between 5 and 255 characters. Use a short symptom and affected component, such as Checkout API returning elevated 5xx responses . 5. Select the affected Service .

sections.heading: Understand the creation result
sections.text: The create operation can return one of three valid outcomes: - Created — OpsKnight made a new incident. - Merged — an active incident already owned the same service and deduplication key, so the event was attached to it. - Reopened — the same deduplication identity matched a recently resolved incident inside the reopen window (30 minutes). For this reason, do not reuse a convenient deduplication k

sections.heading: Verify the initial response state
sections.text: On the incident detail page, confirm: 1. The title, service, urgency, priority, visibility, custom fields, and optional owner match the form. 2. The timeline contains the creation event and identifies the actor or source. 3. The response timer reflects the frozen service target and support-hours rules. 4. The escalation section shows the expected policy generation or clearly explains why escalatio

sections.heading: Change or undo creation
sections.text: Creating an incident is auditable and cannot be made as though it never happened. Correct supported incident fields if they were entered incorrectly. For an accidental exercise, add a clear timeline note and resolve it with an accurate summary; do not use deletion to hide the event.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: The service is missing Confirm that the service is active and that your role grants create access to it. Administrators with broader access can distinguish a missing service from a scope restriction. The form rejects a custom field Read the field-level error and provide a value of the configured type. Select fields must use a configured option; URL and email fields must be syntactically valid; num

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Acknowledge the incident when a responder takes ownership. - Assign the incident when the responsible user or team is known. - Review the complete incident lifecycle.

pages.title: Escalate an incident
pages.description: Request manual escalation from a capability-enabled Microsoft Teams card and verify the resulting pages safely.
pages.intro: Manual escalation asks OpsKnight to execute the current step of an open incident's escalation plan immediately. In 2.0, this action is exposed only by a capability-enabled Microsoft Teams Adaptive Card. The Web incident page is used to inspect the resulting state; it has no manual Escalate control. Standard Slack incident actions do not expose manual escalation.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: Before escalating, confirm: - The incident is Open . Human-requested escalation does not advance acknowledged, snoozed, suppressed, or resolved incidents. - The service has a valid escalation policy with at least one usable step. - You have incident.escalate.scoped or broader access to this incident. - The current step, next scheduled time, and target are appropriate. - The incident is not already

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open the current Microsoft Teams incident card in its configured service destination or war room. Confirm that the card shows Escalate . Its presence is capability- and phase-dependent; do not infer support from an old card.

sections.heading: Configure and request escalation
sections.text: Use the authenticated Microsoft Teams card that exposes Escalate . 1. Open the incident in OpsKnight Web and note its status and the Escalation field in the Details card. 2. In the current Microsoft Teams Adaptive Card, select Escalate once. 3. If prompted, confirm the incident identity. 4. Wait for the result before selecting the action again. 5. Return to the incident page and refresh its timeli

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text: Confirm all applicable outcomes: 1. The audit record identifies who requested manual escalation and the source channel. 2. The incident timeline includes the manual escalation request. 3. The current step and next escalation time reflect the engine result. 4. Resolved targets match the users, schedules, teams, or notification destinations configured on that policy step. 5. Notification history con

sections.heading: Safe retry behavior
sections.text: Microsoft Teams action execution carries an idempotency context internally. A repeated Teams intent reuses the durable operation result where applicable; reusing that key for a different incident or actor is rejected. If the UI times out, inspect the canonical incident timeline, audit log, and notification operations before retrying. Repeated clicks can make the response harder to interpret even t

sections.heading: Undo or correct an escalation
sections.text: An emitted page cannot be recalled. Acknowledge/resolve the incident or correct the policy/service configuration according to the real response state, notify mistakenly paged responders, and document the correction. Do not repeatedly escalate to compensate for an unknown first result.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Escalate is unavailable Confirm the incident is still Open , you can access it, and your role grants escalation. Teams also requires a linked responder identity and a current action card whose capability set and phase permit escalation. Web and standard Slack do not provide this action in 2.0. The result says the incident is not escalatable Refresh the incident. Another responder may have acknowle

sections.heading: Related guides
sections.text: - Configure an escalation policy - Acknowledge an incident - Inspect notification delivery - Incident response

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight serializes the request against current incident state and escalation generation, plans the current policy step, enqueues eligible notifications, and records the result. It does not make an invalid/empty policy usable or bypass authorization.

pages.title: Incident roles
pages.description: Give an incident a commander, ops lead, comms lead and scribe, and understand what each role may do.
pages.intro: Roles say who is doing what during a response. Each incident has four roles, and each role has at most one holder. One person may hold several roles. Role What they do Rights on the incident ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Incident commander Owns the response, makes t

sections.heading: Who can change roles
sections.text: - Responders and Admins can set or clear any role. - Anyone who can work the incident (assignee, on call for it, a member of the owning team, or the ops lead) can take a role themselves. - The commander can hand any role to someone else. - A holder can always step down from their own role.

sections.heading: Assign a role in the web app
sections.text: 1. Open the incident. The Roles chips sit under the title, next to the SLA chips. The Commander chip is always shown, and so is any role someone holds. On a P1 or P2 incident every role is shown; otherwise, if you can fill one of the empty roles, select + N more roles to show them. 2. Hover over a chip to see what the role is for and who holds it. An empty role shows a dashed chip with + and the r

sections.heading: Slack and Microsoft Teams
sections.text: In a war-room channel: /incident who lists the roles above the on-call steps. Role names accept commander (or ic ), ops-lead , comms-lead and scribe . A mentioned person must have a Slack email that matches an active OpsKnight account. Incident cards in Slack and Teams show the role holders and offer Take command until someone is commander. In Teams, Current responders lists the roles too.

sections.heading: Default roles on templates
sections.text: An incident template can name a default holder for each role ( Incidents → Templates → New template → Default Roles ). The roles are applied when an incident is declared from the template in the web app or the mobile app. A default holder whose account is no longer active is skipped.

sections.heading: API and MCP
sections.text: Operation REST v2 MCP tool ----------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ---------------------- List roles and holders GET /api/v2/incidents/{id}/roles incident roles list Assign a role ( { "userId": "…" } ) PUT /api/v2/incidents/{id}/roles/{roleKey} incident role assign Clear a role DELETE /api/v2/incidents/{id}/roles/{roleKey} discoverable operation roleKey

pages.title: Manage incident templates
pages.description: Create, use, and delete reusable incident defaults with the current 2.0 template workflow.
pages.intro: Incident templates provide reusable defaults for common response scenarios. In 2.0, the supported lifecycle is create, use, and delete . There is no template update/edit action; replace a stale template by creating its successor and then deleting the old one.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as an ADMIN or RESPONDER . Decide whether every permitted responder should see the template or only its creator, and confirm access to any default service.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Incidents → Templates . Select an existing template to use/delete, or New Template to create one.

sections.heading: Configure and create a template
sections.text: 1. Open Incidents → Templates . 2. Select New Template . 3. Enter a unique Template name between 3 and 100 characters. This identifies the template in the chooser. 4. Optionally enter an internal Description explaining when responders should use it. 5. Enter the default incident Title , between 5 and 255 characters. 6. Add optional incident description/runbook content. The form previews headings,

sections.heading: Visibility and ownership
sections.text: The listing returns public templates plus private templates created by the current user. ADMIN and RESPONDER can create templates. A non-admin can delete only a template they created; an administrator can delete any template. The creator relationship is ownership metadata. If you plan to disable or delete a creator, inventory private templates first and create public or replacement templates where

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight stores reusable defaults and applies them to the new-incident form. The resulting incident is independent: later template replacement/deletion does not rewrite incidents already created from it.

sections.heading: Verify the template
sections.text: Open Create incident , choose the new template, and confirm its title, description/runbook, urgency, priority, service, visibility, and ownership defaults populate as intended. Cancel the form or create a controlled test incident and verify the resulting incident.

sections.heading: Remove or replace a template
sections.text: Because 2.0 does not support editing: 1. Create a new template with a distinct temporary name and the corrected defaults. 2. Create a synthetic incident and verify every inherited value. 3. Communicate the replacement to responders and update runbooks that name the old template. 4. Delete the old template when it is no longer needed. 5. If desired, recreate the final name only after the old unique

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Create an incident - Respond to an incident - Template Name Conflict: names are unique; choose a different name or delete the obsolete template after validating its replacement. - Template is missing from the chooser: confirm it is public or owned by the current user and that the user can create an incident for the default service. - Delete is denied: only an administrator or the template creato

pages.title: Migrate the SLA scheduler to indexed mode
pages.description: Move safely from legacy scanning through shadow comparison to indexed SLA scheduling.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Back up PostgreSQL, confirm migration access, read Database migrations, and record current due transitions, missing hints, and scheduler health. Only an administrator can change mode.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → Incident SLA → Support & Schedules and locate SLA Scheduler .

sections.heading: Configure shadow mode
sections.text: 1. Leave production scheduling in LEGACY while installing the optional scheduler index with the documented installer. 2. Confirm the PostgreSQL index idx incident next sla transition exists and is valid. 3. Select SHADOW . This resets clean-check counters. 4. Monitor due counts, missing scheduling hints, shadow mismatch count, errors, and job cadence. 5. Investigate every mismatch; do not treat el

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: LEGACY uses the legacy selection path. SHADOW compares indexed candidates with legacy truth while preserving safe behavior and populating hints. INDEXED makes the indexed path authoritative. The transition action uses an advisory lock and refuses a direct LEGACY→INDEXED jump.

sections.heading: Verify indexed readiness
sections.text: Require the configured minimum consecutive clean checks, zero latest mismatches, a valid index, and zero active incidents missing scheduling hints. Then select INDEXED and verify due incidents transition on time without duplicate/missed SLA events.

sections.heading: Roll back
sections.text: If indexed behavior diverges, return to SHADOW or LEGACY , preserve logs and mismatch evidence, and confirm legacy scheduling resumes. Do not drop the index during incident response; it is optional in legacy/shadow and can aid diagnosis.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Run Shadow first: the current mode is not SHADOW . - Resolve mismatches: latest mismatch count is nonzero. - Wait for clean checks: the minimum consecutive comparisons has not completed. - Install index: the required PostgreSQL index is absent/invalid. - Missing hints: keep shadow running and inspect active incidents until the count reaches zero.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - System logs - Prometheus metrics

pages.title: Resolve an incident
pages.description: Close active response with an auditable resolution record and understand how correlated recurrence reopens work.
pages.intro: Resolve an incident only after service health is restored or the triggering condition is conclusively no longer actionable. Resolution ends active response and escalation, but preserves the timeline, first-response measurements, and prior lifecycle history.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: Before resolving, confirm: - The mitigation or permanent fix has been verified using service-level evidence. - Monitoring has remained healthy for the observation period your team requires. - The current owner and relevant responders agree that active response can end. - Required incident custom fields are complete. Human/operator resolution is blocked when required values are missing. - Important

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Incidents → select the incident . Resolve is on the right of the action bar, under the incident's title card. On a phone it is in the bar fixed to the bottom of the screen ( Resolve incident ) once the incident is acknowledged.

sections.heading: Configure and resolve the incident
sections.text: 1. Open the incident and review its latest Timeline entries, status, assignee, and response health. 2. Select Resolve . 3. Enter a resolution note from 10 to 1,000 characters. 4. State what recovered, what action caused or confirmed recovery, and any known remaining risk. Avoid unsupported root-cause conclusions; a postmortem can refine them later. 5. Select Resolve Incident in the dialog once and

sections.heading: Verify resolution
sections.text: Confirm: 1. Status is Resolved and the resolution timestamp is present. 2. The resolution summary shows the note and actor. 3. The timeline contains the terminal event. 4. The Escalation field in the Details card shows Completed and no next escalation is scheduled for the old generation. 5. First acknowledgement and other SLA history remain visible; resolution does not rewrite them. 6. Connected C

sections.heading: When the condition returns
sections.text: The 2.0 Web incident page has no manual Reopen action. Do not look for a button or describe a direct Web reopen procedure. If a new manual incident report is created with the same service and explicit deduplication key within the 30-minute reopen window, OpsKnight reopens the recently resolved incident. Normal monitoring and integration alert trigger ingestion does not reopen a resolved incident;

sections.heading: Undo or correct a resolution
sections.text: There is no Web undo button. If the same condition returned, use a manual creation report with the matching deduplication key within the 30-minute window or an authorized API status update to OPEN . If the resolution note is incomplete, preserve the original audit record and add corrective context to the timeline rather than rewriting history. Create a separate incident when the new event has a di

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Resolve is disabled Make the resolution note at least 10 characters and no more than 1,000. If the note is valid, complete every required custom field and verify your permission and incident scope. Resolution conflicts with another update Refresh and read the new state. Another responder may already have resolved, snoozed, suppressed, or otherwise changed the incident. Do not overwrite newer opera

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: Communicate final status, reconcile any public status incident, review delivery failures, and decide whether a postmortem is required. Track remediation through owned action items with due dates. See Track incident action items, Postmortem workflow, and the incident lifecycle.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight validates required custom fields and current state, records the resolution actor/summary/timing, ends active escalation, and reconciles notifications/ChatOps/status projections while preserving history.

pages.title: Respond to an incident end to end
pages.description: Follow the complete OpsKnight response journey from alert receipt through acknowledgement, ownership, communication, escalation, resolution, and follow-up.
pages.intro: Use this workflow during a real response or controlled exercise. OpsKnight is the authoritative incident state even when you receive and act through email, Slack, Teams, or another notification channel.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as a responder who can view/manage the service incident. Ensure your notification and ChatOps identities are current. Know the service runbook, current on-call/escalation policy, communication destination, and authority for resolving the event.

sections.heading: 1. Open and identify the incident
sections.text: 1. Follow the notification link or open Incidents . 2. Match title, service, environment/context, urgency, priority, and creation time. 3. Read the description, integration payload/context, timeline, SLA/response target, current escalation step, and recent related incidents. 4. Confirm whether the incident is a new failure, duplicate, recurrence, or controlled exercise. Do not act from an old prov

sections.heading: 2. Acknowledge active response
sections.text: Use Acknowledge when you accept response responsibility. Confirm the timeline attributes you and acknowledgement timing/escalation behavior is correct. Acknowledgement is not assignment or resolution. Follow Acknowledge an incident for valid states, concurrency, channel actions, and unacknowledgement.

sections.heading: 3. Assign operational ownership
sections.text: Set one responsible user or team. Assignment communicates coordination ownership but does not prove the assignee has seen/accepted the incident. For handoff, change assignment and record context in the timeline. Follow Assign an incident.

sections.heading: 4. Diagnose and communicate
sections.text: Use the service runbook and observability evidence to bound impact, time, affected users/components, and mitigations. Add concise notes for decisions and results on the Notes tab; the box is one line until you select it, then shows formatting, Preview and Post . The Timeline tab's Activity graph shows when alerts arrived relative to the trigger, and N alerts → 1 incident shows how they were dedupl

sections.heading: 5. Escalate from a supported Teams card when needed
sections.text: Escalate when the current response requires broader/faster attention and the next policy step is appropriate. In 2.0, manual escalation is available only from a capability-enabled Microsoft Teams Adaptive Card—the Web incident page has no manual Escalate control and standard Slack actions do not expose manual escalation. Outside Teams, assign or reassign the incident for immediate handoff. Inspect

sections.heading: 6. Track follow-up work
sections.text: During response, keep immediate operational steps in the timeline/coordination channel. Create action items for durable remediation, ownership, due dates, and optional Jira tracking. Do not hide unresolved response-critical work in a future action item.

sections.heading: 7. Resolve with evidence
sections.text: Resolve only after service health/trigger condition is verified and the observation period has passed. Complete required custom fields, record impact/mitigation/resolution summary, assign remaining action items, and confirm active escalation should end. Follow Resolve an incident. The Postmortem tab appears once the incident is resolved; until then a wide screen shows Postmortem after resolve at t

sections.heading: Verify the completed response
sections.text: Confirm: - final incident state and actor attribution are correct; - acknowledgement/assignment/escalation/resolution timeline is complete; - notifications and Slack/Teams projections converged; - status-page projection is correct when applicable; - action items have owners/dates; - SLA/response measurements and audit history are retained; - responders/customers receive the required closure commun

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Action is unavailable: verify incident current state, user permission/scope, required fields, and concurrent changes. Provider message differs from OpsKnight: treat OpsKnight as authoritative, inspect delivery/projection operation, and reconcile rather than manually fabricating a second message. Escalation or notification is delayed: inspect lane/provider delivery state and oldest queue age; do no

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Review the postmortem/follow-up workflow and action items. - Test the service's on-call, escalation, and notification delivery before the next event.

pages.title: Integration tasks
pages.description: Create, test, and troubleshoot inbound alert integrations, and where the copied integration URLs get their hostname.
pages.intro: Start with the provider page in the integration catalog. After saving the integration, send a test event and verify service mapping, deduplication, urgency, and recovery behavior. If the request is rejected, use integration troubleshooting.

sections.heading: Where the copied URL comes from
sections.text: On a service's Integrations tab, the webhook URL you copy for a provider, the Events API endpoint and the cURL sample all start with OpsKnight's Application URL , resolved in this order: 1. Settings → System → App URL , when an administrator has saved one. 2. NEXT PUBLIC APP URL . 3. NEXTAUTH URL . 4. http://localhost:3000 . A trailing slash on the saved value is ignored, so the copied URL never c

pages.title: Send a test event from the UI
pages.description: Validate an integration key and trigger, acknowledge, and resolve one deduplicated test incident.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Create or obtain a service integration key and use a non-production test window. Treat the key as a secret. Choose one unique deduplication key and reuse it for the full trigger/acknowledge/resolve sequence.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Events → Send Test Alert ( /events/test ). Get the key from Services → service → Manage Integrations .

sections.heading: Configure and send the event
sections.text: 1. Paste the integration key. 2. Select trigger , enter a unique deduplication key, meaningful summary, and severity ( critical , error , warning , or info ). 3. Select Send Test Alert and inspect both HTTP status and JSON response. 4. Find the created incident and confirm service, summary, severity mapping, and dedup key. 5. Return to the test UI, keep the same key/dedup key, send acknowledge , t

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: The UI calls POST /api/events with Authorization: Token token= and a PagerDuty-style event envelope. Matching dedup keys address the same incident lifecycle; changing the key creates or targets a different correlation.

sections.heading: Verify the test
sections.text: Require successful responses for all three actions and one incident whose timeline shows trigger, acknowledgment, and resolution. Review event logs for the request outcome.

sections.heading: Remove or undo
sections.text: Resolve the synthetic incident. Rotate the integration key if it was exposed. Test events are operational records and should not be deleted merely to hide a failed test.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Integration key required/unauthorized: copy the correct service key without whitespace and confirm it is active. - New incident on every action: reuse the exact dedup key. - Error response: read the JSON error code/correlation ID and inspect Events/System Logs.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Events API - Integration catalog

pages.title: Read the AIOps overview
pages.description: See what Intelligence and the noise controls did for your incidents, and fix noisy services from one page.
pages.intro: Open AIOps Overview in the Analytics section of the main navigation, or go to /intelligence . Administrators, responders and auditors can open it. Pick a window at the top: 24h , 7d (the default) or 30d . The window is part of the address, so you can share a link to the same view. Everything on the page covers only the services and incidents you can already open. If your access is limited to your

sections.text: When something is waiting for a decision, a Needs attention list appears above the sections. Each row opens the place where you make that decision. When nothing is waiting, the list is not shown. - Triage : open incidents with triage suggestions nobody has accepted or dismissed, from the last seven days. The row opens the incident. - Related incidents : open incidents with related or duplicate sug

Higher means more alerts were folded into fewer incidents. - Pages avoided : alerts that noise controls actually held back (suppressed, dropped, appended to an open incident or grouped under a parent). Only controls in On mode count here. - Would have avoided : what controls in Shadow mode would have held

sections.heading: Alert quality
sections.text: The noisiest and the most flapping services over the last 30 days, using the same ranking as Settings Intelligence Services & changes Alert quality . A service needs at least five incidents to be ranked. Administrators get one-click fixes on each row: - Create suppression rule opens Noise controls for that service. - Lower severity opens the service's routing and severity settings. - Open Jira iss

sections.text: - Change-linked incidents : incidents in the window that have a suggested change cause, and their share of all incidents. - Changes recorded , and how many have a risk score. - Riskiest recent changes , with a labelled band (high, medium or low risk) and the score. Risk ranks changes by how often similar changes were followed by an incident; it is not a verdict. - Recent change-linked incidents ,

sections.text: Mean time to acknowledge and mean time to resolve for incidents opened in the window, with the change against the window before it (for example "−20% vs previous 7d", marked better or worse). Two small charts show both windows per hour (24h) or per day (7d and 30d), times in UTC. Show data table lists every value.

sections.text: Whether the Intelligence lane on the instance serving the page is healthy, degraded (with the reason) or not running there, and the shared work backlog: ready, running, oldest waiting and failed work. Use Open Intelligence settings to replay failed work.

sections.heading: On a phone
sections.text: In the mobile app, open More AIOps ( /m/intelligence ). It shows Needs attention and Noise with the same window picker. The other sections are on the desktop overview.

sections.heading: When Intelligence is off
sections.text: If the Intelligence master switch is off, the page says so at the top. Administrators get a link to turn it on. Noise, alert quality and response times still show, because they do not depend on it.

pages.title: Browse alerts and changes
pages.description: List every alert with what the noise controls did to it, and every recorded change with its risk score and linked incidents.
pages.intro: Alerts and Changes are in the main navigation, under Runbooks. Administrators, responders and auditors can open them. Both pages only read data, and both show only what you can already open: if your access is limited to your teams, you see your teams' services only. Both lists are newest first and show the last 24 hours until you pick another time range (24 hours, 7 days or 30 days). Filters are p

sections.heading: Alerts
sections.text: Go to /alerts . Each row shows: - the alert's summary (opens the alert) and, when the alert opened or joined an incident, Open incident ; - the service and the severity the integration sent; - up to four labels , with a count of the rest; - the noise decision , if a noise control acted on the alert before paging, and the rule or window that made it: - Suppressed : a suppression or orchestration ru

sections.heading: Changes
sections.text: Go to /changes . Each row shows: - the change's summary (opens the change), its kind (deploy, config, feature flag or infra) and version; - the source that reported it and the service it belongs to, or No service ; - its risk : a labelled band (high, medium or low) with the score, or Not scored . Risk ranks changes by how often similar changes were followed by an incident. It is a signal for where

sections.heading: On a phone
sections.text: Both pages work at phone width: the service, severity, decision, risk and time fold under the summary, and every row link is at least 44 px tall.

pages.title: Confirm actions the assistant suggests
pages.description: Turn on extended assistant actions and confirm escalations, urgency changes, snoozes, watchers, Jira issues, status updates, runbook runs and changes beyond incidents (overrides, maintenance windows, services) from Squire.
pages.intro: Squire never changes anything by itself. When it suggests an action it shows a card that says exactly what will happen. Nothing happens until you press the card's button, and the change then runs with your own permissions, through the same code as the matching button in OpsKnight, and is audited. By default Squire can suggest acknowledging, resolving, adding a note, reassigning and marking inciden

sections.heading: Turn on extended actions (administrators)
sections.text: 1. Open Settings → Intelligence → Assistant . 2. Select Extended assistant actions and save. Turning it off again withdraws any card that is still open: confirming it then reports that the action is turned off.

sections.heading: If a card is refused
sections.text: - Expired : cards are valid for 10 minutes. Ask again. - The incident changed after this suggestion was prepared : someone acknowledged it, changed the urgency, edited the draft, reconfigured the runbook binding, and so on. Review the incident and ask for a fresh card. - Pressing the button twice, or reloading, never repeats the action: the card shows the recorded result. If the result is unknown

sections.heading: Changes beyond incidents
sections.text: With extended actions on, Squire can also suggest changes outside an incident, such as adding a schedule override, creating a maintenance window, renaming a service or setting its escalation policy, tagging an incident, editing a postmortem, or updating an SLO, a dashboard or a status page. It finds the operation in the same reviewed API catalog the MCP server uses, and you get a card with: - what

sections.heading: High-risk changes
sections.text: Deleting a service, schedule, team or escalation policy, and similar changes, are offered only if your role allows them. The card is marked High-risk change , its button reads Confirm high-risk change , and it says that Squire cannot undo it. It runs as you the moment you confirm, like the same action in OpsKnight, and is audited.

sections.heading: Several changes at once
sections.text: When a request needs two to five related changes (for example "create a Payments service and a maintenance window for it"), Squire can suggest them as one Plan card. Each step is listed with the fields it sets; a value that comes from an earlier step (such as the new service's id) shows as from-step-1 . Every step must be a change your role allows, or no card is shown. Apply all runs the steps in

sections.heading: Review what was done
sections.text: Settings → Squire Action History ( /settings/intelligence/ai/actions ) lists every action confirmed from a Squire card, newest first: when, the action, its status (succeeded, failed, unknown or in progress) and the recorded outcome, with a link to the incident. You see your own actions; people who manage intelligence settings can switch to Everyone to see who confirmed what. Filter by status, and

pages.title: Use Squire without an AI provider
pages.description: Ask permission-scoped operational questions and get product guidance in basic mode.
pages.intro: The assistant is on by default ( Settings → Intelligence → Assistant → Show the assistant ), and the Enable AI switch stays off until an administrator turns it on. Basic mode uses deterministic language rules, product instructions and fresh OpsKnight database reads. It does not call a language model, run commands or send a page, and it changes an incident only when you confirm a card it prepared.

sections.heading: Catch me up
sections.text: Ask Catch me up (or “What did I miss?”, or type /catchup ) at the start of a shift. Squire answers for you, from your own access: - The window. By default it starts when your last on-call shift ended, on any schedule you can see and in the last 7 days. If you are on call now, or had no shift, it covers the last 12 hours. Name a window to override it: “catch me up on the past 24 hours”, “since Mond

sections.heading: Understanding, names and clarifications
sections.text: Basic mode tolerates everyday phrasing. Typos in common words are corrected (“incidnets”, “postmortms”), and service, team and person names are matched to the closest one you can see , so “who owns chekout api” answers for Checkout API and says so. When several names fit, Squire lists them and waits for your choice; reply with the name or its number. When a question could mean two things, Squire o

sections.heading: Actions you confirm
sections.text: On an incident page, ask for an action in plain words or with a shortcut and Squire prepares a confirmation card . Nothing changes until you press Confirm, and the change runs with your own permissions through the same commands as the incident page. Say Card ------------------------------------------------------ ---------------------- “acknowledge this” or /ack Acknowledge “resolve this: rolled ba

sections.heading: Suggested checks and feedback
sections.text: Incident answers include suggested checks : investigation prompts chosen by the incident title. Administrators can add their own in Settings → Intelligence → Assistant → Suggested checks (a title pattern and up to six checks); theirs match before the built-in ones. They are prompts only and never run anything. Each answer has thumbs up and down. A thumbs down asks for a short reason. Only the mode

sections.heading: Answers that finish in the background
sections.text: A long answer, such as an investigation, does not need you to wait for it. While Squire is answering, select Keep working in the background under the conversation. Squire stops streaming in the panel, finishes the answer on the server, saves it to the same conversation, and sends you an in-app notification: “Squire finished: your question ” (with your assistant’s name). The notification opens the

sections.heading: Reporting limits
sections.text: Calendar expressions such as today, yesterday, this week and this month use your profile timezone and are labelled in the answer. “Last week” and “past week” mean the past seven days. Rolling windows are supported up to 90 days. Resolution and acknowledgement searches use their recorded event timestamps; ordinary searches use incident creation time. Listings show five results per page by default (

pages.title: See noise decisions and groups on incidents and incident lists

pages.intro: Noise controls (maintenance windows, suppression rules, storm grouping and the others under Settings › Intelligence › Noise controls ) decide before paging whether an alert pages, is grouped under an open incident, or is suppressed. These screens show those decisions where responders work. Everything here respects incident visibility: you only see incidents, parents and precedents you can already

View group opens the Related and group section of the Investigation panel (see Use Intelligence suggestions), which holds the full group view. The line is not shown when intelligence is off for the service. - A mini t

sections.text: With Show intelligence events on (at the end of the filter chips in the Timeline tab's Events view), the timeline also shows, as rows of the same list: - Noise decisions on this incident's alerts: suppressed by a rule, in a maintenance window, deduplicated, grouped into a parent, held during a possible storm. Why? expands the reasons. Shadow-mode decisions are labelled "Shadow" and changed nothing

sections.text: After Summarise this incident (in the Summary section of the Investigation panel) produces a summary, Post summary as note adds it to the incident's notes through the normal note command. Insert summary in the note box's toolbar on the Notes tab (shown once you select the box) drafts the same summary into your note so you can edit it first. It needs the same permission as writing a note (responder

N grouped This incident is a parent with N grouped incidents or alerts. Suppressed by An applied, unreversed suppression, flapping or orches

sections.text: The wallboard ( /wallboard ) shows a Noise reduction tile with the last 24 hours: pages avoided (or, when every policy is in shadow mode, what would be avoided), alerts per incident, grouped alerts and how many were ungrouped, and missing heartbeats. It is shown to roles that may read intelligence. When noise controls are off the tile says so, and administrators get a link to turn them on. The til

pages.title: Investigate incidents with Squire and route models by task
pages.description: Turn on investigation mode, choose which model handles planning and conclusions, and read an investigation answer.
pages.intro: Investigation mode lets the assistant work through a diagnostic question in several steps: it decides what to check, reads several sources at once, and answers with ranked hypotheses tied to the evidence it read. It needs AI to be enabled with at least one provider cleared for Personal data. It is off by default .

sections.heading: Turn it on
sections.text: 1. Open Settings → Intelligence → Assistant (requires the Intelligence manage permission). 2. In Investigation and model routing , select Investigation mode . 3. Optionally route capabilities (below), then select Save investigation and routing . The change is audited as intelligence.ai.routing.updated . If someone else saved AI settings since you opened the page, the save is refused; refresh and t

sections.heading: Ask for an investigation
sections.text: Ask a diagnostic question, usually on an incident page: - "Why is checkout returning 500s?" - "What caused this incident?" - "Investigate the root cause." Questions that ask for a fact or an action ("who is on call?", "acknowledge this") are answered the usual way. A vague symptom question on an incident ("is the latency spike related to the deploy?") is checked by a quick classification call firs

sections.heading: Read the answer
sections.text: - Ranked hypotheses , most likely first, each with a confidence (the model's estimate, not proof) and links to the evidence that supports it. Only sources read during this answer can be cited; an explanation that cited nothing it read is left out and counted. - An evidence level for each hypothesis: speculation, matches a past pattern, supported by evidence, validated by system state, or validated

sections.heading: Automatic investigations
sections.text: Squire can start one investigation by itself when a high-urgency incident opens, so the diagnosis is waiting when responders arrive. It is off by default and set per service: 1. Open the service's Squire settings ( Settings → Intelligence → Services → the service → Squire ). 2. Select Investigate high-urgency incidents automatically , then Save . The change is audited with the service's other proa

sections.heading: Did the fix hold?
sections.text: When you resolve an incident through Squire (an incident action, or the resolve change from the operation catalog, on its own or in a plan) or start a runbook through Squire, Squire checks back 10 minutes later and writes the result on the incident: - Holding: no new alerts in the window. - Not holding: for example "3 new alerts since resolve, the incident reopened, new incident "Checkout down aga

sections.text: Each capability can prefer one provider, and optionally a specific model on it: Capability Used for Typical choice ----------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------- -------------------- Assistant conversation Ordinary answers Your default model Summaries Summarising earlier turns of long saved conversations A small model Investigation conclusions Ranke

sections.heading: Long conversations
sections.text: With saved history on, the last ten turns are replayed as before. Earlier turns are now summarised (by the Summaries route when AI is on, or by a short built-in digest) instead of being dropped. The incident briefing always stays first.

pages.title: Build noise controls and test them against the last week
pages.description: Schedule maintenance windows, write suppression and orchestration rules, add heartbeat monitors, and replay each against the last 7 days before saving.
pages.intro: Open Settings › Intelligence › Noise controls . Anyone with intelligence read access sees the controls, the agenda and the recorded decisions; only intelligence managers can create, change or preview them. Every builder has a Test against the last 7 days button that replays recent incidents with only that control switched on and tells you how many would not have paged. A preview never saves anythi

sections.heading: Maintenance windows
sections.text: Schedule maintenance asks for a name, what it applies to (one service, a team's services, alerts with a label, or everything), the effect (suppress, or page at a lower urgency) and when it runs. Pick a start and a two-hour end is filled in; change it if you need to. A window lasts at most seven days. Repeats offers every day, every week on the start day, every weekday, every weekend, every month o

sections.heading: Suppression rules
sections.text: Add one or more conditions; all of them must match. Each condition picks a field (severity, source, summary, resource, a label, the content fingerprint or the dedup key), an operator (equals, contains, starts with, matches regex, exists) and a value. Matching ignores case. Regular expressions with back-references or nested quantifiers are refused. While you type, the builder counts how many of the

sections.heading: Orchestration rules
sections.text: Orchestration rules are part of the policy and are saved with Save policy . They run top to bottom: the first rule that drops or suppresses an alert wins, and other actions (set urgency, set severity, set a label, route to another service, attach a runbook, add a note) accumulate. Reorder with the arrow buttons, by dragging the handle, or by focusing the handle and pressing the up or down arrow ke

sections.heading: Heartbeat monitors
sections.text: Create a monitor for a scheduled job: its service, how often it should ping, a grace period and the urgency of the incident raised when it goes missing. The ping URL, the token and an example curl command are shown once , each with a Copy button; only a hash of the token is stored. Each monitor shows its status (waiting for first ping, healthy, late, missing, paused), its last ping, when the next

sections.heading: Intelligence on your phone
sections.text: The mobile incident page has a strip of chips, scrolling sideways, directly under the incident's actions; on a desktop the same chips sit in the AI briefing card. Select a chip to open Investigation as a sheet from the bottom: triage suggestions you can apply or dismiss, similar past incidents, related incidents and the group, possible causes, runbooks that have worked on this service, impact and

sections.text: Open a service and choose Intelligence , or go to /services/ /intelligence . The tab loads only when you open it. Each section loads on its own: if one fails it shows a short error and the others still appear. Sections without data are left out; if none has data the tab says "Nothing to report yet". - SLO burn : for each availability or uptime objective, how fast the error budget was spent over th

Hover for the window's name. - SLO burning or SLO burning fast : the availability error budget is being spent faster than planned, or at a paging rate. - Noise controls on or Noise controls: shadow : the mode that applies to the service. When the team has a daily budget, the tile shows how much of it is used and says when it is close to (80%) or at the limit. Administrators get a link to Spend and budgets . - Noise load : alerts received against incidents created for the team's services o

sections.text: The Ops Pulse panel ends with an AIOps pulse row when at least one of these is above zero: - Pages avoided in the last 24 hours by noise controls in On mode (reversed decisions excluded). - Open groups : open or acknowledged incidents that have other incidents grouped under them. - Triage to review : triage suggestions (urgency, owner, duplicate) from the last seven days on open incidents that nob

pages.title: Ask Squire in Slack, Microsoft Teams, MCP and on mobile
pages.description: Turn on Squire outside the web app, ask it in Slack channels and war rooms, confirm its suggestions with a button, and use ask_squire from an AI assistant.
pages.intro: Squire answers the same way everywhere: in basic mode without AI, or with AI when a provider is configured. It always uses your own OpsKnight permissions , cites what it relied on, and never changes anything until you confirm a suggestion yourself.

sections.heading: Turn it on
sections.text: An administrator opens Settings → Intelligence → Assistant . The assistant itself must be on. Under Assistant outside the web app , each surface has its own switch, all off by default: Switch What it adds --------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Slack and Microsoft Teams @OpsKnight in Slack channels (and in incident war roo

sections.text: Mention the OpsKnight app in any channel it is in, or in an incident channel: - @OpsKnight what changed before this started? Squire replies in the thread, visible to the channel. In an incident channel it knows which incident the room is about; in any other channel it answers as a general question. - /incident ask is this related to yesterday's outage? Squire replies only to you, in a war room. Be

sections.heading: Microsoft Teams
sections.text: In an incident war room, mention the OpsKnight bot with your question. Squire replies in the thread. Your Teams account must be linked to OpsKnight (automatically through Entra ID, or with the account-link prompt the incident cards show). Squire answers only in incident war rooms.

sections.heading: Confirm a suggestion from chat
sections.text: When Squire suggests a change (for example "Acknowledge the incident"), the reply carries Confirm and Dismiss buttons (Slack) or a Confirm action (Teams). - Only the person who asked can confirm. Anyone else gets a private message and nothing changes. - Confirming runs the same command and permission checks as the button in OpsKnight. If the incident changed since the suggestion, or your access ch

sections.heading: MCP: ask squire
sections.text: With the MCP switch on, an AI assistant connected to OpsKnight sees an ask squire tool, if its connection was granted the read permissions for incidents, services, schedules, teams, runbooks and postmortems. Pass a question and optionally an incidentId . The answer never reads more than the connection could read itself. Squire looks up people only if the connection also has users:read , escalation

sections.heading: Mobile
sections.text: With the mobile switch on, an Ask Squire button appears on mobile incident pages. It opens full screen and already knows which incident you are looking at.

sections.heading: Page context in the web app
sections.text: Squire knows the page you opened it on: an incident, service, team, schedule, runbook, alert or change. On a change page, "this service" means the service the change was recorded on. A page you cannot read is ignored. The line under the panel header says what the conversation is about: Discussing this incident , this service , this team , this runbook , this schedule , this alert or this change ,

sections.heading: Mention records with @
sections.text: Type @ and at least two letters in the message box to pick an incident, service, schedule, team, runbook or person from the same search as the command palette. Use the arrow keys and Enter (or click) to pick one, and Escape to close the list. The pick is written into your question, such as @Checkout API , and shown as a chip above the box; remove a chip to leave that record out. You can mention up

sections.heading: Dock Squire beside the page
sections.text: On a desktop-width window (1024 px and wider) the panel can sit beside the page instead of on top of it. - Select Dock beside the page in the panel header. The panel becomes a full-height column on the right and the page narrows to make room, so nothing is covered. Select Float over the page to go back. - Your choice is remembered in this browser, like the side the floating panel opens on. - If yo

sections.heading: Pinned incident briefing
sections.text: While the conversation is about an incident, an Incident briefing is pinned above the messages: the likely changes, the most similar past incidents and the runbooks that worked, up to three of each. Each row opens that finding in the incident's insights. Select the heading to collapse or expand it; the panel remembers which you prefer. The briefing is not shown when there is nothing to show: the s

sections.heading: Ask from the command palette
sections.text: Type a question in the search box at the top of the app ( / or ⌘K / Ctrl+K ). Ask Squire appears when the text names the assistant, starts with ask , or reads as a question (it ends with ? or starts with a question word). The entry shows the question it will ask; choosing it opens the panel and asks it straight away. Typing only the assistant's name opens the panel without asking anything.

sections.heading: Links that open Squire
sections.text: Add ?squire=open&q= to any app address to open the panel with that question written in the message box, for example /incidents/ ?squire=open&q=What%20changed%3F . The question is not sent until you send it, so opening a link never starts a conversation or spends AI budget on your behalf. The two parameters are removed from the address once the panel has opened. Links to a single finding use /incid

sections.heading: Charts in answers
sections.text: When Squire reads metrics to answer you (the query metrics read of a connected Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch or base14 Scout backend), it draws the series as a line chart under the answer. This works in ordinary AI answers and in step-by-step investigations. - The chart is built from what the metrics read returned, never from the model's text, so it shows exactly the numbers the answer

sections.heading: Help Squire learn
sections.text: Under every finished answer, rate it with 👍 or 👎. With 👎 you can say what went wrong ( Wrong facts , Missed the point , Too long , Wrong action or Other ) and add a note of up to 300 characters. Leave out secrets: the note is kept as you wrote it. Squire stores the rating, the reason and note, the answer mode and a digest of your question, never the question or answer text. When you asked on an

sections.heading: Language
sections.text: With AI, Squire replies in the language you wrote in. Record names, ids, commands, queries and links stay exactly as they are. Basic mode (no AI) always answers in English.

pages.title: Use Intelligence suggestions and the assistant

On a phone it is one row of chips under the action bar, the strip , and the same panel.

sections.text: Use the thumbs next to a similar incident. If it was not helpful, pick a reason. Your rating is yours to change or withdraw. Ratings help administrators tune how strict matching is.

pages.title: Jira tasks
pages.description: Connect Jira and validate issue creation from OpsKnight incidents.
pages.intro: Use Connect Jira for the end-to-end administrator workflow. Provider details, webhook behavior, permissions, and failure diagnosis are in the Jira integration section.

pages.title: Connect Jira
pages.description: Link OpsKnight services and incidents to Jira projects and issues.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Complete the prerequisites in Connect Jira, including a restricted Jira identity, reachable HTTPS base URL, target project/issue type, and accepted required fields.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → Integrations → Jira and keep a synthetic OpsKnight service and incident ready.

sections.heading: Configure the end-to-end workflow
sections.text: 1. Follow Connect Jira to save encrypted credentials and pass the connection test. 2. Map the synthetic service to the intended Jira project and issue type. 3. Follow Configure Jira webhooks and send a controlled webhook test. 4. Open the synthetic incident and select Link Jira Issue in the action bar under the title card, then Create Jira Issue . 5. Change one supported field from OpsKnight and v

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: Rendering an incident performs no hidden Jira request. Explicit actions, webhooks, and background work update persisted link/sync state. Connection, project mapping, field validation, and webhook delivery therefore need separate verification.

sections.heading: Verify the integration
sections.text: Require the expected Jira key, URL, project, issue type, status, assignee, and last sync direction/time. Confirm repeated webhook delivery does not create a duplicate link or transition. On the incident, linked issues share one Jira button in the action bar. It shows the first issue's key and status, and +N when more are linked. Select it to see every linked issue with its assignee and last sync,

sections.heading: Disconnect or undo
sections.text: Stop webhook delivery, remove/disable mappings, and rotate/revoke credentials according to Jira troubleshooting. Existing Jira issues are not automatically deleted.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Capture the OpsKnight incident ID, Jira key, direction, operation time, correlation ID, and sanitized provider response. Then use the dedicated troubleshooting guide.

pages.title: MCP security and data
pages.description: What reaches your AI assistant's vendor, what the assistant can see, what is always removed, what OpsKnight stores and logs, and the controls.
pages.intro: This page is for the people deciding whether to turn MCP on. The short version: OpsKnight keeps your data in your PostgreSQL, but whatever an assistant reads is sent to that assistant and its model vendor .

sections.heading: Data flow
sections.text: Every tool or resource result goes back to the assistant client and, from there, to its model vendor: incident titles and notes, alert payload summaries, display names, runbook text and anything else the assistant reads. How long the vendor keeps it, and whether it trains on it, depends on your contract with that vendor, not on OpsKnight. Choose assistants and plans whose data terms you accept.

sections.heading: What an assistant can see
sections.text: At most what the signed-in person can see, and usually less. On every request: The permissions reference lists every scope and the roles that can use it. whoami never returns an email address.

sections.heading: What is always removed
sections.text: Results pass through a recursive projection before they leave the server. It removes: - Any field whose name contains secret , password , token , credential , authorization , apikey (with or without a separator), signedurl (with or without a separator), email , phone , payload , rawOutput , stdout , stderr (in any letter case), and any field named exactly definition , config , inputValues , execut

sections.heading: What OpsKnight stores and logs
sections.text: - Connections: grant, token and consent metadata. Tokens are stored only as keyed HMAC digests, never as bearer strings. Expired grant, code, token and consent records are removed after a seven-day replay-detection window. Automatically registered assistants that never signed anyone in are deleted after 30 days. - Reviewed changes: the frozen request is stored as an encrypted envelope until it is

sections.heading: Controls
sections.text: - Enable MCP (Access policy) turns every MCP surface off at once; MCP FORCE DISABLED=true does the same from the deployment, whatever the stored policy says. - Allow reviewed sensitive configuration reads is off by default. - Changes are off by default; configuration changes and runbook runs always wait for a person to approve them in OpsKnight, and an assistant can never approve. - Exposed capabi

pages.title: MCP setup for any self-hosted OpsKnight
pages.description: Turn on AI assistant access, connect assistants, manage connections and review the changes assistants propose.
pages.intro: The same setup applies to Docker, Compose, Swarm, Kubernetes and virtual machines. There is no OpsKnight-hosted registration service, special test domain or separate MCP secret. Your installation publishes its own endpoint and OAuth discovery from its configured App URL. Everything below lives on one page: Settings → Integrations & ChatOps → MCP (AI Assistants) . Its tabs are Overview , Connect ,

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: - Turning MCP on and changing the access policy needs an OpsKnight administrator who signed in within the last two hours. - Users need their own OpsKnight account and an MCP-capable assistant; each signs in as themselves. - OpsKnight must be served from an HTTPS origin that users (and any cloud-hosted assistant) can reach. That origin becomes the App URL .

sections.heading: Administrator: turn it on (about two minutes)

sections.heading: Access policy
sections.text: The Access policy tab holds: - Assistant access : Enable MCP and Automatic connections . - What assistants may do : the permission ceiling. People can approve less on the consent page, and their own OpsKnight permissions always apply on top. - Reviewed actions : changes, the review window and commit window, and sensitive configuration reads. - Sign-in sessions : how long an unused connection stays

sections.heading: Limits an assistant can meet
sections.text: Three separate limits apply, and they are not the same number: - Weighted operations per minute per grant ( Advanced , Workload limits ; 60 by default; a connection is a grant). It is weighted, so a tool that makes several reads in one call counts as several. The optional Requests per minute for one person cap applies across all of that person's connections. Over the limit, the answer is HTTP 429

pages.description: Connect clients that only run local stdio MCP servers, or cannot do remote OAuth, to a self-hosted OpsKnight with the opsknight-mcp bridge.
pages.intro: Some MCP clients only start local servers over standard input and output (stdio), or cannot complete a remote OAuth sign-in. opsknight-mcp is a small local program that such a client starts like any other stdio server. sections.heading: Get the bridge
sections.text: The bridge is not published to a package registry. It lives in the OpsKnight repository under sdk/mcp-bridge . Copy that folder to the machine that runs your MCP client and run node /bin/opsknight-mcp.js , or link it once with npm link from inside the folder to get an opsknight-mcp command. The bridge refuses plain http:// addresses except localhost and 127.0.0.1 , so your token never crosses a ne

sections.text: Choose one: - Personal access token (an administrator must allow personal tokens). Create one under Settings → Integrations & ChatOps → MCP → Connections → Personal access tokens and give it to the bridge in the OPSKNIGHT TOKEN environment variable. Tokens start with okmcp pat . See API-hosted and headless agents. - Device sign-in (an administrator must turn on Device sign-in , and either Automati

sections.heading: Configure your client
sections.text: The command is the same for every stdio client: opsknight-mcp --url , with OPSKNIGHT TOKEN in the environment if you use a personal token. If opsknight-mcp is not on the client's PATH , use node as the command and the full path to bin/opsknight-mcp.js as the first argument. Claude Desktop ( claude desktop config.json , under Settings → Developer → Edit Config ): Leave out env after opsknight-mcp l

sections.heading: Verify the connection
sections.text: 1. Restart or reload your client so it starts the bridge. 2. Ask the assistant "Who am I in OpsKnight, and what can you do for me?". It calls whoami and answers with your role, teams and enabled tools. 3. If the call fails, read the bridge's diagnostics on standard error (your client's MCP log) and see Troubleshooting.

sections.heading: Options
sections.text: Option Meaning ----------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --url Your OpsKnight address (or OPSKNIGHT URL ). A trailing /mcp is accepted. --toolsets a,b Sends X-OpsKnight-Toolsets: a,b so the server offers only those groups of tools, where the server supports it. --channel Claude Code only: pushes your new pages

sections.heading: What the bridge does
sections.text: - Each line the client writes is one HTTP POST /mcp with your bearer token and the protocol headers the server expects: MCP-Protocol-Version (the version in the request's meta , otherwise the one agreed in initialize ), Mcp-Method , and Mcp-Name for tool calls, prompts, resource reads and tasks. - JSON answers and streamed ( text/event-stream ) answers are both written back, one message per line.

sections.heading: Pages in Claude Code (channel)
sections.text: Claude Code channels let a local MCP server push events into a running session. With --channel , the bridge declares the claude/channel capability, holds a subscriptions/listen stream for opsknight://oncall/me/pages and turns each update into a notifications/claude/channel event, so Claude learns that you were paged and can look with oncall catch up . The server ends each stream after ten minutes;

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Refusing http://… : use the https:// address. - No credentials for … : set OPSKNIGHT TOKEN or run opsknight-mcp login . - Device sign-in is turned off on this server : ask an administrator, or use a personal token. - Error codes the server returns are listed in troubleshooting.

pages.title: Understand mobile offline state and updates
pages.description: Distinguish cached, queued, failed, and confirmed mobile state and recover safely after reconnecting.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Treat the server as authoritative. Cached data and locally stored drafts support continuity, but they do not prove a responder action reached OpsKnight.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: The mobile shell displays network and queue banners. Open a banner to inspect pending/failed actions when controls are available.

sections.heading: Configure safe offline use
sections.text: 1. When You're offline. View-only mode appears, use cached pages only for context. 2. Do not tell other responders an action succeeded unless it becomes confirmed after reconnect. 3. Incident creation drafts are encrypted and saved on-device, but creation is not queued while offline. 4. After reconnecting, let Background Sync/page replay run and inspect the queue summary. 5. Treat queued as not ye

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: The page coordinator and service worker coordinate queue restoration/flush. Authentication failure pauses unsafe replay and can redirect to mobile login. Cached-data notices identify stale content; online events trigger recovery but do not make every queued mutation valid.

sections.heading: Verify recovery
sections.text: Require zero pending/failed actions, reload key incidents, and compare their timeline/status with the intended outcome. For a PWA update, close all app windows, reopen, and confirm the new service worker controls the page.

sections.heading: Remove or reset
sections.text: Sign out before clearing site data when possible. Clearing browser storage removes cached data, encrypted drafts, and local queue state; record unresolved actions first. Reinstall only after confirming there is no unsubmitted work.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Queue stays pending: keep one app window online and authenticated, then refresh once. - Queue failed: inspect the action; authorization or lifecycle state may have changed. - Old UI after release: close all windows and reopen; if needed remove/reinstall after preserving drafts. - Draft missing: site-data cleanup, browser eviction, or a different profile/device may have removed local storage.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Install and enable push - Respond on mobile

pages.title: Respond to incidents on mobile
pages.description: Triage, acknowledge, and follow incidents safely from OpsKnight's mobile experience.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Confirm you are signed in as the intended responder and have incident permissions. Use a reliable connection for state-changing actions; the offline banner explicitly places the application in view-only mode.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Tap a push notification, or open Incidents from the mobile navigation. Filter/search the list and select the incident.

sections.heading: Configure and perform the response
sections.text: 1. Confirm service, urgency, priority, status, assignee, timestamps, and current responder ownership. 2. Acknowledge only after you accept response responsibility. 3. Refresh and confirm the server state changed. 4. Follow relevant service, team, schedule, policy, status, analytics, and postmortem views from mobile navigation. 5. Resolve only after recovery is verified through the source and runbo

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: Mobile routes apply the same server authorization and incident lifecycle as desktop. Notifications deep-link to /m/incidents/ . Cached list/detail data may be displayed during a network interruption, but it is labelled and is not proof of current state.

sections.heading: Verify the response
sections.text: Require a confirmed server status after acknowledgment/resolution, then cross-check the incident timeline or another connected session. A disappearing spinner alone is not confirmation.

sections.heading: Undo or correct
sections.text: Incident lifecycle actions are audited and may not be reversible. If an incorrect transition occurs, add context through the supported incident workflow and escalate rather than modifying storage directly.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Action unavailable: check connectivity, current status, permission, and whether another responder already changed it. - Old status displayed: manually refresh after reconnecting. - Push opened login: the session expired; authenticate and return to the original incident link.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Offline behavior and updates - Desktop incident response

pages.title: Search and process in-app notifications
pages.description: Navigate the desktop application, search authorized records, and process the personal notification inbox.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in with the role and team memberships you normally use. Search and inbox results respect the current user's authorization, so missing results may be an access boundary rather than a data problem.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Use the desktop sidebar to move between Dashboard, Incidents, Services, Teams, on-call, analytics, and settings surfaces available to your role. Press Cmd+K on macOS or Ctrl+K elsewhere to open product-wide sidebar search. Press / only in a page that implements a local search shortcut, such as the Incidents list. Select the bell in the top bar to open the personal in-app notification drawer.

sections.heading: Configure and use search
sections.text: 1. Enter at least two meaningful characters. Queries are bounded and normalized. 2. Review the result type before opening a match. Search can return authorized incidents, services, teams, users, escalation policies, and postmortems. 3. Add a more specific title, identifier, service, or person fragment if results are broad. 4. Open the result and verify its record identity before taking an action.

sections.heading: Process the notification inbox
sections.text: 1. Open the top-bar bell and inspect the unread badge. 2. Use All , Unread , Incidents , or Shifts to narrow the drawer. Service notifications remain identifiable by their service type in the list. 3. Select a notification with an incident target to open that incident. 4. Use the inline control to mark one item read, or Mark all as read after reviewing the outstanding items. 5. Interpret Connectin

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: - In-app inbox: a personal, signed-in activity drawer with read/unread state. - Paging providers: email, SMS, voice, push, WhatsApp, Slack, or Teams delivery used to reach responders outside or alongside the web application. - Delivery history/operations: administrator evidence about provider attempts, outcomes, retries, and failures; it is not a user's unread inbox. Reading an in-app item does no

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text: Create or use a controlled event that produces a visible notification. Confirm the unread count changes, the appropriate filter contains the item, the target opens correctly, and marking it read persists after closing and reopening the drawer. Confirm a user without access cannot discover the protected record in search.

sections.heading: Change or undo it
sections.text: Read state can be changed only through the available inbox actions; marking an item read does not mutate the underlying incident. Restore or change access in the owning team/role workflow, not through search. Adjust external channel preferences under Settings → Profile → Notifications .

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Search returns nothing: use two or more characters, simplify punctuation, check spelling, and verify access to the record. - Search is temporarily unavailable: wait for the displayed/retry interval if rate limited, then try a narrower query. - The unread count looks stale: reopen the drawer; check whether it reports Live or Polling, then reload and verify the source event. - A drawer item does n

pages.title: Configure Amazon SES email
pages.description: Configure an SES region, sending identity, and least-privilege credentials for OpsKnight.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Choose the AWS account and region, obtain permission to manage SES identities and IAM credentials, and prepare a controlled recipient.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: In OpsKnight, open Settings → Notifications ( /settings/notifications ) and locate Amazon SES under Email Providers.

sections.heading: Configure Amazon SES
sections.text: 1. In the target AWS region, verify the sending domain or email identity and complete DKIM setup. 2. If the account is in the SES sandbox, verify test recipients or request production access. 3. Create a dedicated IAM principal allowed to send through the chosen identity and region. Record its access-key ID and secret access key. 4. In OpsKnight, open Settings → Notifications and locate Amazon SES

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight encrypts the AWS credentials and submits selected email notifications to SES in the configured region.

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text: Confirm the OpsKnight attempt, SES message ID and delivery event, and controlled inbox receipt.

sections.heading: Change or undo it
sections.text: Rotate the IAM key by validating the replacement in OpsKnight before deactivating the old key. Move routes before disabling SES.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Check region alignment, sandbox status, identity policy, IAM permission, quotas, bounces, and complaints when delivery fails.
