pages.title: Link Microsoft Teams responder identities
pages.description: Map a verified Teams user to the correct OpsKnight responder for authorized and attributable incident actions.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in to OpsKnight as the active responder whose Teams identity is being linked. Never complete another person's link.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Select an incident action in Teams and follow the identity-link prompt, or open Settings → Profile & Preferences ( /settings/profile ) and locate Connected ChatOps Accounts .

sections.heading: Configure the identity
sections.text: Confirm the tenant/account shown is your own and that the OpsKnight session is your intended responder account.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Open the signed link prompt. 2. Complete it while authenticated to OpsKnight as yourself. 3. Return to the original Teams card. 4. Retry the incident action once.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight stores a tenant/provider identity mapping to the responder. It still applies current authorization, service scope, and incident-state rules to each action.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Perform an allowed test action and confirm the incident timeline attributes it to your OpsKnight account. Confirm all cards converge.

sections.heading: Remove or change the link
sections.text: Remove stale mappings when a Teams account or OpsKnight user is deactivated or ownership changes, then complete a new signed link. Never transfer a link URL.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Prompt repeats: verify tenant/account and OpsKnight session match and the user is active. Linked but forbidden: identity succeeded; check product role/capability/service scope and incident state. Wrong actor appears: stop actions, remove the mapping, review audit/timeline, and relink the correct account.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Use incident actions - Troubleshoot Teams

pages.title: Use Microsoft Teams incident actions
pages.description: Act on OpsKnight incidents from verified Adaptive Cards.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Install Teams, map a service destination, and trigger a synthetic incident. Adaptive Card actions enter through the Bot messaging endpoint. OpsKnight validates the Bot token, tenant, trusted service URL, installation, destination, action schema, identity, and product authorization before applying a command. The normal incident card gives responders the incident status, service, urgency, assignee,

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open the current incident Adaptive Card in its routine service destination or incident war-room channel.

sections.heading: Configure the action
sections.text: Confirm the incident, current status, service, urgency, assignee, and priority. Choose only an action that reflects the real operational state. Complete identity linking before a user-attributed action.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Open the incident Adaptive Card. 2. Choose an action available to your responder role. 3. Complete identity linking if prompted. 4. Confirm the OpsKnight timeline and all destination cards converge.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight applies the same authorization and lifecycle transition as the UI, records the actor/timeline, applies escalation/notification effects, and reconciles all card projections. A stale or concurrent action is evaluated against current state.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: After acknowledging, assigning, escalating, or resolving, verify the authoritative OpsKnight status, actor, timeline, escalation effect, and all cards. Preserve activity ID/service URL when reporting failure, but never credentials/tokens.

sections.heading: Change or undo the action
sections.text: Do not edit the Teams post to imply a state change. Use supported OpsKnight lifecycle/follow-up action to correct state or add context.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Identity prompt repeats: relink the matching active responder account. Forbidden: check tenant/installation/destination validation, user mapping, product role/scope, and current state. Teams times out: inspect OpsKnight incident and operation before retrying; the action may already have applied.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Configure war rooms - Troubleshoot Teams

pages.title: Understand Microsoft Teams incident cards
pages.description: Learn the content, lifecycle, delivery, update, and source-of-truth behavior of normal OpsKnight Adaptive Cards.
pages.intro: A normal service-destination Adaptive Card presents current incident context such as status, service, urgency, assignee, priority, description, and creation time. It is not itself a war room. OpsKnight remains authoritative. Cards are provider projections associated with tenant installation, destination, service URL, and activity identity. Lifecycle actions reconcile all projections; manually chan

sections.heading: Normal card versus war-room card
sections.text: Routine destinations receive lifecycle cards. War-room provisioning creates an incident-scoped channel and may show a video bridge plus responder actions. War rooms require additional resource-specific consent and a designated owner destination.

sections.heading: Delivery and identity
sections.text: Viewing does not require an OpsKnight identity link. User-attributed actions do. OpsKnight validates Bot token, tenant, service URL, installation, destination, activity/action schema, mapped user, authorization, and incident transition. Provider throttling, expired credentials, disabled installations, changed service URLs, deleted activities/channels, or worker failures can delay projection withou

pages.title: Microsoft Teams permissions
pages.description: Review base and optional Teams resource-specific consent permissions.
pages.intro: Permissions are split between Bot Framework installation context and Microsoft Graph resource-specific consent (RSC). OpsKnight requests the Graph https://graph.microsoft.com/.default scope; the installed package determines which application RSC permissions exist in each Team.

sections.heading: Base package
sections.text: ChannelSettings.Read.Group is required to discover channels for the destination picker. Ordinary incident Adaptive Cards are sent through Bot Framework Connector transport using the installation service URL and bot recipient identity. OpsKnight therefore does not request ChannelMessage.Send.Group for routine card delivery.

sections.heading: Optional feature permissions

sections.heading: Consent boundaries
sections.text: RSC is granted by installing/consenting to the app in a specific Team. An app uploaded to the tenant catalog or installed in a different Team does not prove the target Team granted the permissions. Generate the package only after selecting the OpsKnight features you intend to enable, install that exact package in every target Team, and review the consent prompt. Do not enable war-room automation b

sections.heading: Verify permission health
sections.text: 1. In OpsKnight, confirm the detected installation belongs to the expected tenant and Team. 2. Review granted RSC permissions and missing-capability messages. 3. Test routine card delivery independently of Graph channel management. 4. Create and close a disposable war room when that feature is enabled. 5. Add/remove a pilot participant only when membership automation is approved. After changing th

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Routine cards work but Team/channel discovery fails: check ChannelSettings.Read.Group on the target Team installation. Channel creation returns 403 : verify Channel.Create.Group and TeamsAppInstallation.Read.Group were consented through the installed package. Creation works but rename/archive fails: add ChannelSettings.ReadWrite.Group , reinstall, and reconfirm consent. Membership does not reconci

pages.title: Send and verify a Microsoft Teams test
pages.description: Test an exact Teams destination and diagnose installation, channel, Bot transport, or delivery failures.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Complete tenant/Bot/app installation and save a non-production service destination.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Services → select the service → Notifications → Microsoft Teams and locate the exact destination.

sections.heading: Configure the test
sections.text: Confirm tenant, team, and channel. Do not use a production incident channel for the first test.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Select Test for the destination. 2. Wait for the operation result; avoid repeated clicks. 3. Open the target Teams channel. 4. Match the received Adaptive Card to the test time/destination.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: The test uses the stored tenant installation, trusted service URL, and Bot Framework Connector transport. It proves basic card delivery to one destination, not incident routing, identity-linked actions, or war-room channel permissions.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: OpsKnight reports success and exactly one test card appears in the intended channel. Then trigger a synthetic incident to validate real lifecycle delivery/update.

sections.heading: Remove the test setup
sections.text: Remove the temporary destination after validation if it is not part of production routing. Follow tenant retention policy for the test card.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Installation not found: confirm bot/app is installed and enabled in the exact tenant/team. Forbidden/untrusted service URL: re-establish a valid installation/conversation and inspect tenant/service URL validation. Timeout/ambiguous response: inspect delivery operation and channel before retrying to avoid duplicates.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Understand incident cards - Use incident actions

pages.title: Troubleshoot Microsoft Teams
pages.description: Diagnose tenant, installation, destination, card, and war-room failures.

sections.heading: Installation is not detected
sections.text: Verify the configured tenant ID, Azure Bot endpoint, application package ID, and that the bot is installed in the target team. Separate the Entra application ID, Azure Bot identity, Teams app manifest bot ID, and configured OpsKnight ID; they must identify the intended application. Confirm the messaging endpoint is public HTTPS and targets the documented OpsKnight activity route. A tenant restrict

sections.heading: Cards are not delivered
sections.text: Test the exact destination. Confirm its installation remains enabled and its service URL is trusted. Inspect the notification operation and provider result. Locate the saved conversation/destination by tenant, team, and channel. A stale service URL or removed installation requires a fresh installation/conversation update; a forbidden response requires destination/app permission review. Test the sa

sections.heading: Card actions return forbidden
sections.text: Check Bot token validation, tenant match, installation and destination scope, identity mapping, and OpsKnight authorization. The inbound activity limit is enforced before processing; oversized requests return 413 . Match the activity ID and timestamp to the OpsKnight request. Validate the Bot Framework token issuer/audience and tenant first, then installation scope, identity mapping, and OpsKnight

sections.heading: War-room creation fails
sections.text: Verify the target team granted the optional war-room RSC permissions. Inspect the collaboration operation before retrying because channel creation can succeed remotely even when the response is ambiguous. Search the target team before retrying. If a channel already exists, reconcile the collaboration operation. If no channel exists, distinguish missing resource- specific consent, insufficient Grap

sections.heading: Verify and escalate
sections.text: Use a non-production service to post a normal incident card and a war-room card, run one action as a linked responder, and create one test room. Preserve tenant, team, channel, activity, and operation IDs plus HTTP status and Microsoft error code. Never attach bot credentials, bearer tokens, or an unredacted card payload.

pages.title: Configure Microsoft Teams war rooms
pages.description: Enable consented channel creation, lifecycle management, and membership sync.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Complete the base Teams installation and obtain permission to grant optional resource-specific consent in the target team. War rooms require additional resource-specific consent beyond ordinary card delivery. Enable war-room permissions in the generated package, reinstall or update it in the target team, then select the war-room destination for the service. In a provisioned incident channel, the c

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: As administrator, open Settings → Integrations → Microsoft Teams to generate/update the app package. Then open Services → select service → Notifications → Microsoft Teams to select the one destination that owns automatic war-room behavior. Responders create/manage the room from the incident collaboration controls.

sections.heading: Configure war-room consent
sections.text: 1. Enable war-room permissions in the generated application package. 2. Reinstall or update the package in the target team. 3. Select the service destination that owns automatic war-room behavior. 4. Create a test incident room and verify its lifecycle. Channel creation needs Channel.Create.Group and TeamsAppInstallation.Read.Group . Lifecycle and membership features add ChannelSettings.ReadWrite.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight creates/links an incident-scoped Teams channel, stores durable identifiers/markers, publishes incident context, reconciles membership and cards, and performs terminal cleanup. The incident remains authoritative. Only one destination per service owns automatic war-room behavior.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Confirm the channel appears in the intended team, normal incident context and optional video bridge/actions are correct, expected members synchronize, card actions update OpsKnight, and closure performs documented cleanup.

sections.heading: Remove or change the war room
sections.text: Close/reconcile it from OpsKnight rather than manually deleting the Teams channel. To change owner destination, finish/open-room coordination, select the new service destination, and test with a new incident; do not assume existing remote rooms migrate.

sections.heading: Squire in the war room
sections.text: When Squire is enabled for chat ( Settings → Intelligence → AI ), mention the bot in the war-room channel to ask about the incident, or send @OpsKnight investigate [focus] to run Squire's investigation on it. Squire replies in the thread, edits that reply with its progress, and finishes with the investigation and links to the evidence, answering as the asker's linked OpsKnight account; unlinked pe

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Channel creation forbidden: verify optional RSC permissions and team-level consent/package update. Room exists but OpsKnight reports ambiguity: inspect collaboration operation/markers before retrying to avoid duplicate channels. Membership fails: verify Team/Channel member read/write RSC and target user availability.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Review permissions - Use incident actions - Troubleshoot Teams

pages.title: Slack ChatOps
pages.description: Connect Slack, route incident messages, act on incidents, and operate war rooms.
pages.intro: Connect one Slack workspace to deliver incident lifecycle messages, accept interactive responder actions, run /incident commands, and create incident war rooms. Start with the complete Slack ChatOps setup, which covers Slack app creation through production acceptance.

sections.heading: Recommended setup sequence
sections.text: 1. Create, connect, and validate the Slack app. 2. Review scopes and reinstall after changes. 3. Configure service channels and test each one. 4. Link responder identities. 5. Validate notifications, actions, and commands with a synthetic incident. 6. Configure and rehearse war rooms when required. 7. Document rate-limit, troubleshooting, and disconnect/reconnect ownership.

sections.heading: Choose a task
sections.text: - Connect and configure Slack ChatOps - Configure service channels - Send and verify a test - Understand incident notifications - Acknowledge and resolve incidents - Use incident actions and commands - Create and operate war rooms - Declare from a message and use the Home tab - Sync on-call to a Slack user group - Link responder identities - Review permissions and scopes - Review rate limits - Dis

sections.heading: Check setup and health
sections.text: Settings → Integrations → Slack has a Setup and health panel with live checks against Slack: the bot token, the workspace, required scopes, optional feature scopes, the signing secret, recent requests from Slack, and whether Squire is on. A guided checklist ticks as OpsKnight sees each step work, and shows the events, interactivity, and slash-command URLs to paste into the Slack app. Select Run ch

sections.heading: How the pieces relate
sections.text: The OAuth installation authorizes the OpsKnight bot. Service destinations control routine lifecycle delivery. Identity links authorize user-attributed actions. War rooms are separate incident-scoped channels with their own lifecycle. Configuring one does not implicitly configure the others.

pages.title: Acknowledge and resolve incidents from Slack
pages.description: Use Slack message actions safely and verify incident, escalation, timeline, and message convergence.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect Slack, configure the service channel, and link your responder identity. You need product permission to perform the action and an incident in a valid starting state.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open the incident's Slack message in a routine destination or war room. Use the action on the current message rather than an old copied link or screenshot.

sections.heading: Configure the action
sections.text: For acknowledgement, confirm the incident is open/triggered and you intend to stop or alter active escalation according to the incident policy. For resolution, confirm the incident is actually mitigated. Resolve asks you to confirm in a dialog, then performs the lifecycle transition directly; it does not prompt for the web resolution-note form. Verify the resolution and timeline in OpsKnight after

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Select Acknowledge or Resolve on the incident message. 2. Complete identity linking if prompted, then retry once. 3. Wait for the card to update (it is edited in place, usually within a few seconds) instead of clicking repeatedly. The card changes as soon as you click, and a thread reply follows. 4. Verify the resolution and timeline in OpsKnight afterward.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight validates the signed Slack request, timestamp, workspace, action schema, identity, authorization, and current incident transition. It updates the authoritative incident/timeline, applies escalation/notification effects, and reconciles all provider projections. Concurrent or stale actions are evaluated against current incident state. A Slack click cannot bypass product lifecycle rules.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Open the OpsKnight incident and confirm status, actor attribution, timeline entry, assignee/escalation effect, and any resolution summary. Confirm every mapped Slack projection converges to the same state.

sections.heading: Change or undo the action
sections.text: Acknowledgement and resolution are lifecycle events, not editable Slack text. Slack offers Escalate while an incident is open, but it does not offer Reopen . If a condition returns, submit a new manual report with the matching deduplication key within 30 minutes or use an authorized API status update; do not manually edit the message to imply a different state.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Identity prompt repeats: ensure the signed link was completed while signed in as the matching active OpsKnight user, then remove stale mapping if needed. Forbidden: verify product permissions/service scope and that the action is valid for the current state. Slack times out but action may have applied: inspect the OpsKnight incident/timeline and operation before retrying to avoid duplicate intent.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Use Slack commands - Operate war rooms

pages.title: Use Slack incident commands
pages.description: Run supported signed slash commands and verify their authoritative OpsKnight incident effects.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Install the current Slack app manifest, link your identity, and open an incident destination/war room where the command context is clear.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: In Slack's message composer, enter /incident help to display the supported command syntax.

sections.heading: Configure the command
sections.text: Three commands work in any channel; the rest work in an incident war room: Command What it does --- --- /incident declare Opens a form to declare a new incident (see below). /incident list [service] Your open incidents, or a service's. If none are assigned to you, it shows the latest open incidents you can see and says so. /incident oncall [service] Who is on call for a service. /incident ack Ackn

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Enter /incident with its argument. 2. Submit once and read the response. 3. Complete identity linking if prompted. 4. Open OpsKnight when the response says the action was queued or cannot confirm final state.

sections.heading: Declare an incident from Slack
sections.text: /incident declare opens a form with the same choices as the web create page: - Title and Service are required. The service list is searchable. - Urgency defaults to High. - Priority is optional. Left empty, the service's policy sets it, as on the web. - Visibility is optional: customer-facing (status pages) or internal only. Left empty, the service's default applies. - Assign to is optional and is

sections.heading: Page, assign, and update
sections.text: These work in a war-room channel and run as you, with your normal permissions. - page pages the target for this incident. A person is assigned the incident; a schedule resolves to whoever is on call now; a team becomes the owning team and the assignee is cleared. A name that isn't @person , team: or schedule: is tried as a team first, then as a schedule. The result is posted in the channel ("Paged

sections.heading: Post a status-page update
sections.text: /incident status and More actions → Post status update publish a customer-facing update. They need the administrator capability and only work for an incident that is public and whose service is on an enabled status page; otherwise they say why in a private message. The update is published as an information announcement linked to the incident on up to five status pages that show the service. Subscr

sections.heading: Run a runbook
sections.text: /incident runbook lists up to five enabled runbooks attached to the incident's service, each with a Preview button. Preview shows the version, the steps, the risk and approval flags, and any check that blocks the run. Confirm and run appears only when nothing blocks it, and the confirmation is valid for five minutes and works once, so a stale preview or a second click is refused. A runbook that ne

sections.heading: Action items
sections.text: /incident action Add a canary to the deploy [@person] [due:2026-12-05] adds a follow-up to the incident's postmortem, creating a draft postmortem if there isn't one. The title is at most 200 characters, a due date must be a real date (up to a day in the past is accepted), and an identical open title is refused as a duplicate. The owner must have an OpsKnight account. /incident actions lists the op

sections.heading: How a command answers
sections.text: A fast command shows only its answer, with no "Processing" note. Who sees the answer depends on the command: - Private to you: the read-only commands ( who , list , oncall , help ), ask and investigate , and any error or refusal. - Posted in the channel: commands that change the incident ( ack , resolve , note , role , page , status , action , and postmortem ) announce the result to everyone in th

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight validates the Slack signature/timestamp, parses only the supported grammar, maps identity, checks authorization/context, and applies the same product transition used by the UI.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Confirm the authoritative incident timeline/state/actor in OpsKnight and the updated Slack projection. For who , confirm the reported ownership matches current OpsKnight state.

sections.heading: Change or undo the command
sections.text: Commands create product actions; deleting Slack command text does not undo them. Use the supported incident workflow to correct state or add a clarifying note.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Command not recognized: use /incident help and confirm the current app package registered the command. Wrong incident/context: open the intended incident message/war room and retry only after confirming no action applied. Temporary queue error: inspect OpsKnight worker health and operation state before retrying.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Acknowledge and resolve - Troubleshoot Slack

pages.title: Configure Slack service channels
pages.description: Route service incident messages to one or more Slack destinations.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect the Slack workspace and ensure the bot can access each target channel.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Services → select the service → Notifications → Slack . Workspace connection and service routing are separate: this page chooses where that service sends incident messages.

sections.heading: Configure destinations
sections.text: 1. Enable Slack delivery for the service. 2. Select a connected workspace channel. 3. Add up to three active channels for the service. 4. Save the service configuration. 5. Use Test for every destination. All linked channels receive lifecycle messages; they are not a fallback chain. At the three-channel limit, unlink an obsolete channel before adding another. Channel destinations are independent f

sections.heading: Limit a channel by priority or urgency
sections.text: Each linked channel can be limited to certain priorities (P1 to P5) and urgencies (high, medium, low). For example, send only P1 and P2 to an incident channel and everything else to a quieter one. Choose the values under the channel on the same page and select Save . Leaving both lists empty means every incident, as before. The limit decides where new incident cards are posted. A card that has alr

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: All active destinations receive lifecycle messages; they are not a priority or fallback chain. OpsKnight stores durable destination identities and updates the incident projection as state changes. Routine service channels are separate from incident war rooms and identity links.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Trigger a synthetic incident. Confirm exactly one message in every mapped channel and verify that later lifecycle changes update the existing projection.

sections.heading: Remove or change a destination
sections.text: Open the same service page, unlink the obsolete destination, save, and send tests to the remaining destinations. Removing a routine destination does not close an existing war room. At the three-channel limit, remove an obsolete channel before adding another.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Channel does not appear: confirm the bot can discover/access it and that required public/private scopes and membership are present. Test succeeds but incidents do not arrive: check service notification routing and the incident's service, then inspect delivery history/provider result. Duplicate messages: confirm the channel is not mapped through multiple active destinations and inspect the incident

pages.title: Connect and configure Slack ChatOps
pages.description: Create the Slack app, configure every callback and permission, connect OAuth, route services, and verify ChatOps end to end.
pages.intro: This is the complete administrator journey from a new Slack application to a verified OpsKnight incident workflow. A successful OAuth callback alone is not production acceptance.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: - Use an OpsKnight administrator account and a Slack account permitted to create and install apps in the target workspace. - Set NEXTAUTH URL and NEXT PUBLIC APP URL to the same public HTTPS origin. - Confirm Slack can reach that origin without private DNS, VPN, or an authentication proxy intercepting /api/slack/ . - Decide whether private-channel support is required; it adds optional scopes. - Cr

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → Integrations → Slack . Use the guided setup and manifest from this deployment, not callback URLs copied from another environment.

sections.heading: Create the Slack application
sections.text: 1. Copy the generated Slack app manifest from OpsKnight. 2. In the Slack API console, select Create New App → From a manifest . 3. Select the intended workspace, paste the manifest, review it, and create the app. Stop if the workspace is wrong. 4. Under Basic Information → App Credentials , record the numeric Client ID , reveal and copy the Client Secret , and copy the separate Signing Secret . Do

sections.heading: Review Slack permissions
sections.text: Core ChatOps requires chat:write , channels:read , channels:join , channels:manage , channels:history , reactions:read , users:read , and users:read.email . Private coverage additionally uses groups:read , groups:write , groups:history , im:read , and mpim:read . channels:manage enables public war-room lifecycle; users:read.email supports responder matching; and reactions:read with channel history

sections.heading: Configure Slack OAuth
sections.text: 1. Select Connect Slack in OpsKnight. 2. Confirm the Slack authorization page names the intended workspace and scopes. 3. Select Allow with an authorized workspace administrator. 4. Return to OpsKnight and confirm the workspace is connected and required scopes are healthy.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight validates OAuth state and encrypts the bot token. Workspace authorization does not grant private-channel membership or create routing. Signed Slack requests are timestamp-checked before identity resolution and normal product authorization. Incident delivery is durable and later lifecycle events update the stored provider projection rather than treating Slack as a second incident database

sections.heading: Configure service delivery
sections.text: 1. Invite the app to private test channels; it can join eligible public channels. 2. Open Services → select service → Notifications → Slack . 3. Enable Slack and add up to three destinations. All active destinations receive lifecycle messages; they are not fallbacks. 4. Save and send a real test to every channel. 5. Configure global/service ChatOps and war-room policy only after routine delivery s

sections.heading: Configure responder actions
sections.text: 1. Ask a pilot responder to link their Slack identity. 2. Confirm an unlinked user is prompted to link. 3. Use one permitted button and /incident help . 4. Confirm a user without product permission is denied. Slack identity establishes the actor; OpsKnight authorization and current incident state still decide whether an action is allowed.

sections.heading: Verify the complete workflow
sections.text: 1. Trigger a synthetic incident on the configured service. 2. Confirm exactly one message reaches every mapped channel. 3. Acknowledge, assign where applicable, add a safe note, and resolve. Standard Slack actions do not expose manual escalation in 2.0. 4. Confirm existing Slack messages update and the OpsKnight timeline records the correct actor and transitions. 5. If enabled, create a war room a

sections.heading: Production acceptance checklist
sections.text: - Correct workspace and installing administrator - Required scopes healthy; optional scopes justified - OAuth, signed buttons, Events API, and /incident independently verified - Every production destination tested - Allowed and denied responder authorization tested - Trigger-through-resolution cards converge without duplicates - War-room lifecycle tested when enabled - Rotation, revocation, discon

sections.heading: Change or undo it
sections.text: For scope changes, update the manifest and reinstall/reconnect. For credential rotation, update OpsKnight and test every destination before revoking the old secret/app. To stop delivery, disable service routing, account for open war rooms and queued operations, then disconnect and revoke deliberately.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: OAuth reports an invalid client: use the numeric Client ID and Client Secret from App Credentials . The Client Secret and Signing Secret differ. Redirect URI mismatch: copy the exact callback displayed by OpsKnight and correct the public URL/proxy instead of registering an internal HTTP callback. Buttons or commands fail: verify Signing Secret, clock, request URL, TLS/proxy body handling, identity

sections.text: - Slack permissions and scopes - Configure service channels - Send and verify a test - Configure war rooms - Troubleshoot Slack - Disconnect or reconnect

pages.title: Disconnect or reconnect Slack
pages.description: Rotate or revoke a Slack workspace connection and safely revalidate destinations, identities, actions, and war rooms.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Use an administrator account and schedule the change when delayed ChatOps delivery is acceptable. Inventory active service destinations, identity links, open war rooms, and queued operations.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → Integrations → Slack and select the connected workspace.

sections.heading: Configure the change
sections.text: Choose reconnection for revoked/rotated authorization or required-scope changes. Choose disconnection when Slack must stop receiving OpsKnight data. Coordinate app revocation in Slack so neither side is assumed active incorrectly.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Record affected destinations/open incidents without recording credentials. 2. Select the disconnect/reconnect control. 3. For reconnect, complete OAuth in the intended workspace and review scopes. 4. Re-run workspace health and destination tests. 5. Trigger one synthetic incident and action.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight replaces/stores encrypted authorization and workspace identity after a validated callback. Stale/revoked authorization cannot deliver. Existing destination identifiers still require access and must be retested.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: For disconnect, confirm tests/delivery no longer succeed and remove obsolete routing. For reconnect, confirm required scopes, every production destination, an interactive action, and selected war-room lifecycle.

sections.heading: Change or undo it
sections.text: Reconnect through OAuth to restore a deliberately disconnected workspace. If the wrong workspace was connected, disconnect it before authorizing the correct one; do not leave ambiguous cross-workspace routing.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Old workspace appears: clear the admin Slack session or explicitly choose the correct workspace during OAuth. Destinations fail after reconnect: verify bot membership/channel identity and newly granted optional scopes. Queued failures persist: inspect whether operations are retryable or terminal after credential replacement; avoid uncontrolled replay.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Send a test - Troubleshoot Slack

pages.title: Use Slack incident actions
pages.description: Acknowledge, resolve, annotate, and inspect incidents from Slack.
pages.intro: This page summarizes the supported action surface. Follow Acknowledge and resolve incidents for lifecycle effects and Slack incident commands for exact slash-command behavior.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect Slack, map a service destination, and link your responder identity. Interactive messages expose only actions allowed by the shared ChatOps policy. Link your Slack identity before performing user-attributed actions. 1. Open the incident message or incident war-room channel. 2. Use a button on the message, or enter /incident with one of the commands below. The channel card offers these butto

pages.title: Understand Slack incident notifications
pages.description: Learn how OpsKnight projects incident lifecycle state to Slack destinations and how updates, identity, and delivery failures behave.
pages.intro: OpsKnight is the source of truth for incident state. Each active service destination receives a projection. Subsequent lifecycle changes update or reconcile that projection using durable provider/message identities and idempotent delivery keys. The message can expose only actions allowed by the shared ChatOps policy. A provider message is not an independent incident record; manually editing or del

sections.heading: One live card per incident
sections.text: A routine service destination gets one card per incident . OpsKnight posts it when the incident triggers and then edits that same message as the incident moves from triggered to acknowledged, snoozed, escalated, and resolved. Each change adds a short reply in the card's thread, so the channel reads as a timeline instead of a stack of repeated alerts. The card shows: - A colour bar and emoji for th

sections.heading: Reminders in the thread
sections.text: Two optional reminders post a reply on the incident's card. Set them under Settings → Integrations → ChatOps ; leaving a field empty turns that reminder off. - Nudge when unacknowledged (minutes): while an incident is open and nobody has acknowledged it, OpsKnight replies "No one has acknowledged this yet" after this many minutes, and again every interval up to six times. - Nudge when there is no

sections.heading: Notification settings
sections.text: The service's notification switches for triggered, acknowledged, and resolved incidents control new posts . With a switch off, OpsKnight does not post a new card or reply for that event, but a card that already exists is still edited so it never shows a stale state. Older messages are not changed. A message posted before you upgraded, and messages sent through an incoming webhook (which cannot be

sections.heading: Routine destinations and war rooms
sections.text: Routine service destinations receive incident lifecycle messages. A war room is a separate incident-scoped channel with provisioning, membership, context, and cleanup. Configuring one does not configure the other.

sections.heading: Delivery and convergence
sections.text: Provider throttling, removed bot access, deleted messages/channels, revoked tokens, or worker/database failures can delay a projection without changing the incident. Use OpsKnight delivery/operation state to diagnose and retry safely; avoid manual duplicate posts.

sections.heading: Identity and actions
sections.text: Viewing a message does not require an OpsKnight identity link. User-attributed actions do. OpsKnight validates Slack signatures/timestamps, maps the Slack user, then applies normal product authorization and incident-state rules.

sections.heading: Related guides
sections.text: - Configure service channels - Acknowledge and resolve - Operate war rooms

pages.title: Sync on-call to a Slack user group
pages.description: Keep a Slack user group equal to whoever is on call for a schedule, so an @oncall mention always reaches the right people.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: User groups are a paid Slack feature. Create the user group in Slack first (for example @oncall-platform ). The Slack app needs the usergroups:write scope, and usergroups:read if you want to pick the group from a list; see permissions and scopes. An app installed before 2.3.0 must have its manifest updated and be reconnected to get them.

sections.heading: Map a schedule
sections.text: 1. Open Settings → Integrations → Slack and find On-call user groups . 2. Choose an on-call schedule and a Slack user group. If OpsKnight can't list user groups, type the group's id. 3. Save. Use Pause and Resume to stop and restart a mapping, or remove it.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: About once a minute OpsKnight works out who is on call for each mapped schedule, finds each person's Slack account by email, and sets the user group's members to those people. Slack replaces a group's whole membership, so OpsKnight never sends an empty list: if nobody is on call, or none of the on-call people matches a Slack account, the group keeps its previous members and the mapping shows the r

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: The mapping shows synced after a successful pass, or the error after a failed one (a missing scope, a disconnected workspace, or nobody to sync). In Slack, check that the user group's members are the people currently on call. This feature needs a paid Slack plan, so it was covered by automated tests but not run against a live workspace.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Slack permissions and scopes - Operate war rooms

pages.title: Slack permissions and scopes
pages.description: Understand the exact required and optional Slack bot scopes, including the commands scope added in 2.2.0.
pages.intro: Core features require chat:write , channels:read , channels:join , channels:manage , channels:history , reactions:read , users:read , users:read.email , and commands . Private-channel and direct-message coverage is optional and uses groups:read , groups:write , groups:history , im:read , and mpim:read . Squire, the OpsKnight assistant, uses two more optional scopes: app mentions:read (receive @Ops

sections.heading: Squire's name and avatar ( chat:write.customize )
sections.text: Slack lets an app post under a different name and icon only when it holds chat:write.customize . With the scope granted, every Squire message (answers to @OpsKnight mentions and Squire's automatic incident-channel updates) is posted under the Squire name set in Settings → Intelligence → AI and the Squire avatar served from your OpsKnight base URL ( /squire/squire-avatar.png ). Without the scope, S

sections.heading: What changed in 2.2.0
sections.text: commands is now a required scope. Slack rejects an app manifest that declares a slash command without it, and a workspace installed without it does not deliver /incident to OpsKnight. Earlier releases declared /incident but did not request the scope.

sections.heading: Upgrading from 2.1
sections.text: Workspaces connected on 2.1 show commands as a missing required scope under Settings → Integrations → Slack . To fix it: 1. If you created the Slack app from the manifest, add commands under OAuth & Permissions → Bot Token Scopes in the Slack app settings, or recreate the app from the new manifest. 2. Select Reconnect to refresh scopes in OpsKnight and approve the updated scopes. 3. Run /incident

sections.heading: Advanced scopes
sections.text: Three more scopes are requested with the rest but are never reported as a gap, because most workspaces don't use the features: Scope What it enables --- --- usergroups:read Lists Slack user groups when you map an on-call schedule to one. usergroups:write Keeps a user group equal to who is on call (see on-call user groups). conversations.connect:write Invites external people to a war room with Slac

sections.text: The current manifest declares two shortcuts named Declare incident , turns on the Home tab, and subscribes to the app home opened event. These need no scope, but an app created before 2.3.0 must have its manifest updated and be reinstalled to get them. See shortcuts and the Home tab.

sections.heading: Slack Enterprise Grid
sections.text: An install made for a whole Enterprise Grid organization stores the organization's id, and requests from any workspace in that organization are accepted for it. To install for the organization, turn on Org Level Apps in the Slack app's settings and reinstall; the generated manifest leaves it off so that ordinary workspaces are unaffected. A normal single-workspace install behaves exactly as before

sections.heading: Update an existing install
sections.text: If the Slack app was installed from an older manifest, Settings → Integrations → Slack shows Slack app manifest out of date with the scopes it is missing and what each one unlocks. Everything that worked before keeps working; those features stay off until you update the app: 1. Select Copy manifest , open your app in the Slack API console, paste it under App Manifest , and save. 2. Select Reconnec

pages.title: Slack rate limits and retry behavior
pages.description: Understand Slack throttling boundaries, queued retries, convergence, and safe operator response.
pages.intro: Slack enforces workspace/API-method limits and can return throttling responses with a retry interval. OpsKnight delivery is asynchronous; an incident remains authoritative while its Slack projection is delayed. Do not repeatedly send tests or manually repost incident messages during throttling. Inspect provider response, operation state, queue oldest age, and credential/channel access. Allow the b

pages.title: Send and verify a Slack test
pages.description: Test an exact Slack service destination and distinguish workspace, channel-access, queue, and delivery failures.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect Slack and save a destination on a non-production service. Ensure the bot is a member of a private target channel.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Services → select the service → Notifications → Slack , then locate the exact saved destination.

sections.heading: Configure the test
sections.text: Confirm the displayed workspace and channel are the intended destination. Do not use a production incident channel for the first test.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Select Test for the destination. 2. Wait for the operation result; do not click repeatedly. 3. Open the target Slack channel. 4. Match the received test to the destination and test time.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: The test uses the stored encrypted workspace credential and selected channel. It validates delivery to that destination, not incident routing, identity linking, interactive actions, or war-room permissions.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: The OpsKnight operation reports success and exactly one test message appears in the selected channel. Then trigger a synthetic incident to validate service routing and lifecycle updates.

sections.heading: Remove the test setup
sections.text: Delete the test message according to workspace policy and unlink the non-production destination if it was temporary.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Channel not found/forbidden: verify channel identity, bot membership, and public/private scopes. Rate limited: wait for the provider retry window; do not generate repeated tests. Inspect operation/provider response. OpsKnight reports success but message is not visible: verify the exact workspace/channel, Slack retention/moderation, and that another destination was not inspected.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Understand incident notifications - Use incident actions

pages.title: Slack shortcuts and the Home tab
pages.description: Declare an incident from any Slack message or the shortcuts menu, and use the OpsKnight Home tab to see who is on call and which incidents are open.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Link your Slack identity (see Link Slack responder identities). An app created before 2.3.0 must be updated first: paste the current manifest under App Manifest in the Slack API console, save, and select Reconnect Slack in OpsKnight. No new scope is needed.

sections.heading: Declare an incident from a message
sections.text: 1. Hover a message, select More actions , and choose Declare incident . 2. The declare form opens with the title set to the first line of the message (200 characters at most) and the description set to the message text, followed by a link to the message when Slack provides one. 3. Choose the service, adjust the priority, visibility, and assignee, and submit. The incident is created as with /incide

sections.heading: Declare an incident from the shortcuts menu
sections.text: Open the shortcuts menu (the ⚡ button under the message box) and choose Declare incident . It opens the same form with nothing filled in.

sections.heading: The Home tab
sections.text: Open OpsKnight under Apps and select Home . It shows: - On call now for you. - My open incidents and Open incidents , up to ten each and limited to what your account may read. Each has View and, for an incident that is still open, Acknowledge . - Declare incident , which opens the form. If your Slack account isn't linked to an OpsKnight account, the Home tab says so instead of listing incidents. T

sections.text: - Use Slack incident commands - Link Slack responder identities

pages.title: Troubleshoot Slack
pages.description: Diagnose OAuth, delivery, interactive-action, identity, and war-room failures.

sections.heading: Workspace will not connect
sections.text: Verify the public application URL, callback URL, Slack app credentials, and administrator installation permission. Reconnect after a revoked installation. Check the failed OAuth callback response and OpsKnight logs at the same time. A redirect mismatch is fixed in the Slack app configuration; invalid client credentials are fixed in the OpsKnight secret; access denied means the installer cancelled

sections.heading: Messages are not delivered
sections.text: Test the destination, confirm the bot can access the channel, inspect the notification operation, and check the provider response. A workspace connection does not grant access to every private channel. Test the exact service destination, not a different public channel. Distinguish channel not found or not in channel from missing scope , revoked token, and rate limit responses. Invite the bot to a

sections.heading: An action or command fails
sections.text: Confirm request-signature validation, required scopes, identity linking, and the responder's OpsKnight permissions. Queue failures return a temporary error and should be retried only after worker health is restored. Use the Slack request timestamp and interaction payload ID to locate the inbound request. Signature failures indicate wrong raw bytes, timestamp, or signing secret. A successful signat

sections.heading: War-room creation fails
sections.text: Check channels:manage ; for private rooms also check the optional groups: scopes. Inspect the incident collaboration operation before manually creating a replacement channel. Before retrying, search Slack and the incident collaboration record for the requested room. A remote create can succeed even if the callback times out. If the room exists, reconcile that result instead of creating a duplicate

sections.heading: Verify and escalate
sections.text: Reconnect only when necessary, send one non-production incident notification, run one authorized action, and create one test war room. Preserve workspace ID, channel ID, request timestamp, operation ID, Slack error code, and granted scope list. Redact tokens, signing secrets, and message content containing customer data.

pages.title: Link Slack responder identities
pages.description: Associate a Slack user with an OpsKnight responder account.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in to OpsKnight as the responder whose Slack account you are linking.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Select an incident action in Slack and follow the identity-link prompt, or open Settings → Profile & Preferences ( /settings/profile ) and locate Connected ChatOps Accounts .

sections.heading: Configure the identity
sections.text: Confirm the Slack workspace/user and signed-in OpsKnight account are your own. Identity linking attributes actions; it does not grant product permission.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Open your identity-link prompt. 2. Complete the signed flow while authenticated as yourself. 3. Retry the Slack action. 4. Verify the OpsKnight timeline attributes the action to your account.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight stores the provider/workspace/user mapping and still evaluates current role, service scope, action policy, and incident state for every request.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Perform an allowed action on a controlled incident. Confirm actor attribution in the OpsKnight timeline and convergence of every Slack projection.

sections.heading: Remove or change the link
sections.text: Administrators should remove stale mappings when a Slack account or OpsKnight user is deactivated or ownership changes, then complete a new signed link. Never share an identity-link URL.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Prompt repeats: confirm the signed link was completed while authenticated as the matching active OpsKnight account. Linked but forbidden: identity succeeded; check OpsKnight permissions/service scope and current incident state. Wrong actor: stop actions, remove the mapping, review timeline/audit evidence, and link the correct account.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Acknowledge and resolve - Use commands

sections.heading: Optional: Slack direct-message paging
sections.text: A responder can also be paged by Slack direct message, with Acknowledge and Resolve buttons. It is off for everyone until each person opts in at Settings → Profile & Preferences → Notifications → Slack DM . It needs the im:write scope on the Slack app (see permissions and scopes), and the OpsKnight account email must match the Slack account email so OpsKnight can find you. The switch stays disable

pages.title: Operate Slack incident war rooms
pages.description: Create, synchronize, and close incident-scoped Slack channels.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect Slack with the required public or private-channel scopes and create an active incident.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Incidents → select incident and locate the Create war room launcher in the incident command bar. A war room is incident-scoped, not a routine service destination.

sections.heading: Configure the room
sections.text: Confirm the Slack provider/workspace, intended public or private channel behavior, incident, and participants. Private rooms require the optional group scopes.

sections.heading: Complete the action
sections.text: 1. Select Create war room in the incident command bar. 2. Confirm Slack as the provider in the dialog and create the war room. 3. Confirm the context and intended participants appear. 4. Close the room from OpsKnight when coordination is complete.

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight creates or links a provider room, stores durable identity, publishes incident context with idempotent delivery keys, reconciles participants/messages, and performs terminal cleanup. The incident remains authoritative.

sections.heading: What the room contains
sections.text: A new room opens with a readable channel name, a plain description, and a topic that tracks the incident's state. OpsKnight then posts: 1. A short welcome that names the incident and its service, who the incident commander is, and the commands to use in the room. 2. A status card , pinned and bookmarked when the app has the pins:write and bookmarks:write scopes. The card shows the incident's state

sections.heading: Room settings
sections.text: Under Settings → Integrations → ChatOps : - Private Slack war rooms creates new Slack rooms as private channels that only invited responders can see. It needs the groups:write scope and is separate from status-page incident visibility. It is off by default. - Close Collaboration on Resolution archives the room when the incident resolves. The optional Archive delay (hours) (1 to 720) keeps the room

sections.heading: Optional room behaviour
sections.text: All of these are off by default and are set under Settings → Integrations → ChatOps . - Invite the on-call responder adds whoever is on call now for the schedules in the service's escalation policy (ten people at most) to new war rooms. It is applied when the room's participants are synchronized; a handover in the middle of an incident is not followed automatically. - Always add people to a servic

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Verify channel creation, topic/initial context, participant synchronization, interactive actions, pinned-note behavior, and closure. Missing channels:manage prevents public-channel lifecycle operations; private rooms also require the optional group scopes described in permissions and scopes.

sections.heading: Remove or change the room
sections.text: Close/reconcile through OpsKnight instead of manually deleting the Slack channel. If a remote room was changed/deleted, inspect the collaboration operation before retrying to avoid duplicate rooms.

sections.heading: Squire in the incident channel
sections.text: When Squire is enabled for chat ( Settings → Intelligence → AI , the assistant and its chat switch), it works inside the war-room channel: - Ask or investigate. Squire also answers @OpsKnight mentions in ordinary channels; in a war room it has the room's incident as context. Mention the app ( @OpsKnight what changed? ), or type @Squire … as plain text at the start of a message. @OpsKnight investig

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Creation forbidden: verify channels:manage ; private rooms also need the documented groups: permissions and bot access. Room exists but operation is ambiguous: inspect durable room ID/operation and provider response before retrying. Membership or actions fail: check user availability, identity mapping, bot membership, scopes, and product authorization.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Use incident actions - Troubleshoot Slack

pages.title: Twilio voice, SMS, and WhatsApp
pages.description: Configure and validate Twilio voice calls, SMS, and WhatsApp incident notifications.
pages.intro: OpsKnight can use one Twilio provider record for SMS and voice, plus independent WhatsApp enablement and credentials. Each channel still requires an eligible responder endpoint and routing selection; configuring Twilio alone does not send incident notifications.

Twilio trial-account recipient restrictions and channel enablement still apply. The stored secrets are the account SID and auth token. WhatsApp may reuse those credentials or use its own account SID and auth token. C

Enable Twilio SMS and run the provider test to an authorized test number. 3. A successful settings save is not delivery verification. Voice paging uses the configured Twilio provider to call a responder for a triggered incident. Voice is an urgent notification cha

Set VOICE CALLBACK SIGNING SECRET to an independent random value of at least 32 characters; when it is absent, the callback token code falls back to a sufficiently long NEXTAUTH SECRET . The externally visible application URL must allow Twilio to reach the voice gather and st

Trigger one incident, confirm the call identifies the service and incident, and exercise the documented acknowledgement input. Then inspect Settings → Notifications → Operations for provider admission, attempts, callback outcome, and terminal state.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - SMS reports an invalid sender: use an SMS-capable Twilio number rather than a WhatsApp-only sender. - A trial-account send is rejected: verify the recipient in Twilio or use an account permitted to contact that recipient. - WhatsApp is unavailable: confirm its independent enablement, sender number, credentials, and responder preference. - A delivery callback is rejected: confirm the public callb

pages.title: Issue-tracking integrations
pages.description: Connect an issue tracker and verify incident and action-item synchronization.
pages.intro: OpsKnight 2.0 provides the Jira integration. Connect Jira, map the intended project and issue types, verify webhook authentication, and create a controlled incident/action-item issue before relying on synchronization in an active response.

pages.title: Jira integration
pages.description: Create and synchronize Jira issues from OpsKnight incidents.
pages.intro: Jira connects incidents to project issues and processes authenticated webhook updates through a fenced synchronization path. - Connect Jira - Configure Jira webhooks - Troubleshoot Jira

pages.title: Configure Jira webhooks
pages.description: Authenticate Jira lifecycle events and synchronize linked incident state.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Connect Jira and generate a webhook secret in the Jira integration settings.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → Integrations → Jira and generate/store a high-entropy webhook secret. In Jira administration, open the webhook configuration for the site.

sections.heading: Configure the webhook
sections.text: 1. In Jira, create a webhook targeting https://YOUR OPSKNIGHT HOST/api/jira/webhook . 2. Configure the same secret using x-jira-webhook-secret or the supported bearer transport. 3. Select only handled issue lifecycle events: created, updated/generic, and deleted according to the workflow. 4. Scope the webhook to intended projects/issues when Jira supports the required filter. 5. Save, update a lin

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: The endpoint rejects missing/mismatched production secrets, applies a 60-request-per-minute client limit, and uses Jira delivery and issue-mutation fences to prevent duplicate/racing updates. It synchronizes only supported events for known linked issues.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Confirm one event updates the linked OpsKnight record once, retains the Jira issue key/URL, and records expected sync/audit state. Repeat/redeliver one event and verify it does not create duplicate links or conflicting transitions.

sections.heading: Revoke or rotate the webhook secret
sections.text: Pause or expect brief sync interruption, replace the secret in OpsKnight and Jira together, send a pilot event, then remove the old value. There is one active shared secret boundary; mismatched rotation fails closed. Production requests fail closed when no webhook secret is configured. The endpoint applies a 60-request-per-minute client limit and uses Jira delivery and issue mutation fences to pre

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Unauthorized: compare configured secret/header or bearer value and confirm proxy preservation. No update after 2xx: verify event type, issue link, project/filter scope, and supported mutation. 429 or concurrency response: stop rapid replay, allow current mutation to finish, then retry one provider delivery.

sections.text: - Create and verify the connection - Troubleshoot Jira

pages.title: Configure the Jira connection
pages.description: Configure Jira credentials, project defaults, and issue creation.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Create Jira credentials with access to the intended project and issue type, and sign in to OpsKnight as an administrator. For Jira Cloud, use the Atlassian account email and an API token created for a dedicated least-privilege integration identity. Confirm it can browse/create/edit/comment in intended projects and use the configured issue types/required fields.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → Integrations → Jira .

sections.heading: Configure the connection
sections.text: 1. Enter the Jira site base URL, without an issue path. 2. Enter the integration account email and API token through the encrypted credential fields. 3. Save, then select Test connection . 4. Open Services → select service → Jira and enter the intended project key plus supported issue mapping/options. 5. Save the service mapping. 6. Open a controlled incident and select the Jira issue action to cr

sections.heading: What OpsKnight does
sections.text: OpsKnight calls Jira REST API v3 with the stored connection, serializes provider/issue mutations, and stores durable issue identity/link/sync state. Rendering an incident does not make hidden Jira requests; synchronization occurs through explicit actions, webhooks, or background work.

sections.heading: Verify it worked
sections.text: Confirm the connection test, service mapping, and issue creation separately. The issue must appear in the intended project/type with expected summary/description/link; the incident must show issue key/URL/provider identity and healthy sync state. Add a controlled comment/status update and verify the configured sync direction.

sections.heading: Remove or rotate the connection
sections.text: Create a replacement API token, update OpsKnight, test, create/update a pilot issue, then revoke the old token. Before disconnecting or changing site/project, inventory linked incidents/action items and service mappings; remote issues are not deleted automatically. Store credentials only through the encrypted settings flow. Project permission and issue-type availability are validated by Jira, not

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Connection test fails: verify base URL, email/token, account activity, outbound DNS/TLS, and Jira response. Issue creation fails after test succeeds: check service project mapping, issue type, required fields/components, and project permissions. Issue may have been created after timeout: inspect incident operation and Jira search before retrying to avoid duplicate work.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: - Configure webhooks - Troubleshoot Jira

pages.title: Troubleshoot Jira
pages.description: Diagnose credentials, project mapping, issue creation, and webhook synchronization.

sections.heading: Connection test fails
sections.text: Confirm the base URL, credentials, project permission, and encrypted settings. Run the test again only after correcting the visible failure. Classify the response: DNS/TLS failure is the network boundary; 401 is the account/token pair; 403 is product or project permission; 404 often means a wrong cloud base URL or project; 429 requires backoff. For Jira Cloud, use the site base URL rather than a c

sections.heading: Issue creation fails
sections.text: Verify the project key and issue type exist and that required Jira fields are available. Inspect the incident operation before retrying. Check the configured project key and issue-type ID against the same Jira site. Inspect Jira's field error response for required custom fields, invalid option IDs, or unavailable reporter/assignee. Before retrying an ambiguous timeout, search Jira and the OpsKnigh

sections.heading: Webhook updates do not appear
sections.text: Confirm the integration is enabled, the shared secret matches, and Jira is sending a handled event. Check for 429 responses and preserve the Atlassian webhook identifier when diagnosing duplicate or delayed delivery. Confirm the Jira webhook URL is the current OpsKnight URL, event subscriptions include the documented issue transitions, and the shared secret is the matching revision. Compare the At

sections.heading: Direction and loop checks
sections.text: Determine whether the missing change is OpsKnight → Jira or Jira → OpsKnight. Check the outbound operation for the former and webhook delivery for the latter. When both directions are enabled, verify origin markers prevent the same update from bouncing repeatedly. Do not fix a loop by disabling all synchronization without preserving the failing event and link evidence.

sections.text: Create a test issue from a non-production incident, change one supported field in Jira, and confirm one correlated update returns to OpsKnight. Preserve incident ID, Jira issue key, operation ID, webhook ID, response status/body, field errors, and timestamps. Redact email addresses and credentials.
