pages.title: Health checks and metrics
pages.description: Build alerts and operational diagnosis from readiness, deep health, Prometheus metrics, and synthetic journeys.
pages.intro: Monitor OpsKnight in layers. Process health removes a failed replica from service; dependency health shows whether a role can work; queue and provider signals show whether work is completing; synthetic response journeys prove the user outcome.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: - Restrict /api/health/deep and /api/metrics to operator networks. - Configure a strong PROMETHEUS SCRAPE TOKEN and store it in the monitoring system's secret store. - Scrape every runtime role/replica where per-process worker state matters. - Label dashboards by environment, deployment identity, runtime role, and instance. - Establish normal queue-age and latency baselines before choosing alert t

sections.heading: Configure platform probes
sections.text: Use: - /api/health for liveness. - /api/health?mode=readiness for startup/readiness. - /api/health/deep for authenticated diagnosis. The shipped Kubernetes and Compose manifests are the baseline for cadence and failure thresholds. Route probes to the local container. Readiness failures should stop new traffic without automatically destroying every replica during a shared database outage; liveness

sections.text: Request metrics with the bearer token and reject non-success responses: Do not put the token in a URL query string. Restrict egress and logs so headers are not captured. See the Prometheus setup and metrics reference for implemented names and labels.

sections.text: Alert on sustained conditions rather than isolated samples: 1. Readiness 503 or JSON unhealthy , grouped by role and deployment. 2. Scheduler missing/stale last-success when that role is expected to schedule. 3. Worker not running or lacking recent successful cycles when expected. 4. Oldest pending critical job age, then general and bulk lane age. 5. Pending/failed notification age and provider fa

sections.heading: Run the diagnostic sequence
sections.text: When OpsKnight appears unhealthy: 1. Check liveness and readiness for each replica, not only the load-balanced endpoint. 2. Compare deploymentId across replicas to detect a mixed rollout. 3. Query deep health and identify the owning role: database, scheduler, worker lane, realtime, notifications, or rollups. 4. Inspect relevant metrics over time, including oldest age and error ratios. 5. Inspect s

sections.heading: Synthetic journey
sections.text: Use a dedicated non-production service in the production control plane with clearly labelled test data: 1. Create or ingest a uniquely keyed test incident. 2. Verify notification delivery to a controlled destination. 3. Acknowledge and confirm escalation completes. 4. Resolve with a synthetic-test note. 5. Verify status projections only if the test service is intentionally included. Do not run a s

sections.heading: Verify monitoring itself
sections.text: At deployment and periodically thereafter: - Prove an unauthorized deep-health and metrics request is rejected. - Temporarily target a safe test alert threshold and confirm routing. - Confirm dashboards distinguish disabled responsibilities from failures. - Confirm alert links open the correct environment and time range. - Confirm retention supports incident and postmortem investigation.

sections.heading: Operate in production
sections.text: Keep readiness probes, Prometheus scraping, durable logs, and synthetic journeys in separate failure domains where practical. Review thresholds after topology, replica, pool, or concurrency changes. Restrict deep-health and metrics endpoints to operator networks, and retain enough history to distinguish a transient provider delay from sustained queue saturation.

pages.title: Use the Health Center

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as an ADMIN , then identify the affected workflow, runtime role, and time window. The page is at Settings → System → Health and is generated on request; it is not a historical monitoring system.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open Settings → System → Health . Record the UTC time, failed or unknown checks, and affected workflow before restarting anything.

sections.heading: Configure the diagnostic context
sections.text: Open Prometheus and centralized logs for the same time window. Determine whether each check is cluster-wide, provider-scoped, or process-local; in split runtime, inspect the role that owns the work.

sections.heading: Understand how Health Center works
sections.text: 1. Open the Health Center and inspect failed, warning, and unknown checks. 2. Identify the owning dependency or runtime role. 3. Correlate the check with metrics and system logs. 4. Apply the relevant runbook and verify recovery with a synthetic workflow. The Health Center summarizes application readiness and operational dependencies. Treat a green page as a point-in-time signal, not proof that de

sections.heading: Interpret statuses
sections.text: - Healthy : the observed condition is within the check's current threshold. - Degraded : the workflow may still operate, but backlog, latency, failures, or incomplete configuration needs attention. - Unhealthy : a measured condition can prevent or materially delay work. - Unknown : the collector had no data or could not read it. Unknown is not healthy; inspect the check details and cited dependenc

sections.heading: What the checks measure
sections.text: - Database tests connectivity. Database capacity inspects connection use against configured/runtime capacity; neither proves query performance. - Migrations compares committed and recorded migration state. Follow the database-migration runbook before changing prisma migrations . - Scheduler reads the singleton scheduler state and heartbeat. A current heartbeat proves only that its owner updated st

sections.heading: Common symptoms
sections.text: - Everything is green but alerts do not arrive: send a synthetic provider event, then inspect inbound delivery, incident creation, paging coverage, notification history, and the relevant worker lane in order. - Scheduler is healthy but jobs are old: the scheduler may be enqueueing correctly while a worker lane is absent, saturated, or repeatedly failing. - A replica check changes on refresh: reque

sections.heading: Verify recovery
sections.text: Refresh until the owning check is healthy, then run the smallest synthetic workflow that proves the user outcome: ingest an alert, create or correlate an incident, deliver to a controlled destination, acknowledge, and resolve.

sections.heading: Undo the mitigation
sections.text: Roll back temporary replica, concurrency, log-level, or provider-routing changes through their source of truth. Keep a mitigation only after its capacity and security effects are reviewed.

sections.text: The result changes on refresh: requests are probably reaching different web replicas; use instance-labelled metrics and centralized logs. Everything is green but delivery fails: inspect inbound integration, incident, paging coverage, notification operation, and provider outcome in order. Unknown has no details: inspect the serving process logs and permissions for the underlying query; unknown is n

pages.title: Scrape OpsKnight with Prometheus
pages.description: Securely collect OpsKnight metrics in Compose, Swarm, Helm, and Kustomize deployments.
pages.intro: GET /api/metrics returns Prometheus text format. A request is authorized by either an authenticated OpsKnight ADMIN session or the single value in PROMETHEUS SCRAPE TOKEN , supplied as an exact Bearer token. Missing, malformed, or incorrect credentials return 401 Unauthorized .

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Generate a high-entropy token, set the same PROMETHEUS SCRAPE TOKEN on every web replica, restart them, and permit the Prometheus network path to the web service. Do not expose /api/metrics directly to the public Internet. Verify the endpoint before configuring Prometheus: Success is HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/plain; version=0.0.4 and lines such as opsknight build info , opsknight active inc

sections.heading: Configure a scrape
sections.text: For a Compose deployment on a private Docker network: - Compose and Swarm: attach Prometheus to a controlled network path and scrape the web runtime through its service address. - Helm: render the selected values and create a ServiceMonitor only when the Prometheus Operator is installed. - Kustomize: keep the Service, authentication secret, and scraper policy in an owned overlay. For a Prometheus

sections.heading: Run the first scrape
sections.text: Trigger one collection from the Prometheus target page or query the endpoint with the configured bearer token. Confirm the target is up before relying on dashboards.

sections.heading: Validation and alert configuration
sections.text: Run the authenticated scrape shown above before enabling collection. A successful response is Prometheus text, not an HTML login page or JSON authorization error. Use rate() or increase() for counters ending in total ; do not sum gauges across replicas unless the metric represents replica-local work that should be aggregated. Group only by labels actually emitted. Start with alerts for oldest pend

sections.heading: Rotate the token
sections.text: OpsKnight accepts one scrape token; it has no overlap set. Update the secret and all web replicas, then update Prometheus. Expect a short scrape interruption unless your deployment can coordinate those changes atomically. Confirm a 200 response with the new token and verify the old token returns 401.

sections.heading: Operate in production
sections.text: Scrape every Web target required by the metric scope in the metrics reference. Protect the token in the monitoring secret store, alert on scrape absence separately from application health, and retain enough history to compare queue age and provider latency across deployments.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: - Prometheus returns 401: check for the exact Authorization: Bearer header and confirm every web replica was restarted with the same value. - The connection is refused or times out: check the Service target, ingress path, Docker/Kubernetes network, TLS trust, and NetworkPolicy. - A series is missing: some series exist only after the corresponding code path runs; also inspect collector-error metric

pages.title: Scale OpsKnight
pages.description: Scale each runtime role from measured demand while preserving database, queue, and provider headroom.
pages.intro: Scale the constrained runtime role, not the deployment as one undifferentiated unit. Web requests, critical/general/bulk jobs, scheduling, and status projection have different bottlenecks. Adding replicas without recalculating database demand can turn queue latency into connection exhaustion.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: Before changing capacity, collect a representative baseline covering a normal peak and at least one failure/retry period: - Request rate and p95/p99 web latency. - Pending jobs and oldest-pending age by worker lane. - Notification backlog, delivery latency, failure rate, and provider throttling. - Scheduler last-success age and missed/stale work. - Status projector backlog and publication latency.

sections.heading: Configure the scaling target
sections.text: Use the symptom to identify the constrained role: - Scale web for sustained request saturation or high request latency after excluding database contention. - Scale critical workers when time-sensitive incident/escalation work ages while database and provider capacity remain healthy. - Scale general workers for sustained ordinary background-job age. - Scale bulk workers for export, maintenance, or

sections.text: 1. Record the baseline, hypothesis, old values, proposed values, and rollback threshold. 2. Change one constrained role or concurrency control at a time. 3. Run the capacity validator against the exact candidate environment. 4. Apply the topology-specific replica change using Compose, Kubernetes/Helm/Kustomize, or Swarm procedures. 5. Wait for new replicas to become ready and for old work to settl

sections.text: Confirm: 1. GET /api/health?mode=readiness is healthy for every required role. 2. Deep health shows expected worker/scheduler state and decreasing oldest-pending ages. 3. Provider throttling and delivery failures do not increase. 6. CPU, memory, rest

sections.text: Return to the recorded replica/concurrency values when database headroom falls below the approved threshold, tail latency or errors rise, readiness becomes unstable, or provider throttling increases. Wait for excess replicas to terminate cleanly, then confirm queue claims and scheduled work still have an active owner. Do not reduce a worker role to zero unless that role is intentionally disabled a

sections.text: Record each accepted change with its workload window, database budget, provider headroom, and rollback threshold. Repeat the same synthetic workload after upgrades or topology changes; a replica count that was safe for one runtime contract is not automatically safe for another.

sections.heading: Recovery procedure
sections.text: 1. Preserve incident IDs, active/candidate IDs, effective mode, fallback reasons, and the relevant audit entries. Do not copy sensitive payloads into tickets. 2. For an incorrect candidate, discard it; leave the known-good active version routing. 3. For active service misrouting, disable that service. Accepted work can retain its original pointers; for an emergency affecting enabled backlog, use g

pages.title: Operate with system logs
pages.description: Use OpsKnight's process-local log viewer and durable container logs without confusing them with audit history.
pages.intro: OpsKnight writes application logs to stdout/stderr and retains a small copy in each Node.js process. System Logs displays that in-process copy. Use it for immediate diagnosis on a single web replica; use your container logging platform for durable, searchable, multi-replica history.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as an ADMIN . Record the affected workflow, UTC time, visible error, runtime role, and any request, incident, notification, delivery, or job identifier before restarting a container or changing log levels.

sections.heading: Open the feature
sections.text: Open System Logs ( /system-logs ) on the affected environment. Keep the platform log explorer open beside it because the UI buffer represents only the web process serving the request.

sections.heading: Supported boundary
sections.text: - The page is available to ADMIN users at System Logs ( /system-logs ). - Entries are newest first. The page requests at most 500 entries from the process serving that request. - The buffer is memory-only. It is erased by a restart and is not shared between web, scheduler, or worker replicas. - The page is not a durable audit record and does not prove that an event did or did not occur elsewhere i

sections.heading: Configure logging
sections.text: Set these variables on every runtime role and restart that role: - LOG LEVEL : debug , info , warn , or error . The default is info . - LOG FORMAT : json for structured output or pretty for human-oriented local output. Production defaults to JSON; other environments default to pretty output. - LOG BUFFER MAX : number of entries retained by each process. The default is 500, values above 5000 are ca

sections.heading: Investigate an error
sections.text: 1. Record the UTC time, visible error, affected incident or job identifier, and the x-request-id response header when available. 2. Open System Logs on the web replica you are inspecting. 3. Select Errors , Warnings , Info , or Debug , or use the level query parameter. 4. Search message, component, or error text. The Component filter performs a case-insensitive partial match. 5. Expand an entry to

sections.heading: Redaction and security
sections.text: The logger redacts context keys associated with passwords, tokens, secrets, authorization, credentials, signatures, email, phone, sessions, cookies, JWTs, and webhook URLs. It also replaces recognized bearer/basic credentials, OpsKnight keys, Slack tokens, AWS access keys, email addresses, and sensitive URL query values inside strings. Redaction is defense in depth, not permission to log secrets.

sections.heading: Verify the diagnosis
sections.text: Reproduce the safe test once, confirm the expected log transition across owning roles, and verify the user workflow recovers. Preserve relevant centralized records before a restart clears process-local evidence.

sections.heading: Undo temporary logging changes
sections.text: Return LOG LEVEL to the approved production value, roll the affected roles, and confirm debug volume stops. Do not reduce durable retention or delete incident evidence as part of cleanup.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: The page says “No logs captured yet” The current web process may have just restarted, LOG BUFFER MAX may be 0 , or no entry at the active LOG LEVEL has occurred. Check that replica's stdout/stderr and configuration. An event appears in container logs but not in System Logs It probably occurred in another replica or runtime role, fell out of the bounded buffer, or preceded a restart. Query the clus

pages.title: Security operations
pages.description: Apply the supported production hardening baseline.
pages.intro: Follow Harden an OpsKnight deployment before exposing the service. Revisit the baseline after changes to identity, proxying, secrets, providers, database access, or runtime topology, and preserve evidence of each control decision.

pages.title: Harden an OpsKnight deployment
pages.description: Establish and verify identity, transport, network, secret, database, runtime, and audit security boundaries.
pages.intro: Hardening is a deployment property, not one application switch. Protect the public edge, internal services, identities, stored credentials, database, runtime roles, and operational evidence. Validate denied paths as deliberately as successful ones.

sections.heading: Prerequisites before production exposure
sections.text: Record the deployment topology, public hostnames, trusted proxy path, database location, secret store, runtime roles, administrative identities, monitoring source networks, and backup encryption/recovery owner. Use a non-production environment with the same boundary design to test changes. Generate unique secrets for this installation. Never copy session, encryption, provider, or database credenti

sections.heading: Configure and protect the external edge
sections.text: 1. Terminate TLS at a maintained ingress, reverse proxy, or load balancer and redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS. 2. Set the public application/authentication URLs to the canonical HTTPS origin. Avoid aliases that create unexpected callback or cookie scope. 3. Forward only required headers and strip client-supplied forwarding headers before adding trusted values. 4. Enable TRUST PROXY HEADERS only when

sections.heading: Protect sessions and authentication
sections.text: - Require secure cookies in production and verify browser cookies carry the intended Secure , HttpOnly , and same-site behavior. - Use a high-entropy authentication/session secret stored outside the image and repository. - Configure idle, maximum-age, and update-age settings according to organizational risk. - Prefer OIDC with MFA enforced by the identity provider for human access. - Restrict OIDC

sections.heading: Protect application encryption keys
sections.text: ENCRYPTION KEY accepts one 64-character hexadecimal key. ENCRYPTION KEYS accepts a bounded keyring in id:64-hex-key entries separated by commas. Key identifiers may contain letters, digits, . , , and - and must be unique. Do not add whitespace. Keep key material in a secret manager or orchestrator secret, never an environment file committed to source. Back it up separately from PostgreSQL while re

sections.heading: Segment networks
sections.text: - Expose only the web/ingress service publicly. - Restrict PostgreSQL and PgBouncer to application and approved administration networks. - Restrict /api/metrics and /api/health/deep to monitoring/operator access and require the scrape bearer token or administrator session as applicable. - Keep worker, scheduler, migration, and projector roles private. - Limit outbound traffic to required identity,

sections.heading: Harden the database
sections.text: 1. Use dedicated application and migration accounts where the deployment supports separation. 2. Give the runtime only the permissions it needs; reserve schema-changing privileges for the controlled migration owner. 3. Require encrypted database transport and validate the server CA when crossing an untrusted network. 4. Keep DIRECT DATABASE URL away from web traffic and transaction-mode PgBouncer;

sections.heading: Harden containers and orchestrators
sections.text: - Pin application images by immutable digest and verify provenance before rollout. - Run as the image's non-root user and prevent privilege escalation. - Drop Linux capabilities not required by the workload; use a read-only root filesystem where validated. - Mount secrets as controlled secrets rather than baking them into images or ConfigMaps. - Give each runtime role the smallest ServiceAccount/R

sections.heading: Minimize application authorization
sections.text: Use the least-privileged role and resource scope for administrators, responders, API keys, SCIM, ChatOps, and integrations. Review: - Global versus scoped incident capabilities. - Service/team membership and private-incident visibility. - API-key scopes, last use, owner, expiry, and revocation. - Slack/Teams identity links and app permissions. - SCIM token storage and provisioning scope. - Notific

sections.heading: Protect inbound and outbound integrations
sections.text: - Use provider signatures or the documented authentication mechanism on every inbound webhook. - Rotate webhook/API secrets after exposure and verify both rejection of the old secret and acceptance of the new one. - Use HTTPS provider endpoints and validate the expected host/tenant. - Scope OAuth applications and bot permissions to documented requirements. - Treat notification contents as potentia

sections.heading: Logging, audit, and evidence
sections.text: Ship application, ingress, orchestrator, database, and identity-provider logs to access-controlled storage with synchronized time. Retain the OpsKnight audit trail according to policy and verify administrators cannot silently modify external copies. Do not log session cookies, bearer tokens, webhook secrets, encryption keys, database URLs, or full sensitive payloads. Validate redaction after confi

sections.heading: Run production acceptance
sections.text: Execute the checks below from both trusted operator networks and an untrusted client path. Record the denied and successful outcomes with the deployment evidence.

sections.heading: Validation checklist
sections.text: Before go-live and after material security changes, prove: 1. HTTP redirects to the canonical HTTPS origin and direct-origin bypass is blocked or controlled. 2. Secure session behavior and OIDC tenant restrictions work. 3. An unauthenticated user cannot reach administration, deep health, or metrics. 4. A lower-privileged user is denied a representative cross-scope incident and administrator action

sections.heading: Incident response and rotation
sections.text: If a secret or administrative identity may be compromised, contain access first, preserve audit evidence, rotate at both OpsKnight and the external provider, revoke sessions/API keys, and verify denied use of the old credential. Encryption-key compromise can require rotation of the keyring plus every credential whose plaintext may have been exposed.

sections.heading: Operate the hardened deployment
sections.text: Review the trust-boundary inventory after every new integration, ingress, identity provider, or runtime role. Re-run denied-path tests, restore tests, audit export checks, and secret-rotation exercises on a defined schedule and after security-sensitive upgrades.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Login loops after enabling HTTPS Check canonical URLs, secure-cookie settings, proxy scheme headers, trusted hop count, and OIDC redirect URI. Do not disable cookie security as a permanent workaround. Requests show the wrong client address or scheme Disable proxy trust until the proxy chain is understood. Strip inbound forwarding headers at the edge, then configure the exact trusted hop count. A w

Back up first, pin artifacts by digest, verify every runtime role, and

pages.title: Operate database migrations
pages.description: Validate, apply, verify, and recover OpsKnight PostgreSQL migrations safely.
pages.intro: OpsKnight ships ordered Prisma migrations in prisma/migrations . Treat schema changes as a deployment operation: take a restorable backup, run one migration owner through a direct PostgreSQL connection, verify the schema, and only then roll out all application replicas.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text: You need the target OpsKnight image or checkout, a PostgreSQL account permitted to alter the OpsKnight schema, and a recent backup that has been restored in an isolated environment. Record the current image digest and application version. Set DIRECT DATABASE URL to PostgreSQL itself. Do not point migration commands at a transaction-mode PgBouncer endpoint. DATABASE URL may still point to PgBouncer

sections.heading: Configure and validate the migration set
sections.text: From the release checkout, with database variables set for the target: prisma:validate inspects committed SQL and migration naming for known unsafe patterns. prisma:health compares the local migration directories with prisma migrations ; unapplied migrations are warnings, while unfinished migrations or database records absent from the release are errors. For a source-based deployment, the complete

sections.heading: Apply migrations by deployment type
sections.text: Docker Compose Use the release image as a one-shot migration owner before updating the long-running services. The packaged entrypoint recognizes OPSKNIGHT MIGRATION ONLY=true , applies migrations and online indexes, then exits instead of starting the application: Use the actual web service name from your Compose file. A zero exit code and the final Migrations and online indexes completed successfu

sections.heading: What container startup does
sections.text: Unless OPSKNIGHT SKIP MIGRATIONS=true (or legacy SKIP MIGRATIONS=true ) is set, the image runs prisma migrate deploy . It retries up to three times with five seconds between attempts and invokes the recovery helper after a failed attempt. If all attempts fail, the container refuses to start against an unknown schema. After migration it enforces required online indexes. The default MIGRATION RECOVE

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text: Run the health check again and inspect the migration table: Success means there are no active records with finished at IS NULL and rolled back at IS NULL . Then verify application readiness, administrator login, incident read/write, scheduler and worker health, queue processing, and one synthetic notification before ending the rollout soak period.

sections.heading: Operate migrations in production
sections.text: Retain migration logs, image digest, schema-health output, and approval with the release record. Run exactly one migration owner, preserve a direct database route, and rehearse restore-based recovery whenever the previous image is incompatible with the new schema.

sections.heading: If a migration fails
sections.text: 1. Stop the rollout and prevent old and new replicas from writing concurrently. 2. Preserve the migration-owner logs and query the failing row in prisma migrations , including its logs column. 3. Compare the database objects with the exact migration.sql from the image. 4. Prefer a reviewed forward fix when committed SQL partially succeeded. 5. Restore the validated pre-upgrade backup only when for

pages.title: Roll back an upgrade
pages.description: Select and execute an image, configuration, forward-fix, or restore recovery path without corrupting schema or losing hidden work.
pages.intro: Rollback is a compatibility decision, not simply selecting an older image. Application specifications can be reversed quickly; committed PostgreSQL migrations and new-version writes are not automatically reversed. Choose the least destructive recovery path that restores safe service.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: Before every upgrade, retain: - Previous immutable image digest and complete configuration. - Migration compatibility assessment for the previous runtime on the new schema. - Verified pre-upgrade backup plus matching encryption keys and secrets. - Current and target schema/migration records. - Rollback triggers, decision owner, RPO/RTO, and communication path. - Commands for the exact Compose, Kub

sections.heading: Configure the recovery path
sections.text: Image/configuration rollback Use when the previous application is explicitly compatible with the current database schema and no new data requires a newer interpretation. Restore the previous digest and configuration without reversing migrations. Forward fix Use when the schema is healthy, data written by the new version must be preserved, and a reviewed patch can restore service faster and more sa

sections.heading: Contain the failed rollout
sections.text: 1. Declare rollback/recovery and record the decision time. 2. Stop further rollout and configuration automation. 3. Preserve application, migration, database, ingress, and orchestrator logs. 4. Record running digests, replica states, current deploymentId , migration rows, and queue ages. 5. If schema/data compatibility is uncertain, stop Web and all write-capable background roles. Keep no mixed-ve

sections.heading: Image-only rollback by topology
sections.text: Docker Compose Restore the previous digest and configuration, render the exact file set, and confirm no migration owner will run: For split mode, ensure all long-running roles return to mutually compatible versions and still use OPSKNIGHT SKIP MIGRATIONS=true . Do not run the old image's migrations against a newer schema. Helm Inspect release history and the candidate previous manifest: Use helm r

sections.heading: Restore-based recovery
sections.text: When image-only rollback is unsafe: 1. Stop ingress and every application role that can write. 2. Preserve the failed database separately for investigation; do not overwrite the only copy. 3. Provision an isolated target database or follow the database provider's controlled point-in-time restore process. 4. Restore the last approved backup and the matching encryption key/keyring and application se

sections.heading: Validation after rollback
sections.text: Verify the same surfaces used to accept an upgrade: - Every runtime role runs the intended previous digest and configuration. - Readiness is healthy; deep health shows scheduler/worker ownership and normal queue ages. - Migration health matches the chosen recovery path. - Database connections, locks, latency, and errors stabilize. - Login and authorization work, including a denied-path check. - A

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: The old application starts but readiness fails Check schema compatibility, configuration/secret version, database connectivity, and runtime role. Stop repeated restarts if logs show unknown columns, enum values, or migration state; the image-only path may be invalid. Helm rollback re-runs an unsafe hook Stop and inspect the historical chart hooks. Recover with a reviewed manifest/configuration tha

sections.heading: Operate after recovery
sections.text: Record trigger, decision, digests, schema state, backup recovery point, lost/reconciled writes, commands, evidence, verification result, and follow-up actions. Preserve the failed artifacts for postmortem analysis and update the rehearsal so the same ambiguity cannot recur. See Upgrade OpsKnight, Database migrations, and Migration troubleshooting.

pages.title: Upgrade to OpsKnight 2.2.0
pages.description: What changes when you upgrade from 2.1.x to 2.2.0, how to prepare, apply, and verify the upgrade, the known limitations, and how to roll back.
pages.intro: This page covers what is different about the 2.1.x to 2.2.0 upgrade. Follow it together with the general upgrade runbook, which covers backups, digests, migration ownership, and topology-specific commands, and keep the rollback runbook open during the change.

sections.heading: What is new in 2.2.0
sections.text: - AI assistants (MCP) : a native MCP server at /mcp with per-person sign-in and human-approved changes. It is off by default ; an administrator turns it on. See AI assistants and its release status. - Guided single sign-on in four steps, specific sign-in messages, role rules v2, group-to-team rules, and linking at scale. See single sign-on. - Service maintenance windows , one-off or recurring. See

From 1.x, first follow Migrate from 1.x. - A recent backup that you have restored in an isolated environment, with the matching encryption keys and secrets. - The previous image digest and its full configuration, recorded so you can return to them. - A maintenance window: an image upgrade from 2.1.x needs the application stopped while migrations run (see Apply the upgrad

sections.text: Read each change below and decide whether it needs action before you upgrade. Database migrations 2.2.0 adds 68 migrations since 2.1.2 (durable event ingestion, MCP, single sign-on, access control, SCIM group roles, Analytics views and weekly digest, theme preference, maintenance windows, live views after renames, and the two release fixes below). They add tables, columns, and indexes and backfill

sections.heading: Apply the upgrade
sections.text: 1. Take and verify the backup, and record the current image digest and configuration. 2. Stop every application role (integrated, web, workers, scheduler). On Helm, the pre-upgrade runtime gate refuses an image upgrade until every application Deployment is at zero replicas; on Compose, Swarm, and Kustomize, stop the roles yourself so no 2.1 process writes to the new schema. 3. Run the migrations o

sections.text: 1. Complete the checks in verify the upgrade, including GET /api/health?mode=readiness on every role and npm run prisma:health reporting no unfinished migration. Settings → System → Health should show no new failures. 2. Send a test event to an existing integration with its existing key and confirm an incident opens and pages. 3. Trigger an existing outgoing service webhook and confirm it is deliv

sections.text: - MCP stays off until an administrator turns it on. Read self-hosted setup and security and data before enabling it, and set up MCP monitoring. - Review the HTTPS webhook switch and legacy integration keys from the steps above and retire them on your own schedule.

sections.text: - Export downloads show no size or progress. Next.js 16.4.5 and later drop a route handler's Content-Length header (vercel/next.js 101854). Audit, report, and dashboard exports still complete and can be checked with their X-Content-SHA256 header; browsers show no size or progress until a Next.js release includes the upstream fix. - Service automation browser certification. The browser suite for se

If you take it, stop every

sections.text: - Helm upgrade fails at -opsknight-auth-cutover : an application Deployment still has replicas or pods. Scale them to zero and retry; see the runtime gate. - A monitoring tool stopped creating incidents: confirm it still sends the same key. Keys rotated after the upgrade no longer accept the old displayed value. - An outgoing webhook is refused: the URL uses http:// , or points at a private or int

pages.title: Upgrade to OpsKnight 2.3.0
pages.description: What changes when you upgrade from 2.2.x to 2.3.0 (Node.js 22 and Prisma 7.3.0 on the node-postgres driver), how to check your database connections first, apply the upgrade, and recover from a failed migration, plus the Slack and Microsoft Teams ChatOps changes and the optional steps to switch them on.
pages.intro: This page covers what is different about the 2.2.x to 2.3.0 upgrade. Follow it together with the general upgrade runbook, and keep the rollback runbook open during the change.

sections.heading: What changes in 2.3.0
sections.text: - Prisma 5.22 to Prisma 7.3.0. The database layer now runs on the node-postgres ( pg ) driver through Prisma's driver adapter. Your existing DATABASE URL , DIRECT DATABASE URL , WEB DATABASE URL , and MCP DATABASE URL values keep working, and the Prisma URL parameters ( connection limit , pool timeout , connect timeout , schema , options , pgbouncer , and the ssl parameters) keep their meaning. Th

sections.heading: Behaviour changes to prepare for
sections.text: Database TLS now verifies certificates Earlier releases treated sslmode=verify-ca and sslmode=verify-full like prefer : the certificate was never verified and the connection could fall back to plaintext. 2.3.0 applies libpq semantics: sslmode 2.3.0 behaviour --- --- disable No TLS. allow / prefer Negotiated like libpq; the certificate is not verified. require TLS, certificate not verified unless s

sections.heading: Slack and Microsoft Teams ChatOps
sections.text: 2.3.0 also brings the Slack and Teams integrations up to date. Nothing here needs action on upgrade; the optional steps below switch on the extra features. What changes for responders: - Slack channel alerts are one live card per incident. The card is edited as the incident is acknowledged, snoozed, escalated, and resolved, with a short thread reply for each change, instead of a new message for ev

sections.heading: Password hashes remain compatible
sections.text: bcryptjs 3 writes new local-password hashes with the $2b$ prefix instead of $2a$ . Existing password hashes remain valid; no password reset or database rewrite is required. The hashing cost stays at 12, and the password policy keeps its 72-byte UTF-8 limit.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: - You run OpsKnight 2.2.x. From earlier versions, upgrade to 2.2.x first. - A restored-and-verified backup with the matching encryption keys and secrets. - The previous image digest and its full configuration. - A maintenance window: the application is stopped while migrations run.

sections.heading: Check database connections before upgrading
sections.text: Run the new image with your existing configuration. It connects every configured database URL with 2.3.0's TLS rules, and reports encryption, certificate verification, and a hint when something would fail (for example a missing sslrootcert ). It never prints credentials. It exits 1 if any configured URL cannot connect. Fix the URL or mount the CA, and rerun until it exits 0 .

sections.heading: Apply the upgrade
sections.text: Follow the upgrade runbook for your topology (Compose, Kubernetes/Helm/Kustomize, Swarm). The image runs prisma migrate deploy through prisma.config.ts , the same migration ownership as before: one migration owner (the Helm migration Job, or the single migration container), never every replica. Migrations stay atomic: the pinned Prisma 7.3.0 CLI applies each migration file in one transaction, as 2

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text: 1. GET /api/health reports healthy on every runtime role, and /api/health/deep confirms the database path. 2. npm run prisma:validate and npm run prisma:health pass against the upgraded database. 3. The logs contain no db.config.warning or db.config.invalid events. These name a URL setting that 2.3.0 ignored or rejected, with the target (never the password). 4. Send a synthetic alert and confirm t

sections.heading: Roll back
sections.text: Prisma 7 does not change the schema, but 2.3.0 includes forward migrations; use the rollback runbook.

sections.heading: Known limits
sections.text: - Prisma is held at 7.3.0 on purpose (see above). Newer 7.x releases and Prisma 8 (a release candidate when 2.3.0 was cut) are separate, certified changes. - The $metrics client API no longer exists in Prisma 7. OpsKnight's pool-pressure checks read the pg pool's waiting-connection count instead, and they report "unknown" (never zero) for clients it did not create.

pages.title: Accessibility support and validation
pages.description: Current accessibility behavior, known boundaries, and an acceptance workflow for critical incident response.
pages.intro: OpsKnight implements keyboard-accessible navigation patterns, a skip-to-main link, visible focus treatment, semantic labels on many icon controls, dialog focus management, screen-reader-only text, and reduced-motion styles. These are implemented behaviors, not a claim that every workflow is conformant with every browser, device, or assistive-technology combination.

sections.heading: Interaction support
sections.text: - Use the skip link to move directly to the main content region. - Use Tab and Shift+Tab to reach controls; dialogs and sheets should expose a named surface and a close path. - Interactive notification rows support keyboard activation when they have a target. Icon-only controls include accessible names in reviewed surfaces. - Keyboard shortcuts supplement visible controls and are disabled in commo

sections.heading: Zoom, reflow, and mobile
sections.text: Navigation and sheets use responsive layouts, and mobile routes provide focused operational workflows. Browser zoom, OS text scaling, long translated labels, virtual keyboards, and narrow devices can still expose local reflow issues. Test the exact pages responders will use rather than treating one responsive page as evidence for the whole product.

sections.heading: Organization acceptance test
sections.text: Before production rollout and after a significant UI/theme upgrade: 1. Choose the supported browser, operating system, screen reader, magnification, voice-control, or switch-control combinations used by your responders. 2. pages.description: Trigger, acknowledge, and resolve deduplicated events through the supported ingestion API.
pages.intro: POST /api/events accepts a normalized event and returns HTTP 202 after it is committed to the durable ingestion inbox. Asynchronous processing is the default; no OPSKNIGHT INGESTION MODE setting is required. The default quota is 120 requests per minute per integration or API key. Administrators can configure shared refill rates and burst limits in ingestion settings. These limits are admission pol

sections.text: - event action is trigger , acknowledge , or resolve . - dedup key is required and is 1–200 characters. Reuse it for every state transition of the same signal. - payload.summary is required and is 1–500 characters. - payload.source is required and is 1–200 characters. - payload.severity is critical , error , warning , or info . - payload.custom details is optional and may contain provider-specific

pages.title: Incidents API
pages.description: List, create, read, and update incidents through the supported REST contract.
pages.intro: All incident endpoints require an API key. Authorization is evaluated as the key owner, including team and incident visibility. The limit is 60 requests per minute per key and operation; creation also enforces a burst ceiling of 120.

sections.heading: List and read
sections.text: GET /api/incidents?limit=50 returns the newest visible incidents. limit defaults to 50, invalid or non-positive values fall back to 50, and values over 200 are capped at 200. GET /api/incidents/{id} returns one visible incident.

sections.heading: Create
sections.text: POST /api/incidents accepts: title (1–500 characters), serviceId , and urgency are required. Urgency is LOW , MEDIUM , or HIGH ; description is at most 10,000 characters and priority at most 20. The service must exist and be accessible to the key owner. Success returns HTTP 201 with data.incident and data.outcome . Send a unique Idempotency-Key for retried create requests. Reusing the key for the

sections.heading: Update
sections.text: PATCH /api/incidents/{id} accepts at least one of: Status is OPEN , ACKNOWLEDGED , RESOLVED , SNOOZED , or SUPPRESSED . Set assigneeId to null to unassign. Updates also support Idempotency-Key . Success returns HTTP 200 with data.incident . Every success response includes both the canonical data object and legacy top-level aliases. New clients should read data .

pages.title: Health endpoint reference
pages.description: HTTP status, authentication, fields, and intended use of liveness, readiness, and deep diagnostics.
pages.intro: OpsKnight exposes a cheap liveness mode, dependency-aware readiness mode, and authenticated deep diagnostics. They answer different questions and should not share the same polling policy.

sections.heading: GET /api/health
sections.text: Without a query parameter, the endpoint runs in liveness mode. It reports process identity, uptime, version, deployment identity, environment, memory, and overall state. Liveness always returns HTTP 200 when the handler responds, even when the JSON status is unhealthy . A liveness consumer must parse the response body if it needs semantic state. Deployment probes use this endpoint to decide whethe

sections.heading: GET /api/health?mode=readiness
sections.text: Readiness checks dependencies required by the current runtime role: The response includes: - database — a SELECT 1 check with a five-second timeout. - notificationControlPlane — provider admission/control-plane certification. - scheduler — healthy, unhealthy, or disabled based on role and ENABLE INTERNAL CRON . - worker — present when the role owns a local worker; evaluates running state and recen

sections.heading: Standard response fields
sections.text: - status : healthy , degraded , or unhealthy . - mode : requested mode; deployments should use only documented liveness and readiness behavior. - timestamp : server timestamp in ISO format. - checks : component results with status plus optional latency, error, and expected fields. - uptime : rounded process uptime in seconds. - version : application version. - deploymentId : build/deployment ident

sections.heading: GET /api/health/deep
sections.text: Deep health is an operator diagnostic endpoint. It requires either: - Authorization: Bearer when the token is configured, or - an authenticated OpsKnight administrator session. An unauthorized request returns HTTP 401 . Do not expose this endpoint through an unauthenticated public ingress. Deep health reports worker, scheduler, realtime control plane, dashboard analytics, pending jobs and oldest a

sections.heading: Probe guidance
sections.text: - Liveness: /api/health - Readiness and startup: /api/health?mode=readiness - Operator diagnosis: /api/health/deep Use the timing and failure thresholds from the selected deployment manifests as the starting point. Ensure the probe reaches the local runtime instance rather than a load balancer that can hide one unhealthy replica.

sections.heading: Interpretation cautions
sections.text: - HTTP 200 alone does not mean liveness JSON is healthy. - A readiness 200 may be degraded ; alert on the JSON state as well as HTTP failures. - disabled means the current role is not expected to own that responsibility. - Healthy readiness does not prove queue latency, provider delivery, or every end-to-end journey is healthy. Combine it with deep health, metrics, and synthetic checks. See Health

pages.title: MCP permissions reference

pages.intro: Assistants act as the person who connected them. A permission (OAuth scope) only narrows what that person can already do; it never adds authority.

sections.heading: Effective access
sections.text: What a connection can do right now is computed on every request: - The ceiling for automatically connected assistants (registration or metadata document) is the current What assistants may do list, not the copy stored when the assistant registered. Lowering it takes effect on the next request; raising it does not widen existing connections. - A connection gives no access at all while it is revoked

sections.heading: On the consent page
sections.text: - View permissions are pre-selected. Change permissions are pre-selected only when the assistant asked for them by name, or the connection being replaced had them. - Any permission can be unticked; Allow needs at least one. - Permissions the person's role can never use are hidden and noted on the page.

sections.heading: Why some changes run directly and others wait for approval
sections.text: Each change is reviewed once and given a risk tier. The tier, not the tool, decides whether it waits for a person. - Routine incident actions run directly (acknowledge, resolve, assign, escalate, reopen, unsnooze, add a note, create an incident, add a watcher or tag). They are what a responder does all night; they already require the person to hold the permission; each is recorded in the audit log

sections.text: Operation columns count catalog operations that need the permission: plain reads, sensitive reads (only while an administrator allows sensitive reads), routine changes (run directly when changes are allowed) and reviewed changes (need human approval first). sections.text: Signing identities rotate through ACTIVE → RETIRING → RETIRED with NEXT staged alongside ACTIVE. Distribute OPSKNIGHT EXECUTION PUBLIC KEYS before activating NEXT. Every enrolled non-revoked Agent must acknowledge its ID. Private keys remain encrypted; the UI exposes only public pins. Agents probe configured binaries and runtime access before heartbeats. Scheduling uses effective capabilities and

sections.heading: Rule and readiness contracts
sections.text: ServiceAutomationRule is an independent configuration identity. Readiness states: PAUSED, BLOCKED, CHECKS REQUIRED, CONFIGURATION VALID, UNKNOWN. Worker health states: HEALTHY, DEGRADED, UNKNOWN. Shared PostgreSQL evidence establishes dispatch and reconciliation freshness. Automatic starts are recorded as skips, not failures, in these cases: - BINDING RATE LIMITED : the rule already started 5 auto

sections.heading: Bounded nonce maintenance
sections.text: Replay nonces are purged using an isolated one-connection maintenance pool. Each batch selects at most 1,000 expired IDs through the createdAt index using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED , its own advisory lock, a one-second statement deadline, 100 ms lock deadline, and 2.5-second transaction deadline. Maintenance alerts The bundled Prometheus rules include alerts for stalled, lagging, and failing maintena

sections.heading: Enterprise safety
sections.text: Deadline handling is shared by worker advancement and recovery. UNKNOWN writes require independent target verification. Agent output passes through shared credential sanitization. Docker inspect/health and Kubernetes diagnostics project operational state rather than dumping payloads.

sections.heading: Idle Agent claim behavior
sections.text: A process-local negative queue hint coalesces concurrent availability probes and expires after one second. Every actual claim checks live Agent status, policy, permissions, and lease fences. Newly available work can incur the one-second hint delay plus the 2–5 second polling cadence.

sections.heading: Current boundaries
sections.text: Runbooks remains Beta in v2.1. Configuration checks, policy evidence, browser journeys, and candidate deployment tests each establish a limited property. Release qualification requires the published server/Agent pair, physical write and recovery evidence, HA/fault scenarios, sustained workload measurements, and human accessibility review. Follow Agent operations for deployment prerequisites.

pages.title: Service automation reference
pages.description: Exact field, condition, action, version, readiness, privacy, and failure contracts for service automation.
pages.intro: For the operator workflow, see Configure and roll out service automation. For a complete snapshot and scripted lifecycle, see the API authoring walkthrough. For the execution model, see Service automation.

sections.heading: Snapshot and field definitions
sections.text: An authoring snapshot contains schemaVersion: 1 , fields , and rules . These objects use strict schemas: unknown properties are rejected. Field and rule identities must be unique. Custom field keys match ^[a-z][a-z0-9 ]{0,63}$ and cannot duplicate built-ins or use sensitive/reserved names. Built-ins are priority (P1–P5), urgency , severity , integration , and source . Custom fields use STRING , EN

sections.heading: Conditions and three-valued matching
sections.text: All conditions within a rule are ANDed. An empty condition list is true. A rule runs only when its combined result is TRUE ; FALSE and UNKNOWN do not match. Supported operators: - Equality: EQ , NE with a canonical scalar value. - Membership: IN , NOT IN with a list of canonical values. - Numeric comparison: LT , LTE , GT , GTE with a number on a numeric field. - State checks: IS SET , IS MISSING

sections.heading: Actions and rule ordering
sections.text: Enrichment ( ENRICH ) allows: - SET PRIORITY : set P1–P5. - SET CONTEXT : write a canonical value into a declared custom field. - ADD TAG : add a tag, deduplicated within the evaluation. All matching enrichment rules run in order, with later field writers winning. Routing evaluates the resulting context and stops at the first matching rule. Routing ( ROUTE ) requires exactly one of: - USE SERVICE

sections.heading: Bounds
sections.text: - UI automation actions and the shared validation/simulation helpers enforce a 256 KiB serialized UTF-8 JSON limit. Validation checks the snapshot; simulation also checks its full input, and UI actions check their full action input. - v2 API requests have a separate 1 MiB body limit. Draft PUT and publication do not invoke the 256 KiB helper: a schema-valid draft above 256 KiB may be saved and pub

sections.text: Draft save requires the current draft revision. Publication checks the expected active version and creates immutable history with a compiled checksum. - Disabled/Shadow publication updates the active version and clears any candidate. - Live publication stages a candidate while the active version keeps routing. If a candidate already exists, publication must supply its expected identity; omission o

sections.text: Global settings control enablement, trace/observation retention, diagnostic value previews, and candidate readiness policy. Retention defaults to 90 days and accepts 1–3,650 days. Observation previews default to false. With previews disabled, discovery retains keyed service-scoped value identities and counts with empty previews. Preview opt-in permits bounded examples, subject to sensitive-value f

pages.title: Migrate from OpsKnight 1.x
pages.description: Inventory, rehearse, execute, verify, and recover a controlled OpsKnight 1.x to 2.0 migration.
pages.intro: Treat this as a data, configuration, and runtime-topology migration—not a container-tag swap.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Schedule a change window and identify migration, database, identity, notification, and rollback owners. Retain the current immutable image, configuration, encryption/authentication secrets, and a database backup proven through an isolated restore. Do not proceed without the exact key needed to decrypt stored provider credentials.

sections.heading: Open the migration inventory
sections.text: Record the 1.x image digest, PostgreSQL version, deployment topology, replica counts, environment, proxy, custom manifests, integrations, identity settings, notification providers, schedules, policies, status configuration, and current migration health. Export audit/configuration records required for comparison.

sections.heading: Understand what changes
sections.text: 2.0 introduces explicit runtime roles, expanded configuration and authorization contracts, durable delivery/control-plane behavior, and additional database/index requirements. Existing data is upgraded in place by ordered Prisma migrations; there is no assumed down migration. A rollback after incompatible writes can require restoring the pre-upgrade database.

sections.heading: Preserve secrets and encryption keys
sections.text: 2.0 refuses to start in production with missing, placeholder, or reused signing secrets. Prepare the secret set before the window: Setting 1.x state Action for 2.0 --- --- --- NEXTAUTH SECRET Set Keep the exact value. Do not rotate it in the same window. Run npm run prisma:validate and npm run pr

sections.text: 1. Open Services → your service → Integrations . 2. Select Add integration , then Generic Webhook . 3. Enter a recognizable name such as Quickstart webhook and create it. 4. Copy the generated webhook URL and integration key from the service page. Treat the key as a credential. Do not paste it into tickets, chat, source control, or screenshots. The URL includes the integration identifier; authenti

sections.text: Configure your test sender to issue POST to the copied URL. Supply the key using the exact transport displayed by OpsKnight; Authorization: Bearer is supported. Send a representative trigger payload from the Generic webhook guide. The body must be valid JSON and no larger than 1 MiB. The integration permits 100 requests per 60 seconds. Do not retry a validation error in a tight loop.

sections.text: Open Incidents and select the new incident. Confirm: - the incident belongs to the intended service; - the title and source match the test event; - its timeline contains the trigger; - the escalation policy started; - the current responder received the expected personal notification. If no incident appears, inspect the HTTP response returned by the endpoint or check system logs and Settings → Syst

sections.text: Send the same logical alert again using the same provider correlation identity. It should update or converge on the existing incident rather than create unrelated incidents. Then send the adapter's recovery action and verify that the correlated incident resolves. Keep the trigger/recovery identity identical. Changing it creates a different correlation stream and may legitimately create another inc

sections.text: 401 Unauthorized: recopy the key, check the authentication header, and confirm the integration is enabled and belongs to the URL's service. A duplicate incident appears: compare the correlation identity in both payloads. Retries must preserve the provider event or alert identity.
