pages.intro: Finish the newcomer journey by responding exactly as an on-call engineer would, then verify the delivery and audit trail.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.text: Sign in as the responder targeted by the test policy and send the trigger from Receive your first alert. Keep the provider event available so you can send recovery after the manual exercise.

sections.heading: 1. Verify notification delivery
sections.text: Open the notification on the configured channel. Confirm its incident title, service, urgency, and link all match the test event. If the provider supports an acknowledgement action, you may use it; otherwise open OpsKnight from the link. In OpsKnight, open Settings → Notifications → History and locate the delivery. Distinguish a queued attempt from a provider-confirmed success. A queued record pro

sections.heading: 2. Inspect and acknowledge
sections.text: 1. Open Incidents and select the triggered incident. 2. Review its service, priority, urgency, description, source, creation time, SLA state, and timeline. 3. Select Acknowledge . 4. Confirm the status and timeline record the acknowledgement and active escalation no longer advances. Acknowledgement means response has begun. It does not assign long-term ownership or resolve the underlying condition

sections.heading: 3. Assign and communicate
sections.text: Assign the incident to the test responder when explicit ownership is needed. Add an investigation note stating that this is a quickstart test and record what was verified. If ChatOps is configured, confirm the incident card updates; do not create a production war room for this exercise. Expected result: assignment and notes appear as separate timeline events. Assignment does not replace acknowledg

sections.heading: 4. Resolve the incident
sections.text: 1. Select Resolve . 2. Enter a useful summary, for example Quickstart webhook and responder delivery verified; no production impact . 3. Confirm resolution. 4. Verify the incident is Resolved , the timeline retains creation, acknowledgement, assignment, notes, and resolution, and no later policy step fires. If you also send provider recovery, use the same correlation identity. Repeated recovery sh

sections.heading: 5. Review the operational evidence
sections.text: Check the incident delivery details and notification history for each attempted channel. Confirm the policy target and resolved responder were the ones expected. An Admin can also review Audit Logs for the configuration and lifecycle actions performed during setup. The newcomer journey is complete only when all of these are true: - the external event created one incident on the correct service; -

sections.heading: If a step fails
sections.text: Use the focused guides for acknowledgement, assignment, resolution, delivery inspection, and notification troubleshooting.

pages.title: What is OpsKnight?
pages.description: Understand the product model before configuring your first response workflow.
pages.intro: OpsKnight receives operational events, correlates them into incidents owned by services and teams, escalates to on-call responders, delivers notifications, and records the response lifecycle. The core flow is: Services define operational ownership. Teams group responders. Schedules decide who is on call. Escalation policies decide who is contacted and when. Notification routing chooses the deliver

pages.title: Troubleshooting
pages.description: Diagnose OpsKnight symptoms using observable evidence.
pages.intro: Troubleshooting is organized by symptom rather than component internals. Each page must identify observable signals, safe diagnostic steps, likely causes, recovery actions, and escalation evidence. Choose the symptom area: - Installation - Login and access - Notification delivery - Incident processing - Runbook execution and Agent health - Inbound integrations - Status pages - Workers - Scheduler

pages.title: Troubleshoot database failures
pages.description: Diagnose database and PgBouncer connectivity before changing application state.
pages.intro: For connection errors, pool exhaustion, or startup timeouts, use Database or PgBouncer connections fail. Capture the failing runtime role, redacted connection target, database health, pool metrics, and exact error before changing credentials or pool size.

pages.title: Database or PgBouncer connections fail
pages.description: Diagnose URLs, TLS, authentication, pool mode, and connection budgets.
pages.intro: Test name resolution and TCP reachability from the failing runtime, then validate URI encoding, database name, credentials, TLS mode, CA material, and PgBouncer user list. Compare pool mode and direct migration URL requirements. Sum configured connections across replicas and workers; saturation can resemble an authentication failure. Never print full database URLs in shared logs.

sections.heading: Diagnostic sequence
sections.text: 1. Identify whether the failure affects the web, scheduler, migration, or worker role. 2. From that container or pod, resolve the database hostname and test TCP port 5432. 3. Run the readiness endpoint and inspect the first database error in runtime logs. 4. Compare DATABASE URL with DIRECT DATABASE URL ; migrations must not use a transaction-pooling endpoint when a direct endpoint is required. 5.

sections.heading: Recover and verify
sections.text: Correct the secret or connection budget, restart only affected roles, and confirm readiness plus a successful migration-health check. Preserve redacted URLs, runtime role, PostgreSQL/PgBouncer logs, and connection counts for escalation. Observe at least two readiness intervals and one real read/write workflow. For a pool-capacity fix, also confirm waiting clients return to baseline instead of mere

pages.title: Troubleshoot incident processing
pages.description: Diagnose incident lifecycle actions that do not complete.
pages.intro: Use Incident lifecycle action is stuck when acknowledge, assign, escalate, resolve, or related processing does not converge. Record the incident ID, attempted action, timestamp, actor, UI/API result, worker health, and relevant logs.

pages.title: Incident lifecycle action is stuck
pages.description: Diagnose an acknowledgement, assignment, escalation, or resolution that does not converge.
pages.intro: Refresh the canonical incident, inspect the latest timeline and audit entries, and identify whether the request failed before or after the database mutation. Check authorization, current status, idempotency key, outbox state, and worker health. Do not directly edit lifecycle columns. Preserve the incident identifier, request identifier, actor, attempted transition, and timestamps.

sections.heading: Determine where progress stopped
sections.text: 1. Reload the incident and compare its canonical status with the action response. 2. Inspect timeline and audit entries for the same actor and request identifier. 3. Check the HTTP response: 403 indicates authorization, 409 indicates a stale/conflicting transition, and 5xx requires server and worker inspection. 4. Inspect queued side effects only after confirming the database transition. Canonical

sections.heading: Verify recovery
sections.text: Confirm one canonical transition, one matching audit entry, and eventual message, status-page, and ChatOps convergence. Escalation evidence should include incident ID, old/new status, request ID, actor, response code, and relevant worker errors.

pages.title: Troubleshoot installation
pages.description: Diagnose startup and first-run failures systematically.
pages.intro: Begin with Application startup fails. Identify the failing container or runtime role, preserve its first error, then check configuration, secrets, database reachability, migrations, filesystem permissions, and dependency health in that order. If the application responds but shows HTTP 421, use Recover from Misdirected Request. It covers Application URL, environment origins, proxy trust, aliases, a

pages.title: Recover from 421 Misdirected Request
pages.description: Diagnose and safely repair canonical-host, proxy-header, alias, and Application URL mismatches.
pages.intro: HTTP 421 means the request reached OpsKnight, but its application host was not authorized. This firewall prevents an attacker-controlled Host header from influencing links, redirects, cookies, or callbacks. Do not disable it by exposing the application port directly.

sections.heading: 1. Identify the host OpsKnight receives
sections.text: Record the browser URL, proxy/ingress host rule, direct Host , and—when proxy trust is enabled—the final X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto . Inspect sanitized proxy and application logs; never log cookies, authorization headers, or secrets. If TRUST PROXY HEADERS=false , OpsKnight ignores forwarded host/protocol for authoritative routing. If it is true , the trusted edge must overwrite X-Forw

sections.heading: 2. Compare every configured origin
sections.text: Compare: - Settings → System → App URL ( SystemSettings.appUrl ); - NEXTAUTH URL ; - NEXT PUBLIC APP URL ; - exact comma-separated APP HOST ALIASES ; - DNS, TLS certificate, and proxy/ingress host. Include a public non-standard port consistently. Remember that TRUSTED PROXY HOPS affects client IP only and cannot fix a host/protocol mismatch.

sections.heading: 3. Check expected special cases
sections.text: The canonical apex and its www counterpart receive special handling. Arbitrary subdomains do not: app.example.com does not implicitly authorize www.app.example.com , admin.example.com , or any wildcard. REDIRECT TO CANONICAL HOST=false changes redirection, not authorization. Before the first user exists, /setup remains reachable so you can establish the correct canonical host. Verify its Applicati

sections.heading: 4. Restore an authorized path
sections.text: Use this supported order: 1. Try the saved Application URL host or either configured environment URL host. 2. If DNS changed, temporarily restore routing/TLS for one already-authorized host. 3. Otherwise add the exact recovery hostname to APP HOST ALIASES in deployment configuration and roll out Web/application. 4. Sign in through that valid host and correct Settings → System → App URL . 5. Align

sections.heading: Expected result
sections.text: The intended public HTTPS host serves readiness, login, and the application; redirects and generated links stay on it; provider callbacks match it; and an unrelated host still returns 421.

sections.heading: Related guides
sections.text: - Application URL and host routing - Reverse-proxy contract - Initial setup

pages.title: Application startup fails
pages.description: Diagnose migration, configuration, database, and runtime startup failures.
pages.intro: Capture the failing runtime role and first causal error. Validate required secrets, external URLs, database URLs, encryption-key format, database reachability, and migration health. Confirm that a migration-only process is not being used as a web or worker runtime. Correct one boundary at a time and preserve the original logs; repeated blind restarts can hide a deterministic configuration failure.

sections.heading: Triage by startup phase
sections.text: 1. Inspect the first fatal line, not the final restart-loop message. 2. If environment validation failed, correct the named value and its secret mount. 3. If database readiness failed, use the database connection runbook. 4. If migration failed, stop competing migration owners and use the migration runbook. 5. If Next.js starts but readiness fails, query /api/health?mode=readiness from inside the

sections.heading: Completion criteria
sections.text: The runtime remains healthy through multiple probe intervals, the migration health check is clean, the login page loads through the public origin, and the expected scheduler/worker ownership is visible for the selected topology.

pages.title: Troubleshoot integrations
pages.description: Diagnose rejected or misclassified inbound webhook events.
pages.intro: Use Integration webhook is rejected for authentication, signature, schema, size, or rate-limit failures. Preserve the provider delivery ID, timestamp, HTTP status, response body, target integration, and a redacted payload; never paste the webhook secret into a ticket.

pages.title: Integration webhook is rejected
pages.description: Diagnose authentication, signature, replay, rate-limit, and payload failures.
pages.intro: Record the provider, endpoint, status code, delivery identifier, and timestamp. Confirm the integration exists, is enabled, and matches the route type. Then check key resolution, signature secret and timestamp, replay claim, rate limit, content type, and schema validation. Redact credentials and payload secrets before sharing evidence. Replaying the same genuine delivery identifier may be intentio

sections.heading: Interpret the response
sections.text: - 400 : missing integration ID, malformed JSON, or provider schema mismatch. - 401 or 403 : invalid key/signature, disabled integration, or type mismatch. - 413 : request exceeds the ingestion body limit. - 429 : per-integration rate limit; honor the returned retry guidance. - 503 : an identical delivery is already being processed or a dependency is unavailable. Do not assume every route uses ever

sections.heading: Verify recovery
sections.text: Send one trigger and its matching recovery event to a non-production service. Confirm one incident is created, recovery updates that incident, and replaying the same signed delivery does not create a second lifecycle mutation.

pages.title: Troubleshoot Kubernetes deployments
pages.description: Diagnose OpsKnight pods that do not become ready.
pages.intro: Use Kubernetes pods are not ready. Check events, pod status, the failing container, probes, configuration and secret mounts, database/DNS/network reachability, and migration state before restarting workloads.

pages.title: Kubernetes pods are not ready
pages.description: Diagnose migrations, probes, configuration, policy, resources, and dependencies.
pages.intro: Identify the workload and inspect events, termination reason, logs, rendered configuration, secret references, migration job, and readiness response. Check NetworkPolicy, ServiceAccount, resources, database DNS and TLS, ingress origin, and runtime-role ownership. Do not weaken probes until the underlying readiness dependency is understood.

sections.heading: Diagnostic commands
sections.text: Start with the pod status rather than deleting it: Pod state Next check Healthy result --- --- --- Pending describe pod , quota, node selectors, taints, PVCs A node is assigned and all volumes bind ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff Event message, image digest, pull-secret reference Registry authentication succeeds and the pinned digest pulls Init: Init-container or migration Job logs Migration exits

pages.title: Sign-in troubleshooting
pages.description: Fix single sign-on, administrator test and emergency access problems.
pages.intro: - Sign-in problems with single sign-on — every message a person can see, by the message and code shown on screen. - Administrator test failures — why your test sign-in failed and how to fix it. - Emergency access — problems with emergency recovery identities.

pages.title: Administrator test failures
pages.description: Why your test sign-in in Test & activate failed, how to read the claims OpsKnight received, and how to fix each cause.
pages.intro: When your test sign-in in 4 · Test & activate fails, the result page names the cause, shows What OpsKnight received , and has a button that opens the step where you fix it. Production sign-in is never changed by a test. What OpsKnight received lists every claim name in the ID token and the values of the claims OpsKnight uses: email (masked), email verified , hd , org id , tid , groups , roles and

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text: The OpsKnight address changed during the test Code ORIGIN CHANGED . The test started on one application URL and finished on another. Fix: Make sure everyone uses the same canonical URL, then run the test again. The Review the application URL button opens 1 · Connect provider . Your identity provider account is outside the allowed organization Code ORGANIZATION REJECTED . The organization ID in you

pages.title: Troubleshoot emergency access
pages.description: Diagnose emergency password, hardware-key enrollment, drill, session and alert failures.
pages.intro: For custodians using /login/emergency and administrators using Settings → System → Emergency Access . See setup and custody and lockout recovery.

sections.heading: Enrollment or sign-in fails
sections.text: Use the recorded account identifier and an active independently held hardware key. Complete its PIN/user-verification ceremony. Synced passkeys are rejected. Verify HTTPS, the exact canonical origin and original RP hostname; reverse-proxy host changes and credentials enrolled on another hostname fail origin/RP verification. Request a new challenge after cancellation, expiry, browser changes or reu

sections.heading: Readiness disappears
sections.text: Enrollment/revocation invalidates that identity's previous drill and all its sessions. Sign in again using the identity's current configured credential. Disabled identities and drills older than 90 days do not count. Required activation needs two independently held ready identities; repeat drills after changes. A browser login test for SSO is separate from both independent recovery drills and disc

sections.heading: Session ends while the page stays open
sections.text: A recovery session expires after 60 minutes absolutely or 15 minutes without deliberate visible interaction. Background requests and passive reads do not refresh idle time. Sensitive operations need a fresh credential proof within five minutes. Reauthenticate the current identity; this rotates the capability while retaining the absolute cap. An expired session requires a new sign-in.

sections.heading: Email alerts remain pending
sections.text: Inspect Diagnostics and the active administrators' in-app security alerts. Durable email intents remain pending when the provider/worker is unavailable and retry with backoff and leases. Restore configured email delivery and scheduler maintenance, then verify delivery. Authentication mutations must commit their mandatory audit and alert intents; database write failures reject the mutation.

sections.heading: No identity or database is available
sections.text: Use the separately held backup/second identity, or the imported legacy password bridge if it has not been retired. That bridge opens only recovery. If all credentials are lost or PostgreSQL is unavailable, follow the external infrastructure recovery procedure. Environment edits and import-record deletion are not supported application recovery.

sections.heading: Alert bursts and distributed failure traffic
sections.text: Every failed attempt retains an individual security event and mandatory audit. Anonymous failure notifications are aggregated in a shared PostgreSQL five-minute window across IPs and web replicas: the first failure and twentieth failure generate alerts to at most 100 active administrators each. Further attempts remain searchable in Diagnostics without another email/in-app fan-out in that window. S

sections.heading: A stale recovery cookie accompanies a valid administrator session
sections.text: Expired or revoked recovery cookies are ignored when a separately valid ordinary administrator session exists. Authentication dashboard responses clear the stale cookie. This does not convert a recovery principal into an administrator. If the normal session was also revoked by policy or the user was demoted, sign in again through an allowed method. Never preserve an old rotated cookie for automati

sections.heading: Origin conflict and infrastructure outage
sections.text: Use the pinned-origin recovery procedure. The pin must be the exact trusted WebAuthn origin; a different hostname cannot reuse old hardware credentials. Database outage, missing policy, and missing encryption keys remain infrastructure incidents. Restore from governed backups and account for previously revoked state reappearing. Test the repaired public ingress on each replica before closing the i

sections.heading: Independent emergency password fails
sections.text: Select Password and use the emergency account identifier and generated recovery secret, not an ordinary user's email/password. Passwords are displayed once during creation or rotation and cannot be recovered from their salted hash. Check the vault copy and current method with an authorized custodian; a rotated password or disabled identity fails immediately. Failure messages do not confirm whether

pages.title: Sign-in problems with single sign-on
pages.description: Every message a person can see when signing in with single sign-on, what it means, and how to fix it.
pages.intro: When a single sign-on sign-in does not work, the sign-in page names the problem, says what to do next, and shows a reference ID . The person can select Copy details for your administrator to send you the message, code and reference. To investigate: search the server log for the reference ID. The log entry [Auth] OIDC sign-in rejected holds the internal reason, and the audit log has a matching LOGI

sections.heading: Messages on the sign-in page
sections.text: Your administrator needs to approve your first SSO sign-in Code SSO LINK NOT APPROVED . An OpsKnight account already uses this email address. For safety, it is connected to single sign-on only after an administrator approves it. What the person sees next: Your administrators have been notified. Try again after they approve the request, or contact them directly. What an administrator can do: Approv

sections.heading: Messages after being signed out
sections.text: When a session ends, the sign-in page says why: Reason Message Detail ------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- SESSION REVOKED BY POLICY Your organization changed how you sign in Your administrator changed the sign-in policy, which ended earlier sessions. AUTHENTICATION POLICY DE

sections.heading: Password sign-in
sections.text: - Incorrect email or password — the email or password is wrong, the account has no password, or password sign-in is blocked by policy. It never reveals which. - Your OpsKnight account is disabled — shown only after the correct password, so it cannot be used to probe accounts.

sections.heading: Still stuck
sections.text: - Your own test sign-in fails: see administrator test failures. - You are locked out: see SSO lockout recovery.

pages.title: Troubleshoot notification delivery
pages.description: Locate failures across routing, queues, providers, and recipient endpoints.
pages.intro: Use Notifications are not delivered. Trace one notification from routing decision to intent, queue claim, provider attempt, provider response, and recipient endpoint. Do not retry blindly until you know whether the prior attempt may already have reached the user.

pages.title: Notifications are not delivered
pages.description: Trace recipient eligibility, endpoint state, worker attempts, and provider feedback.
pages.intro: Confirm that the event is enabled for the service, the escalation target resolves, the recipient and channel are eligible, and the endpoint is healthy. Then inspect the notification intent, worker claim, attempt history, provider response, and feedback status. Check quiet hours, opt-out, capacity limits, and retry schedule. Retry only transient failures; repair or replace invalid endpoints first.

sections.heading: Trace one durable notification
sections.text: 1. In Settings → Notifications → Operations , filter by incident, recipient, channel, and the event time. 2. If no intent exists, verify service routing, escalation target resolution, event type, user preferences, and endpoint eligibility. 3. If an intent is deferred, inspect quiet hours and provider admission capacity. 4. If attempts are retrying, inspect the provider code and next-attempt time.

pages.title: Troubleshoot Runbooks
pages.description: Diagnose waiting executions, unavailable Agents, confidential transport errors, ambiguous targets, uncertain outcomes, and common configuration problems.
pages.intro: Begin with the incident execution timeline and Runbooks → Health . Record the execution/version, affected step, target, timestamps, and error code without including secret values or enrollment tokens.

sections.heading: Execution is waiting for approval
sections.text: Symptoms : Step status shows WAITING APPROVAL . Diagnosis : 1. Check that the responder has runbook.approve and access to the incident. 2. Inspect the resolved plan before approving. Resolution : - If the responder has permission, inspect and approve the exact plan. - A changed-plan error requires reviewing the current plan; do not bypass the digest check or reuse old approval. - If the circuit br

sections.heading: Execution is waiting for an Agent
sections.text: Symptoms : Step status shows WAITING AGENT . Diagnosis : 1. Check the binding's resolved target. 2. Check Agent heartbeat (must be within 90 seconds). 3. Check configured vs. effective capabilities. 4. Check local policy and platform permissions. 5. Confirm Agent is not revoked. 6. For a pool, check membership and shared-target assumptions. Resolution : - Review Agent errors and control-plane conn

sections.heading: HTTPS required for secret-backed steps
sections.text: Symptoms : Execution fails with confidential transport error. Diagnosis : 1. Check the Agent's control-plane URL configuration. 2. Verify HTTPS is being used (not HTTP). 3. Verify certificate trust on the Agent host. Resolution : - Configure the Agent with a trusted HTTPS control-plane URL. - Verify certificate trust, ingress/TLS termination, and correct trusted-proxy configuration. - Check the se

sections.heading: Ambiguous LOCAL HOSTS write target
sections.text: Symptoms : Write fails because target is ambiguous. Diagnosis : A multi-member LOCAL HOSTS pool represents multiple machines and cannot determine which should execute the write. Resolution : - Change the service binding to target a specific Agent . - Only use a SHARED TARGET pool when its members genuinely operate the same shared target. - Relabeling a pool mode is not a safety fix.

sections.heading: UNKNOWN outcome or lost lease
sections.text: Symptoms : Step shows UNKNOWN status. Cause : The Agent lost contact or its lease expired after a write started. The write may or may not have executed. Resolution : 1. Inspect the actual target before any retry — the write may have already executed. 2. Preserve logs and durable Agent state, including identity and spool. 3. Do not delete the identity volume to clear an error. 4. Cancellation is a

sections.heading: Spool or worker attention required
sections.text: Symptoms : Health page shows spool depth, dead letters, or worker issues. Diagnosis : 1. Check pending results and dead letters on the Agent. 2. Check storage availability on the Agent host. 3. Check Agent connectivity to control plane. Resolution : - Follow Agent operations for spool recovery. - In split deployments, inspect the Runbook Worker readiness and logs separately — web-process status is

sections.heading: JSON edits did not save
sections.text: Symptoms : Changes made in Advanced JSON editor are lost. Cause : JSON was not applied to the builder before saving. Resolution : 1. Apply Advanced JSON to the builder before saving. 2. The unapplied-changes warning blocks saving across tabs. 3. Refresh JSON from the builder only if you intend to discard unapplied edits. 4. Publishing publishes the saved draft , not unsaved editor contents.

sections.heading: Preview changed or prerequisites are blocked
sections.text: Symptoms : PREVIEW STALE error or blocked capability/secret check. PREVIEW STALE The immutable version selection, resolved inputs, target, or planned actions changed after preview. Generate a fresh preview and review it before executing. Blocked prerequisites A blocked capability/secret check prevents execution from the preview panel: 1. Check Agent heartbeat and capabilities. 2. Check the target'

sections.heading: A rule save conflicts
sections.text: Symptoms : Error when saving rule configuration. Cause : A configuration revision conflict — someone changed the rule after you loaded it. Resolution : 1. Reload the page. 2. Review the saved version. 3. Reapply your intended changes. 4. A successful trigger save affects future incident events only.

sections.heading: A suggestion cannot execute
sections.text: Symptoms : Suggestion shows but preview/execution are disabled. Rule detached - The suggestion is retained for history with Rule detached label. - Preview and execution are disabled. - Dismiss it if no longer useful. Rule paused - Paused rules cannot start their suggestions until reactivated. - Detach archives the rule instead of deleting its historical identity.

sections.heading: v2 API execution returns HTTP 400
sections.text: Symptoms : RUNBOOK DEFINITION INVALID error from API. Cause : A non-empty parameters object was sent with a resolved rule. Resolution : - Omit parameters or send {} for bound executions. - Use the rule's saved inputs. - Or deliberately execute an unbound workflow with validated inputs.

sections.heading: Replay nonce maintenance is falling behind
sections.text: Symptoms : Rising oldest-expired-age gauge or failed-batch counter. Diagnosis : 1. Inspect nonce purge metrics. 2. Check database latency, lock contention, and worker logs. 3. Purging runs in a separate one-connection maintenance pool; slow batches do not overlap. Resolution : - Investigate database and maintenance throughput. - Skipped or failed batches preserve the last successful age observatio

sections.heading: Setup commands cannot be copied
sections.text: Symptoms : Installation page does not show commands. Cause : Missing verified release manifest, unconfirmed Agent-reachable HTTPS URL, or expired token. Resolution : - Review the verified release manifest. - Confirm Agent-reachable HTTPS URL. - If the token expired or was abandoned, revoke the enrollment and create a fresh token. - A consumed token cannot substitute for a lost private identity.

sections.heading: Worker health shows UNKNOWN
sections.text: Symptoms : Health page shows UNKNOWN worker status. Diagnosis : 1. Inspect durable worker heartbeats in the database. 2. Check if the Runbook lane and scheduler are deployed and running. 3. Confirm successful dispatch and reconciliation within 90 seconds. Resolution : - An empty queue alone is insufficient evidence of health. - Deploy or restart the Runbook Worker. - For Agent readiness failures,

sections.heading: Execution evidence
sections.text: The execution detail page shows step and attempt status, queue time, claim time, start/completion, claimed Agent, target, lease expiry, approval identity/digest, bounded output, and artifacts. Troubleshooting guidance separates: Category Examples ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------- Configuration errors Invalid inputs, missing steps Policy rejection Agent policy

sections.heading: Quick reference
sections.text: Problem First check ---------------------- ---------------------------------------- Step waiting Agent heartbeat + capabilities UNKNOWN outcome Inspect actual target Secret transport error HTTPS + certificate trust Ambiguous target Use specific Agent for writes Stale preview Regenerate preview Save conflict Reload and reapply API 400 error Remove parameters for bound executions Worker UNKNOWN Chec

sections.text: - Health monitoring for the health dashboard. - Runbook reference for limits and state machines. - Agent operations for deployment troubleshooting.

pages.title: Troubleshoot the scheduler
pages.description: Diagnose maintenance and scheduled work that is not processing.
pages.intro: Use Scheduler is not processing maintenance. Verify that exactly the intended scheduler role is running, its health and database lease are current, clocks agree, and queued work is eligible before forcing or duplicating execution.

pages.title: Scheduler is not processing maintenance
pages.description: Diagnose missing ownership, stale progress, locks, and database failures.
pages.intro: Confirm exactly one intended scheduler ownership model is active. Inspect runtime role, readiness, scheduler profile, last successful progress, locks, database errors, and queued downstream work. Verify clock and time-zone assumptions. Do not run ad hoc duplicate schedulers against production to compensate for a broken owner.

sections.heading: Diagnostic sequence
sections.text: 1. Confirm the deployment topology and which runtime owns scheduling. 2. Check readiness and the last successful scheduler heartbeat/progress time. 3. Inspect database advisory locks and errors around the first missed interval. 4. Verify system time, configured time zones, and the affected schedule window. 5. Confirm downstream jobs are being enqueued and that their worker lane is healthy. Build a

pages.title: Troubleshoot service automation
pages.description: Diagnose access, draft recovery, extraction, routing, candidate evidence, delivery, Runbook context, and privacy cleanup failures.
pages.intro: Start by recording the service ID, incident ID, active/candidate version IDs, effective mode, and exact failure message. Keep source payloads and credentials out of diagnostic tickets. Use the production procedure for global changes and the reference for exact contracts.

sections.heading: The workspace is read-only or unavailable
sections.text: Confirm the actor is active and has automation read capability. Administrators, Responders, and Auditors can read automation under their resource authorization; Auditors do not gain draft editing or sensitive sample access. A Responder needs membership in the service's owning team to edit. Publication, candidate activation, and mode changes require administrator privilege; API scopes cannot elevat

sections.heading: Draft changes disappeared or publishing is paused
sections.text: Check whether the UI showed Saved, Unsaved, Offline, Save failed, or Conflict. A local recovery copy depends on browser storage and is scoped to account/service. Review both copies before choosing Keep my copy or Reload their changes; download local work before replacing it. An API 412 means a reviewed precondition is stale. Refetch and reconcile rather than automatically overwriting the newer dra

sections.heading: A field is missing, unmapped, or absent from discovery
sections.text: Inspect the actual integration type, EVENT/PROVIDER source, ordered mapping paths, canonical type, and aliases. The first nonblank selected value is normalized; a later mapping does not repair an earlier invalid scalar. Test the same input with the intended integration ID and an explicit provider sample. A missing discovery suggestion can be caused by traversal/cardinality limits, sensitive filter

sections.heading: A rule matches in Test but production differs
sections.text: Verify you tested the same snapshot as the published active version and supplied the same classification/integration context. Test is not event ingestion and does not certify deduplication, provider delivery, or an active mode. Check global enablement and the stored/effective service modes. A draft does not route. While Live, a new publication is only a candidate until activation. An accepted queu

sections.heading: A negative condition did not match
sections.text: Missing/unmapped values do not satisfy ordinary negative comparisons. Inspect IS MISSING or IS UNMAPPED explicitly. IS SET includes Unmapped; use a recognized value comparison when valid canonical data is required. All conditions in a rule are ANDed. For OR, create separate rules and review their order.

sections.heading: Routing or priority is unexpectedly overridden
sections.text: All matching enrichment rules run in order; later writers to the same field win. Routing stops at the first matching rule. Move an overly broad rule or catch-all below specific rules. Check warnings about priority conflicts or shadowed rules. Changing priority does not change urgency. Selecting no escalation suppresses responder escalation but does not discard the incident or mute every notificati

sections.heading: Publication or activation rejects a dependency
sections.text: Check referenced escalation policies, valid responder targets, service default policy safety, and destination ownership/enablement. Disabled rules are still validated. A restored historical snapshot can reference a policy/destination that is no longer usable. Repair the dependency or draft, validate again, and repeat the reviewed publication/activation flow; do not bypass database guards.

sections.heading: Live reactivation asks for review again
sections.text: Every request selecting Live repeats mode activation checks, including recovery from Disabled or Shadow and requests while already Live. The current active version needs valid dependencies, and absent Shadow evidence/errors can require explicit acknowledgement. Candidate promotion additionally uses its own readiness policy. Prior Live usage is not a permanent waiver.

sections.heading: Candidate activation is blocked or counts look inconsistent
sections.text: Confirm evidence belongs to the candidate being reviewed. Review the seven-day window, daily-bucket age, quantity floor, error/fallback rate, and pending/processing allowance. Pending-work samples can be truncated lower bounds. Overlapping route/priority/suppression/error counters must not be added as independent events. Let workers drain a backlog above policy; acknowledgement does not bypass it.

sections.heading: A channel notification is missing or appears duplicated
sections.text: Separate route matching, durable intent creation, and provider delivery. Confirm an enabled destination owned by the service, then inspect Slack/Teams delivery records and worker/provider health. Retries are accounted for by the respective pipelines, but service notifications and supplemental automation messages can be independent intended sends. Inspect each message's origin before concluding a s

sections.heading: Runbook conditions cannot use expected context
sections.text: Confirm the incident has an intact successful Live decision. No Live decision, fallback, missing captured context, and checksum failure make response context unavailable. Historical incidents are not rebuilt from the current draft. A field removed from the captured schema or a type-incompatible condition is invalid. Runbook EXISTS means Recognized, unlike automation IS SET. Review the binding's ow

sections.heading: Preview cleanup is failed or observations stopped changing
sections.text: Keep preview storage disabled before retrying failed cleanup as an administrator. Check cleanup status and worker health until COMPLETE; SUPERSEDED indicates a later opt-in, not proof of physical removal. Preview hiding precedes physical cleanup. Observation cardinality bounds can stop admitting new identities while existing counts continue; retention is asynchronous. Diagnose worker lag, privacy

sections.heading: Confirm recovery
sections.text: After correcting the cause, send one controlled new incident for each affected route and one missing/unmapped case. Verify effective mode, pinned version, final priority, responder outcome, intended provider delivery, and Runbook eligibility where applicable. Confirm backlog/cleanup progress separately. Preserve the reviewed change and evidence in the audit trail.

pages.title: Troubleshoot status pages
pages.description: Diagnose a public status page that does not reflect current incidents or service state.
pages.intro: Use Status page is not updating. Confirm the single configured page, service inclusion, incident visibility and status, projection/worker health, cache behavior, and public route before editing incident data.

pages.title: Status page is not updating
pages.description: Diagnose projection, routing, caching, and privacy configuration.
pages.intro: Confirm the intended page is enabled and the service is linked. Inspect the source announcement, projector health, pending projection work, latest snapshot, route operation, hostname resolution, and cache behavior. Review privacy filters when data exists internally but is absent publicly. Do not bypass projection by editing the public snapshot directly.

sections.heading: Locate the stale boundary
sections.text: 1. Confirm the incident or announcement is visible internally and linked to the page. 2. Compare the page's current projection cursor and latest generated snapshot. 3. Inspect status-projector readiness, oldest projector work, and last error. 4. Resolve the public slug/custom hostname and request it without an authenticated session. 5. Compare origin output with CDN/proxy output and its cache head

sections.heading: Understand stale-serving and maintenance behavior
sections.text: During a snapshot rebuild, the public route can deliberately serve the last known-good snapshot instead of returning an empty/error page. Treat that as a continuity safeguard, not proof that projection is healthy: compare the served snapshot revision/time with the current page revision and repair the rebuild failure. Do not purge the last-known-good snapshot before a replacement has been generated

pages.title: Troubleshoot upgrades
pages.description: Diagnose and safely recover from a failed database migration.
pages.intro: Use Upgrade migration fails. Stop further rollout, preserve the migration name and database error, confirm whether it committed partially, and follow the documented recovery path. Do not mark or rerun a migration blindly.

pages.title: Upgrade migration fails
pages.description: Preserve data and diagnose migration ordering, drift, locks, and compatibility.
pages.intro: Stop additional migration owners and preserve the first failure. Record the application revision, migration name, database revision, lock state, and exact error. Run the repository migration validation and health checks. Do not use destructive drift repair, force flags, or manual schema edits. Follow the tested rollback or restore decision established before the upgrade.

sections.heading: Safe decision path
sections.text: 1. Stop every additional migration owner while leaving the database available. 2. Capture the failed migration name, SQLSTATE, application image digest, and migration-table state. 3. Determine whether the migration made no change, committed fully, or partially changed data outside a transaction. 4. Compare against the pre-upgrade backup and the release rollback compatibility notes. 5. Choose resum

pages.title: Troubleshoot workers
pages.description: Diagnose an unhealthy worker or a queue that is not draining.
pages.intro: Use Worker is unhealthy. Identify the runtime role and lane, then check health, queue age/depth, claim leases, database connections, provider latency, concurrency, and recent logs. Scale only after identifying the actual bottleneck.

pages.title: Worker is unhealthy
pages.description: Diagnose stalled claims, queue age, concurrency, and database capacity.
pages.intro: Identify the process role and traffic class. Inspect readiness, oldest queued work, claim leases, attempts, last error, database connections, provider latency, and configured batch and concurrency. Check for a duplicate or missing owner. Scale only after proving capacity; reclaim expired work through supported recovery logic rather than modifying claim state manually.

sections.heading: Diagnose by lane
sections.text: 1. Identify all , general , critical , bulk , or projector and confirm that the deployment actually owns that lane. 2. Compare readiness, last success, oldest eligible job, active leases, and attempts. 3. Check PostgreSQL connection pressure before increasing concurrency or replicas. 4. Separate provider latency/admission pressure from database claim failures. 5. Look for duplicate owners, expired
